Description: The *Pāñcarātrarakṣā* by Vedāntadeśika, edited by M. Duraiswamy Aiyangar and T. Venugopālacārya.

The author of this work was Veṅkaṭanātha, popularly known as Vedānta Deśika. He was a Śrīvaiṣṇava and a great scholar who lived between 1269 and 1369 CE. He was the son of Anantasūri of Tuppil, located near...

Conjeevaram. Tradition regards him as an incarnation of the bell of Lord Tirupati. His first and primary teacher was his uncle. His first work dates to 1290. Thereafter, he composed more than one hundred works. The...
The *Pāñcarātrarakṣā* is a fundamental introductory treatise on the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra system, in which Vedānta Deśika cites from numerous Vaiṣṇava and other sources. His concern is to establish—

He establishes the authority of the Pāñcarātra and demonstrates its superiority over other traditions. In doing so, he references various Śaiva schools and texts; thus, this work is also of great importance for the historian.
Of those traditions.

*Śrīpañcarātrarakṣā*
Edited by Śrī Vedāntadeśika.
Paṇḍita M. Duraiswamy Āiyangār and Paṇḍita T. Venugopālacārya.
The Adyar Library and Research Centre, Madras, 1942.
*Śrīpāñcarātrarakṣā*,
composed by Śrīmad Vedāntadeśika.
May the illustrious Veṅkaṭanāthārya, the lion among poets and logicians,
the preeminent teacher of Vedānta, ever abide within my heart.
The first section, titled "Establishing the Final Doctrine," begins with the invocation.
We worship the Supreme Brahman, who is manifested in fourfold forms, perfected by the six divine attributes,
and the source of the entire Pañcarātra.
We take refuge in you, who abide in the principle of having no other deity,
and who are a virtuous person capable of seeing the further shore of the great ocean of the Pañcarātra.
May those whose feet have been placed upon the path of faultless reasoning— the very limit of vision for those like me— ascend, surpassing others who fall from that position.

The well-spoken verses are like evening lamps, held by those who see the essence of all that is heard, who nod their heads, who devour the double-tongued, and who wear as crest-jewels the serpents coiled in play.
Regarding the authority of the Pāñcarātra,

the universal authority of the Lord’s scripture was established in the Mahābhārata and other works by Vyāsa and others, who had directly realized the true state of the meaning of the entirety of the Vedas.
And in the Śārīraka [Bhāṣya],
immediately after the refutation of the systems of Kapila, Kaṇabhakṣa, the Bhikṣu, the Kṣapaṇaka, and Paśupati,

[the author] acted for the sake of dispelling the delusion of those of dull intellect who might otherwise be confused by the possibility of [the Vedānta] being studied alongside other systems (tantrāntara).

Having introduced the prima facie (pūrvapakṣa) position by means of the two sūtras, "Because of the impossibility of origination" and "And because an instrument [cannot originate] from an agent," the established conclusion (siddhānta) has been supported by the two sūtras, "Or, if there were the state of being consciousness and so forth, there would be no prohibition of that" and "And because of contradiction," by way of demonstrating the non-mention and the prohibition of the origination of the individual soul (jīva) and other such things.
By the venerable Yāmunamuni and the commentators,
this Mahopaniṣad has been declared to be consistent with the four Vedas and expounded through the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and the established conclusions of the Pañcarātra.
Having extracted the essence from the Vedantas as it is, the learned Lord Hari,
out of compassion for his devotees, condensed [the teachings] for their ease.

By means of the methodology established by this collection of proofs, such as those beginning with "iti," [the validity of] the scripture— which emerged from the mouth of the Blessed One, which consists of a compendium of the supreme human goal, its means, and the manner of its performance, situated at the pinnacle of hundreds of Vedas that are exceedingly vast, profound, and deep— is free from defects in its cause and so forth.

It was determined that non-authoritativeness (aprāmāṇya) should not be suspected in any instance whatsoever. Even in the section on ritual action (karmakāṇḍa), within the definition of valid means of knowledge (pramāṇalakṣaṇa), he formulated the aphorism that non-authoritativeness applies only to those Smṛtis that contradict the Vedas and are not accepted by Vyāsa and others. As for those later Mīmāṃsaka scholars of the final age who [rely] on other systems (tantrāntara)...
They consider the *Sāttvata* scripture to share the same status as [the Veda];
their boastful claims were refuted in the *Āgamaprāmāṇya*. And it has been said:
"If this [scripture] is equal to that [Veda], then it is the same in its system which has strayed from the path of the Śruti."
That which is designated as the Pañcarātra was composed by the final authority of Sāṃkhya and Yoga.
Having extracted the essence from the Vedāntas as it is, the wise Lord Hari,
out of compassion for his devotees, condensed [the teaching] for their ease.

By means of the method established by this collection of proofs beginning with these words, [the author proceeds] with respect to the scripture issued from the mouth of the Blessed Lord— which consists of a compendium of the supreme human goal, its means, and the manner of its performance, situated at the pinnacle of hundreds of Vedas that are exceedingly vast, dense, and profound— and which is free from defects in its cause and so forth.

It was determined that non-authoritativeness (*aprāmāṇya*) is not to be suspected in any instance whatsoever. Furthermore, in the section on ritual (*karmakāṇḍa*), within the definition of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇalakṣaṇa*), [Jaimini] sūtra-ed the non-authoritativeness of those *smṛtis* alone that are contradicted by the Veda and not accepted by Vyāsa and others. As for those later-era Mīmāṃsakas who [rely] on other systems (*tantrāntara*),...

They consider the Sāttvata scripture to be of equal status [to the Vedas]; their boastful claims were refuted in the *Āgamaprāmāṇya*. And it has been said: "If this [Sāttvata] were identical to those systems that have strayed from the path of the Śruti..."
In that case, those who drink soma would also be drinkers of liquor by virtue of being drinkers.
Thus it is said. Regarding the occasion of the worship of Śūdras and so forth, the venerable Kṛṣṇa-muni has stated this counter-argument:

"Just as in the case of a Śūdra who prepares the sacrificial oblation, or as in the case of one who performs many sacrifices, the ritual procedure is carried out; in the same way, the practice of this scripture is also maintained, and not otherwise."

Thus, the meaning is this: just as in such scriptural passages as "Let the preparer of the oblation run! or "From the house of one who performs many sacrifices, excluding a Śūdra," a resolution is reached by resorting to either eligibility for a specific ritual or a particular figurative usage, so too is it here.
And by the Bhaṭṭārakas, this was distinguished from other tantras as possessing universal authority:
"Therefore, Sāṃkhya with Yoga, along with the doctrine of Paśupati, and in some places Pañcarātra—
this is understood to be authoritative everywhere, derived precisely from the fifth Veda."
Regarding the "four Siddhāntas":

this very [system] is the great root of the vast tree of the Veda; thus, it is the nourishment for that portion of the root of the tree of the Nigamas—which consists of the trunk of the Ṛgveda and other branches, and which supports infinite branches as previously described.

The nature of the *haṇa* (the *ha*-syllable) remains established as fourfold, according to the division of its own root-mantra portions (*mūlanigamabhāga*)— namely, the portions such as the *ṛc* and so forth—
just like the *ṛc*, etc.: namely, the *Āgama-siddhānta*, the *Mantra-siddhānta*,
the *Tantra-siddhānta*, and the *Tantrāntara-siddhānta*.
The establishment of the non-confusion of the tenets: these four tenets are divided into sub-systems according to their various branches, just like the *Ṛgveda* and the others.
In this regard, just as there are different Vedas such as the *Ṛgveda* and different branches within each of them, so it is here.

Just as things are established according to their successive prior acquisitions and are subsequently taken possession of by sons and others, so too do the various philosophical systems (*siddhānta*) and their sub-divisions remain fixed according to the sequence of their initial adoption. And just as... [the word *ca* appears in the manuscript].

There is no fault in the mixing of other Vedic branches, other recensions, or other Sūtras beyond what is expressly stated; likewise here, there is no fault in the mixing of Siddhāntas, the mixing of Tantras, or the mixing of specific optional (vaikalpika) dharmas and so forth that fall within the scope of individual Tantras. And this systematic arrangement remains unmixed.
It is to be established through a sequential investigation supported by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
And this [is so] because of the practice of other purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), beginning with conception (*garbhādhāna*) and ending with cremation (*dāha*).
The Bhagavatas, while refuting the objection raised by the opponent regarding their lack of Brahminhood, have effectively established their status in the following sense: "These [people],
who study the Vājasaneya Śākhā through an unbroken lineage of preceptors..."

They perform the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna* according to the path taught in the *Gṛhyasūtras* of Kātyāyana and others; whereas those who, by abandoning the *trayīdharma*— beginning with the recitation of the *Sāvitrī* [the reading "nyāyapariśuddhau" appears in the *Dharmātyaga* manuscript]— perform only the forty sacraments prescribed in the *Ekāyana-śruti*.

Those who perform [the rites]— that is, those who carry out the matter prescribed in their own branch's *Gṛhya-sūtra* correctly— do not fall away from Brahminhood merely because they do not perform the rituals belonging to other branches,
nor do others [fall away].

Because there would follow the undesirable consequence of losing one's Brahminhood due to the non-performance of rites prescribed in other recensions (*śākhā*). In all cases, ritual practices are observed to be established according to distinctions such as caste (*jāti*), school (*caraṇa*), lineage (*gotra*), and qualification (*adhikāra*).
Even though a single rite is recognized across all recensions, nevertheless...
Dharmas connected to mutually distinct classes of qualified practitioners are never to be combined;
for these [classes] are distinct from those qualified for rites such as the *indrāgneya*, which are means for attaining the enjoyment of objects like heaven and sons as prescribed by the three Vedas.

Those Brāhmaṇas who, desiring liberation, are entitled to the performance of rituals— the sole means for attaining the Lord— consisting of approach (*abhigamana*), acquisition (*upādāna*), sacrifice (*ijyā*), and so forth, as prescribed by the *Trayyantakāyana* Śruti; these are the [qualified] twice-born.
The non-performance of the rites prescribed in each other's branches does not cause either group to lose their Brahminhood.

Furthermore, just as the authorless nature (*apauruṣeyatva*) of the Ekāyana branch has been explained in detail within the *Kāśmīrāgamaprāmāṇya*, it is not introduced here. However, regarding the Bhāgavatas who are the subject at hand...
The clear perception of the connection with the dharma of the three Vedas, beginning with the recitation of the Sāvitrī,
does not tolerate any doubt regarding such states as *vrātyatva* (loss of caste) caused by the abandonment of that [dharma].
Here, by the word "knowledge" (*vijñāna*), one refers to the specific knowledge established by [the author] himself in works such as the *Saṃvitsiddhi*.
This is what is intended to be expressed. For it has been said:
"Just as 'The King of Chola is the sole emperor on earth'—such speech is intent upon excluding any other king equal to him."
But it does not ward off [the suffering of] one's sons, servants, wives, and so forth;
likewise, there are hundreds of millions of cosmic eggs containing gods, asuras, and humans.
These [powers] belong to the Lord of all, who is untouched by afflictions, karma, its maturation, and the like;
he is a treasury of the sixfold qualities beginning with knowledge, and his majesty is inconceivable.
"A mere drop or spray from the ocean of the majesty and power of Viṣṇu."
And Bhojarāja, Baladevācārya, and others analyze this division of the Vedas:
"He who was planting that Veda-tree— which has many roots and branches, is served by hosts of twice-born men seeking various fruits,
and is divided into the categories of *pūrva* (revealed) and *anuśrava* (traditionally heard)..."
I shall praise Puruṣa.
By such statements as these, the absence of confusion in all cases has been demonstrated in summary form in the Śrīsāttvata:
"There is no subversion of the meaning of the scriptures or of the scriptures themselves through intentional intellect;
here, one should act only out of ignorance, without the traditional succession."

Thus, those ritual acts which have their foundations in clearly perceived means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and are embraced by the tradition of practice (*ācāraparaṃparā*), being recognized through an unbroken lineage, must not be abandoned even in the slightest degree, nor should they be neglected.
It is thus stated that those [doctrines] opposed to it are to be rejected.

Furthermore, in the *Śrīpauṣkara*, in the chapter on the definition of the qualified aspirant (*adhikārinirūpaṇādhyāya*), the distinction between the various systems (*siddhānta*) and their internal subdivisions is shown precisely with the intention of defining the specific domain of each respective qualified aspirant; there is no confusion among them.
As stated in the Pauṣkara: "That scripture in which the Fourfold Self is worshipped as something to be practiced,
by means of its own traditional designations passed down through lineage, is indeed the Brāhmaṇa [tradition]."
Know that, O Pauṣkara, it was previously designated as the Siddhānta;
it is indeed composed of various arrays and consists of twelve forms.
Likewise, that multitude of manifestations which is endowed with other forms,
and which is joined with other manifestations, was indeed maintained within the primordial lotus.

Know that, O Lotus-born One, he is accompanied by Lakṣmī and the others— those known as Śaṅkha, Cakra, Gada, and Garuḍa— as well as the lords of the directions together with their hosts, all intent upon their respective weapons.
And there is the scripture known as the Mantrasiddhānta, which bestows all fruits;
in it, nothing else is practiced apart from the four forms.
O Pauṣkara, the form of the Blessed One, consisting solely of mantra and enveloped by speech, is joined with the assembly of beloved goddesses such as Śrī and the others.
O Lotus-born One, that scripture known as Tantra should indeed be understood as being covered with various ornaments and weapons in embodied forms.

[The section on the non-application of the price: Where lions and other such animals are indeed distinguished by their primary or secondary application, they are joined according to a ratio of four, three, two, and so forth, as requested.
Whether they are surrounded by their respective retinues or abandoned by them,
know that whatever is propitiated according to its capacity is indeed another tantra.
In this way, always know the commonality of the various Āgamas:
the two names, or the pair [gha, ṅ, cha, ja], as the *Siddhānta* and the *Pañcarātra* in the *Pauṣkara*.
Each one exists from its very root with many divisions,
made manifest by the perfected ones (siddhas) according to the power of various dispositions.
The third [type] consists of both the concise and the detailed;
it is composed of the Vedas along with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas, together with the Vedāntas.
"Those who have attained perfection through ten million births, their final abiding is here.

By this statement, which declares that each and every Siddhānta is established from its very root in many divisions, [it follows] that there are four Siddhāntas and their intermediate tantric subdivisions.
It is indicated that one should always remain while avoiding the confusion of different Siddhāntas and Tantras;
furthermore, all four Siddhāntas grant liberation (the word *ca* does not appear in the manuscripts).

It was stated immediately prior that these four, known as the Siddhāntas, bestow liberation: "Therefore, from this scripture, the supreme, imperishable Brahman called Vāsudeva is attained through action preceded by knowledge."
"O Brahmins, his designations for the Siddhāntas are indeed three and a half.

Here, because of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the plural ending in "three and a half" (*sārthakāḥ*), the word *siddhāntasaṃjñā* must also be plural; thus, through its connection with the specific categories such as the Āgamas and so forth, it is fourfold.

He intends the state of *saṃjñā*. It has already been stated here previously that, just like the word *pañcarātra*, the word *siddhānta* is common to all four [systems]. Furthermore, in the *Pādme*, regarding the fourfold *siddhāntas* beginning with *sadāgama*, it is said:

"They bestow the state of the True" (*satpadaprade*), meaning they grant the state of the Blessed One (*bhagavatpada*)—that is, the attainment of the Blessed One—which is denoted by the term *satpada* for all four.

The state of being a means for attainment has been stated. In the Hayagrīvasaṃhitā as well, it is stated that for some [this system] grants liberation exclusively, while for others it grants liberation along with other fruits:
"For the Siddhānta, which is the essence of all Āgamas, grants the fruit of liberation alone."
For this established doctrine, known as mantra, bestows both spiritual accomplishment and liberation upon human beings.
The designation "Tantra" refers to the Siddhānta,
which bestows the fruits of the four aims of life;
indeed, this Tantra and the Siddhānta grant the fruits of one's desired objects.

Thus it is said. Here, by the term "desired object" (*vāñchitārtha*), liberation (*apavarga*) is included without distinction, just like the three aims of life (*trivarga*). Therefore, since all four of these lead to Vāsudeva, who is the Supreme Brahman, they are [to be practiced] by those seeking liberation in the sections teaching the means to liberation (as found in the *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *jha* manuscripts of the *Upadeśa*).
There is no option [between them], because the fruit is non-distinct; according to this principle,

there is an optional adoption [of one or the other] as in the case of the Sadvidyā, Akṣaravidyā, Daharavidyā, Madhubhūmavidyā, Vaiśvānaravidyā, Śāṇḍilyavidyā, Nāciketa, Upakosala, Pratardana, Saṃvargavidyā, Antarādityavidyā, Ānandamayavidyā, and so forth.

Just as there is no mutual inclusion of the specific qualities restricted to their respective meditations (*vidyās*)—which are distinct from the attributes that define the very nature of Brahman—in those various meditations, so it is here as well; thus, the application of the individually restricted ritual procedures is established without mutual confusion. However, in cases such as the Madhu-vidyā, etc., [the situation is different].

Just as the attainment of Brahman is preceded by the attainment of the stages beginning with *vaśa*, the attainment of Vāsudeva is here described as occurring through a succession; in that case as well,
those who desire the attainment of the ultimate goal as mediated by each of those preceding stages possess the qualification [for this path].
[The qualification for desire is established as "gha"]. With that intention, it is stated in the Bhāṣya:

"For that which is called Vāsudeva is the Supreme Brahman, whose body consists of the six perfections in their entirety, and who is divided into the subtle, the vyuha, and the vibhava forms; He is to be known by devotees according to their respective qualifications through knowledge preceded by devotion."

It is said that by properly worshipping through ritual action (*karma*), one attains [the result]; by worshipping the *vibhava* [manifestations], one attains the *vyūha*; and by worshipping the *vyūha*, one attains the supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva, which is subtle.
Therefore, all four [forms] have liberation (*apavarga*) as their ultimate purpose. The statement regarding them as means for other fruits has a different intent.

It has been stated by [the Lord] himself [as quoted in the Pauṣkara]: "And for the sake of providing conviction regarding liberation, the supernatural powers (siddhis) have been fully proclaimed. Thus, since it is established that all four [Vedas] bestow liberation, their nature as a supplement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) to the essence of the Upaniṣads (*trayyantāsāra*) also becomes entirely consistent.
Regarding the confusion of Siddhāntas and the confusion of Tantras, there is an investigation of the *Pādma* statement:
in the *Caryāpāda* of the *Pādme*, the mutual distinction between these four is explained, as well as the fault in the confusion of Siddhāntas and the confusion of Tantras.
That scripture exists in four divisions, yet like the *Ṛg* and other Vedas, it is manifold;
each individual *tantra* is further divided extensively by way of various branches.
The first is the Siddhānta of Mantra, the second is called Āma,
the third is the Siddhānta of Tantra, and the fourth is Tantrāntara.

Thus [it is said]. Here, the mention of the Āgama and Mantra Siddhāntas in reverse order from the sequence stated in the Pauṣkara is because the intent is to praise the superiority of the Mantra and Siddhānta systems, which bestow both supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mokṣa*). For even here, the excellence of the Āgama Siddhānta is characterized by its granting of liberation alone [this phrase appears in the Ka, Kha, Ga, and Jha manuscripts].
It has already been shown that even regarding actions, renunciation is not taught in that scripture (*āgama*). Here, however,

the renunciation of optional (*kāmya*) actions is intended by their very nature, whereas for those duties prescribed according to one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*), [the renunciation is not].
According to the method established in the eighteenth chapter of the Bhagavadgītā, there is the renunciation of action characterized by *sattva*,
while the undertaking of all obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites is performed according to the rules prescribed in one's own Vedic branch (*sva-śākhā-gṛhya*). Therefore,
it should not be maintained that in the Siddhānta of the Āgama, there is a total renunciation of the essential nature of all actions.
Because of the abundance of specific types of action; for it was with reference to those established in that very state that it was said:
"The virtuous perform thirteenfold action, free from desire and the like, endowed with the qualities of self-restraint."

Thus [it is said]. Herein, according to the sequence indicated, four Siddhāntas will be discussed: "The definition of the Siddhāntas as stated in the Padma [Purāṇa] is that only one form is to be worshipped primarily, while the others..."
The goddesses, Śrī and the others, should also be worshipped as part of the retinue.
She is surrounded by weapons such as the conch and the discus, and by ornaments such as the Śrīvatsa, all personified; or she may be alone, seated upon a lotus.
Wherein this is explained, that is declared to be the foremost Siddhānta of Mantra;
therein the four emanations (vyūhas), beginning with Vāsudeva, are also [described] by the practitioners.
Those who have come through lineage are equal in rank to those who have come through lineage; they are indeed worthy of worship in the presence of the source.
Furthermore, in that scripture (Āgama), renunciation is also described as being achieved through ritual action.
O Lotus-seated One, that which is declared as the established doctrine of the Tantras and Āgamas is that wherein the preeminence of all nine forms is described.
The twelve limbs are the forms (mūrtis), and likewise others are their manifestations;
there are also groups of manifestations and groups within the forms themselves.
Accompanied by other manifestations, together with the gods of the quarters and the gods themselves, bearing their weapons,
and clearly joined by the goddesses in embodied form, such as Lakṣmī and the others.
That which is called the *Tantrasiddhānta* is again the fourth and supreme [tantra],
O Four-faced One, who possesses a multitude of faces such as the gentle lion and others.
Whether she has two, three, or more distinct faces, her single form alone is worshipped;
accompanied by her retinue or without them, she grants all desires.
O Four-faced One, that which is another tantra would be the fourth,
by means of which the ritual actions such as summoning (*karṣaṇa*) and so forth are performed according to the path of the *siddhānta*.
In the beginning, everything was established by him alone, and not by the path of any other system;
for even in another tantra, that which is spoken of there but not mentioned here must certainly be accepted.
Therefore, a confusion of tenets and likewise a confusion of tantras leads to calamity,
consisting in the destruction of the king, the kingdom, and the royal residence.
When a confusion of established doctrines has arisen through negligence, for its pacification,
one should first perform a ritual sprinkling and then an ablution with a thousand jars.
If a confusion of tantras occurs, one should perform the ritual bath;
at the conclusion, one should hold a great festival preceded by the hoisting of the banner.

Thus. Here, the definition of *tantra* and *tantrāntara* stated in the *Pādma-tantra*—which is not found in the *Gha* manuscript of the *Tantra-kośa*—is to be interpreted in a manner that does not contradict what is stated in the *Pauṣkara*. If the identity of meaning between these two texts is possible, then there is no contradiction; otherwise, the definition of *tantra* and *tantrāntara* [applies to] other *tantras*.

The definition of the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* (accepted tenet), *tantra* (system), and *tantrāntara* (other system) should be understood as being of two kinds. For example, in the *Nyāyavistara*, among the *sarvatantra-siddhānta* (tenets common to all systems), *pratitantra-siddhānta* (tenets specific to a particular system), and *abhyupagama-ādhāra-siddhānta* (tenets accepted for the sake of argument), the *abhyupagama-siddhānta* is twofold.
They describe the definition intended by Akṣapāda as follows:
"That which is established in another system (paratantra) and yet relied upon in one's own system (svatantra)—
that indeed is an *abhyupagama* (acknowledged tenet) in Nyāya, such as the non-deviation of the mind."
Or, when its existence has been established elsewhere, there may be an examination of its specific qualities;
just as, once the mind's existence is established elsewhere, there is an examination of its being a sense-organ.

Thus, the definition of the various tantras as stated in the *Pārameśvara* is indeed identical to that stated in the *Pauṣkara*. For instance, in the chapter on expiation (*prāyaścitta*), when the established doctrines (*siddhāntas*) are being distinguished for the purpose of avoiding defects such as the mixing of lineages (*saṃkara*), [it is said]: [The text continues: "In this regard, the *Siddhānta* is that which is taught by Śiva himself; it is not mixed with other systems, nor does it contradict them. It is free from the defects of *saṃkara*, *saṅkīrṇa*, *apabhraṃśa*, and *viparyaya*. The *Siddhānta* is characterized by the five categories (*pañcārtha*), the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), the fourfold means (*catuṣpāda*), and the three-fold initiation (*trividhā dīkṣā*). It is the teaching of the Supreme Lord, consisting of the *Mantra-tantra*, the *Vidyā-tantra*, and the *Mudrā-tantra*. It is the essence of all scriptures, the source of all success, and the means to liberation. Thus, the characteristics of the tantras described in the *Pārameśvara* are exactly the same as those described in the *Pauṣkara*. To illustrate: in the section concerning expiation, while the established doctrines are being analyzed to eliminate faults such as the confusion of traditions, [the text states]: [The text continues: "Among these, the *Siddhānta* is the doctrine revealed by Śiva, which is unmixed with other systems and does not contradict them. It is devoid of the defects of *saṃkara*, *saṅkīrṇa*, *apabhraṃśa*, and *viparyaya*. The *Siddhānta* possesses the five categories, the six limbs, the four divisions, and the three types of initiation. It is the teaching of the Supreme Lord, comprising the *Mantra-tantra*, the *Vidyā-tantra*, and the *Mudrā-tantra*. It is the core of all scriptures, the root of all accomplishments, and the path to liberation. Following the elaboration of the *āgama*, *mantra*, and *siddhānta*, it is said:

"Whether by means of each individual form (*mūrti*)— distinguished as the Supreme (*para*), the Manifested (*vyūha*), and so forth— or by the Embellished (*sāṅga*), the Solitary (*kevala*), or the Beloved Manifestation (*kāntā-vyūha*) with its ornaments."
Likewise, with weapons and bodies endowed with form, there is the whirlpool known as Tantra;
[these include] Nṛsiṃha, Kapila, Kroḍa, Haṃsa, Vātīśvara, and others.
The Devalas, endowed with limbs, appear through the various modes of primary and other functions,
equipped with excellent weapons such as the discus and others, and adorned with ornaments such as crowns and the like.
That other tantra is proclaimed as that wherein she is worshipped according to the prescribed rite by hosts of beloved ones, Yakṣīs and others, and by retinues such as the sky-goers (gandharvas).
Thus, the avoidance of confusion among these established doctrines (*siddhāntas*) is set forth in the sixth chapter of the *Pādma[tantra]*. In that very chapter,

it is stated in certain instances regarding a particular doctrine or its internal subdivisions that one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*) lacks the authority (*anadhikāra*) to perform rites prescribed in other doctrines or other tantras.
One who has been initiated into one Siddhānta has no authority in another.
O Four-faced One, a supreme twice-born man who has been initiated into one Tantra or Siddhānta should not perform rituals elsewhere, such as plowing and so forth.
And [he is] four-faced.
Furthermore, the office of teacher (ācāryaka), the role of officiating priest (ārtvijya), worship and so forth belonging to the Enemy of Madhu (Viṣṇu),
as well as the various Tantras and the various Siddhāntas, are not applicable [to him].

Having said this, the status of being the presiding authority for the lower tantras was again declared for those who hold the authority of the higher tantras [the sequence ka, kha, ga, ca, jha]; [thus the authority was demonstrated ka,
kha, ga, ṅ, ca, ja, jha].
Those who hold authority in the higher tantras have the right to practice in the lower tantras according to their respective paths,
as well as in other tantras, and likewise on the path of the systems of Tantra and Mantra (or Mantra and Siddhānta).
For those who have been initiated, the bestower of yoga indeed proceeds step by step, higher and higher;
for others, there may be eligibility provided it is preceded by the respective purificatory rites.
It should always be worshipped by three others who are established in the Siddhāntas of Karaṇa and Āgama,
as well as by another who is established in the Siddhānta of Mantra.
Furthermore, it should be worshipped constantly by another follower of a Tantric system;
however, within one's own home, it should be worshipped according to one's own specific Tantra alone.

Thus it is said. Here too, it is stated that even for one established in a superior system (*siddhānta*), worship must be performed according to the specific manner of each respective system when situated in locations belonging to inferior systems;
for there is no possibility of one established in a superior system falling into an inferior system within their own domain. Precisely for this reason—
It is said that there is no interval [between these]: "If there are secondary initiates (gauṇādhikārin),
they should enter the independent temple by means of an independent [initiation], provided that primary initiates (mukhyādhikārin) exist."

Thus [it is said]. "By one's own independent [scripture]" means by one's own previously established scripture. Furthermore, regarding the entry into other [paths] from the prescription of the Ekāyana, an exceeding degree of transgression (*pratyavāya*) has been stated in that very [text]: [the *ca* is not present in the *gha*, *cha*, *ja* manuscripts].
There is a transgression in entering elsewhere that which is prescribed for the Ekāyana; the image established by its own tenets on another path [is to be placed] in the ālaya.
Whether through ignorance or delusion, [one must act] according to the rule of the Ekāyana.
By honoring [him], one attains freedom from all calamities both in this world and in the next.

Thus, when it has been established by the aforementioned method that those adhering to each individual system lack authority regarding the ritual practices of other systems, [it follows that] for those established in one system,
[there is no authority] regarding the Bhagavad-āgamas established in other systems.

Fearing the undesirable consequence that even common religious duties— such as circumambulation, prostration, offering garlands, lighting lamps, sweeping, sprinkling water, smearing the ground, decorating, protecting, nurturing, and the offering of oblations (havir) and hymns of praise (stotra)— might also be prohibited; [fearing such a prohibition, in versions ka, kha, ga, and ca].
One should perform the circumambulation, prostration, and other rites only at the conclusion of the worship;
one must not perform worship elsewhere, as it brings fear to the king and the kingdom.
Thus,
having explained at length the transgression resulting from the confusion of established doctrines in the twenty-ninth chapter of that very [work], beginning with "cha ja":

It has been established that only those qualified persons whose principles and dharmas are unconfused possess the fitness for mutual association and so forth; whereas for others, however, even the avoidance [of them] is prescribed, just as in the case of outsiders.
Confusion among the four philosophical systems (siddhāntas) brings about calamity;
among these four systems, one has been practiced by men of former times.
Having abandoned [his own duty], a man who would resort to another becomes a sinner;
therefore, from birth until the end of his life, he should remain disciplined.
Otherwise, one personally destroys one's entire family by means of the mantra,
maṇḍala, sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and other rituals, mudrās, and offerings.
He who, out of delusion, leads yoga away from the path prescribed in his own established doctrine—
even he [leads] all the dharmas born of his own lineage to the Supreme Self (the compound *paramātmānaṃ* is analyzed as *parama-ātmānaṃ*; see marginal note).
That lowest of men would lead men to a most terrible hell;
his actions would be fruitless and, on the contrary, would cause harm.
If he fails to perform this rite, the deity becomes enraged; his wrath brings fear to the king and the kingdom.
Both the one who performs it and the one who causes it to be performed shall perish, along with their entire lineage.
There shall be no lack of proximity to the abode of Hari, nor any loss of spiritual riches;
one must not practice the doctrines or rituals of other schools that lead to confusion regarding Rādhā.
Those who, according to their respective traditions, perform the rites of propitiation for Acyuta within all four principal systems of Mantra and Siddhānta without mutual confusion,
are indeed worthy of being connected with one another.
The supreme among men.

Thus [it is said]. "They practice without confusion" is the connection [of the words]. Regarding the detailed exposition of the faults in the confusion of established tenets (*siddhānta*), it is stated in that very same [work], the *Jīrṇoddhāra*:
Whatever form [is prescribed] by whatever tantra for whichever type of qualified practitioner in the first kalpanā, that very same [form] shall be used in the second kalpanā.
The image is itself the Tantra, and it is that very same image which is the consecrator.
If an exchange is conceived between the Tantras, the officiants, and the images,
there will be destruction for men, for the king, and for the kingdom as well.
Thus it is said. Later, in that very same chapter on expiation and so forth, [it states]:
"In the event of birth or death, or when the image is touched by dogs, jackals, donkeys, and the like, or when a confusion of tantras has occurred."
In these and other such cases, the procedure for sprinkling (saṃprokṣaṇa) should be performed.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Narādīya*:

"O Gautama, when there is a reversal of the attendants and the enjoyments and so forth, one should perform the ritual bathing as before and then carry out the propitiatory fire-offering (*śāntihoma*)."

Thus [it is said]. Here, by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the inclusion of *siddhāntavyatyaya*, *tantravyatyaya*, and so forth is intended, because they are required and there is no distinction [between them]. For this very reason, it is stated right here: "O Nārada, in the case of ploughing and other such acts, one should perform them by means of a single *tantra*."
Whatever has been commenced according to a particular tantra, one should carry it out according to that very same tantra.
And those not mentioned—having observed them in other tantras, one should apply them here;
and having observed them elsewhere, one should employ them. Furthermore, O best of sages, [if one acts] otherwise than this...
It causes the destruction of the kingdom.
Thus it is stated. And in the *Pārameśvara*, in the chapter on Installation (*Pratiṣṭhādhyāya*):
"Especially in a self-manifested (*svayaṃvyakta*) [liṅga], in a divine (*divya*), in one established by a *siddha* (*saiddha*), or even in one established by a *ṛṣi* (*ārṣaka*)."
However, one should not effect a transposition of the positions of the ritual icons,
nor of the deities of the doors, the limbs, and the enclosure, nor of the worship, the temple, or the fire-oblation.
Beginning with these words:
"One should not establish another characteristic, nor likewise another means of valid cognition;
nor indeed another substance, nor should one establish another action."
One should not perform another mantra [or another tantra, as indicated by the variants ka, kha, ga, ṅ]; one should do everything exactly as before.
O Mahāmati, if one were to perform such things in reverse order, [the result would be ruin].
There would be the destruction of the king, of the kingdom, and of his entire lineage.
Thus it is said in that very same [text]:
"O Mahāmati, there is the inversion of enjoyments and the inversion of mantras."
One should not practice the transposition of the *dyānas*, the *mudrās*, the deities, or others such as these.
Thus it is said. Likewise, later in the chapter on expiation (prāyaścitta), it is stated: "The temple and the image should be constructed according to whichever scripture [is followed];
having consecrated them, one should worship Hari with that very same [scripture] during the daily rites and so forth."
He who worships by another path, as well as he who is a detractor of the image—
both of them are defiled souls, [and they bring harm] to the king, the kingdom, and indeed to the preceptor.
Both a family affliction and an illness will swiftly cause upheaval and suffering,
and they will especially bring about the loss of wealth and the ruin of one's dwelling.
One devoted to the Pañcarātra should not perform a rite that causes a confusion of tantras;
if a confusion of tantras has occurred, the consecration must be performed again.
Thus it is said. Having explained therein at length the various differences of established tenets (*siddhāntabheda*), it is stated immediately thereafter:
"Of the scriptures, mantras, rituals, and so forth, as well as of the manifestations (*mūrti*) and their arising..."
The acceptance of a noble guide is just as it was before.
In that very same manner, one must not act otherwise for as long as it lasts;
if these are performed in reverse order here, they will cause harm to the king, the kingdom, and others.
Therefore, one should diligently perform the consecration according to the previously mentioned method;
thereafter, those of perfected self should never practice a confusion of the Siddhāntas.
Whatever is most beloved in the world, provided it does not conflict with what was established before—that should be accepted; otherwise, a wise person should mutually abandon what is contradictory.
Thus, in the *Kālottara*, in the chapter on the determination of the fourfold worship,
it is said: "O best of the twice-born, [O most excellent of the twice-born], whether by means of Vedic, Tantric, or Śrauta rites."
In a temple that is self-manifested, one should worship the deity with mixed materials.
In a place honored by sages and others, one should not perform any special rite without following the traditional succession, even for the sake of the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.
Thus [it is said]. These same two verses are also recited later in this very chapter on expiation (*prāyaścitta*). In that very place:
"O twice-born one, whatever image was commenced by which scripture in the past, or likewise a temple (*prāsāda*), one should worship it according to that very scripture."
One should worship that [with the syllables] gha, cha, and ja.
He who performs a sacrifice by another path, without that very scripture,
desires the destruction of the king, the kingdom, and the performer alike.
A wise person should never cause a confusion of scriptures;
through the fault of confusing scriptures, a great evil will certainly arise.

Thus [it is said]. Although it might be argued that this statement is intended to avoid the confusion between the Vaikhānasa and Pañcarātra traditions—since such a refutation is indeed set forth in this very scripture—nevertheless, because of the general expression "by which scripture," it pertains to all subjects. For it is stated therein:
In all great festivals, according to the requirements of place and time [or according to the best of teachers],
one should not perform any special rite for the sake of the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.
Thus it is concluded [and stated].

In this way, since the internal mixing of even a single scripture among the *Pañcarātra* texts is utterly condemned, the mixing of the *Vaikhānasa* and *Pañcarātra* is prohibited by the principle of "how much more so" (*kaimutya*). [This is established by the logic of the "how much more so" (*kaimutikanyāya*).]

And in both cases, [the validity] of each other is clearly negated. However, the *Pañcarātra* is, in certain instances, even relied upon by the *Vaikhānasa*s. For instance, according to the *Vaikhānasa*, there is a fault in the mixing (*saṃkara*) of the *Pañcarātra*. Yet, the *Pañcarātra* is that which is relied upon by all.
He is to be worshipped and served by Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who possess the proper marks and are ever-diligent in their own duties,
according to the Sātvata injunction proclaimed by Saṃkarṣaṇa.

By such statements as these, it is declared in the *Mahābhārata* and other texts that the worship of the Lord and so forth must be performed by Brāhmaṇas and others alike, according to the path taught in the venerable *Pañcarātra*; indeed, no restriction regarding specific *sūtras* or the like has been made anywhere.
On the contrary, the culmination of all the Sūtras is set forth in that very treatise as being subordinate to it:
"One should perform the purificatory rites, beginning with the impregnation ceremony, as prescribed in one's own Sūtra."
Or even those rites proclaimed in the Pañcarātra which have been performed by their own kinsmen.

Thus it is said. Nor should it be argued: "Since the installation and worship of the Lord and so forth have already been taught by Bodhāyana, Vikhanas, Śaunaka, and others, what need is there for another? For those who adhere strictly to the *sūtras* that lack such specific instructions, the adoption of a common scripture (*sādhāraṇa-śāstra*) is justified due to their dependence on other sources. Indeed, a complete instruction is not found anywhere.

When it is possible for one who is capable [of performing the rite] to adopt the complete [text], it is not proper for that same capable person to adopt an incomplete version when a complete instruction is available. For this very reason, even Adhvaryus adopt the *hautra* (the duties of the Hotṛ) as prescribed in the *hotṛ-śākhā*. Therefore, regarding those sūtras...

The worship of the Blessed One and so forth was established; even for those devoted to that [Vedic path], the performance of propitiation and other rites according to the procedure taught in the scriptures of the Blessed One is most highly praised. And thus it is practiced by the learned.
Now, as for those who follow the Vaikhānasa-sūtras [Kāśyapīya, Gha, Ja]:

[Opponent: What is the use of the Pañcarātra, given that the installation and worship of the Blessed One and so forth are fully taught in the scriptures of Kāśyapa, Marīci, Bhārgava, Ātreya, and others, as well as in their related treatises and compendiums, both in brief and in detail? [Proponent: Not so; for those teachings are intended only for those who adhere to those specific sūtras. If that is so, then...

If it is argued that if the system of the *Pañcarātra* were not to be accepted by those devoted to that [Veda], its common applicability to all who abide by the Sūtras would be lost—this is not so, because the answer has already been given (the answer has been provided). For even the *Kāśyapīya* and other such systems [are included]. (The variants *ka*, *kha*, *gha*, *ca*, *jha* appear in the manuscripts.)

There are no treatises that teach a systematic framework regarding various subjects while remaining entirely independent of other treatises; likewise, even that which is taught in the *Pañcarātra* sometimes relies upon others. As it is stated in the *Kriyādhikāra* proclaimed by Bṛgu:
Some say that one should worship by means of the ritual manuals and mantras perfected through the instructions of the guru, or even with offerings such as the seat and other services.

Thus [it is said]. Here, by the term *kalpamantra*, only those mantras taught in the scriptures of the Blessed One (*bhagavat*) are intended. For this very reason, it is specified that they are "perfected through the instruction of the Guru" for the sake of the *vaikhānasa* householders who have studied the Vedas. Furthermore, the ritual manuals (*tantra-kalpa*) for those respective mantras are not distinct from the *Pañcarātra* tantras; for [the latter] is indeed expanded fourfold.

In that scripture, which is divided into various distinct *saṃhitās*, all the ritual manuals (*kalpas*) for the mantras of the Lord (*bhagavat*), as well as the ritual manuals for their ancillary mantras, are appropriately contained. For this very reason, learned authorities refer to those respective ritual manuals of the Lord’s mantras as the "Ārṣa Pañcarātra."

[They describe them as *ka kha ga a ja jha*]; and those who are devoted to that [tradition] are designated by the term *kalpabhāgavatas*. Likewise, even among the Bhārgavas and others, those who are endowed with the rites beginning with conception (*niṣeka*) according to the *Vaikhānasa-sūtra* [are so designated].
Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas, pure, and experts in the ritual application of mantras.

In such passages as these, the mention of "knowledge of the ritual manuals" (*mantrakalpa*) in various places is intended for the purpose of grasping what is required therein. Likewise, in the *Bhārgava* [text], within the section on ritual action (*kriyādhikāra*), after introducing the installation of Sarasvatī and other rites, it is stated: "Having installed [the deity] according to this rule, one should worship with the ritual manual's mantra. Yet, neither the nature of the ritual manual's mantra nor its ancillary components (*aṅga*) and so forth are taught here.

Therefore, the procedure taught in the *Kalpa* itself must be followed here. Thus, when the installation (*pratiṣṭhā*) and worship (*arcana*) of the Lord in the form of Sudarśana have been completed, another procedure is proposed with a view toward the distinction of results:
"This has been declared as Vedic, bestowing the fruits of enjoyment (*bhukti*) and liberation (*mukti*)."
If one desires enjoyment, one should remember Devala while reciting the six-syllable mantra.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, there is no detailed exposition of the procedure for the six-syllable mantra here;
therefore, the procedure taught in the *Vāsiṣṭha*, *Gārgya*, *Vihagendra*, *Ahirbudhnya*, and other *Saṃhitās* is the only recourse.
Likewise, even regarding the instruction on forms ranging from two arms up to sixteen arms, although not explicitly stated [here], [it should be understood from those sources].

[It is] not found in the *Kośa*; it must be taken from elsewhere. For this very reason, one desists after stating "the black forms are infinite" and so forth, because since the forms such as Kṛṣṇa-Narasiṃha and others are innumerable, they cannot be fully described.
Among those, some are mentioned in other scriptures [indicated by the variants *ka*, *kha*, *ga*].

These alone are to be collected. Therefore, having extracted the essence from the Vedāntas according to their substance, the Blessed Lord Hari—acting as one who desires the welfare of all people through the aforementioned method of extracting the quintessence of all Vedāntas—himself composed the glorious Pāñcarātra Śāstra. This is that which must be relied upon by all those who are established in the Sūtras.
Success! As for the position that the passages in the Śrīvaikhānasa containing mutual condemnations of the Vaikhānasa and Pāñcarātra traditions are interpolations:
The *Āgneya-pañcarātra*, however, is tantric and associated with initiation;
because it is non-Vedic, one should abandon that tantra and worship the God of gods according to the *Vaikhānasa* tradition alone, which is gentle and Vedic.

Regarding what has been stated in the *Śrīpāñcarātra-tantrasārasamuccaya*: "The Vaikhānasa [tradition] brings about a lack of prosperity (*aśrīkara*), is not gentle (*asaumya*), and is non-sāttvika" (with variants *atāttvika* in manuscripts *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *jha*), and so forth; beginning from that point, [it says] "having abandoned its ritual procedure, one should worship according to the Pañcarātra," and other such passages.

Those statements from the *Pādmapārameśvara* and other such texts were surely interpolated by those desiring to eat sugarcane— or perhaps by clever young students eager to seize one another's positions.
These were established by the lowest of worshippers.

For the establishment of the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*) as dharma was performed by those who remained impartial toward both scriptures, through their non-contradictory application. [The reading *niveśanam* is found in manuscripts Ka and Kha.]
And what [is that]?
Otherwise,

[this would apply] to those [shrines] such as Śrīraṅga, Śrīmad-Veṅkaṭādri, Śrī-Hastiśaila, Vṛṣabhagiri, and others, which are more widely renowned and possess an abundance of accepted authority regarding their established sanctity.
In the successive traditions of the *Vāsādini-baddha-Śrīvaiṣṇava-dharmaśāstra-kāṇḍa* and others [i.e.,
the *Dharmaśāstra-karmakāṇḍa* and others],...
The Blessed One said:
"Listen, O Pāṇḍava, to all that regarding the sequence of one's own worship:
having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus with a pericarp upon a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila)."
Either by means of the eight-syllable formula, or with twelve-syllable [mantras],
or with Vedic mantras, or again with my own hymn (sūkta).
Then, O Yudhiṣṭhira, having honored me who was established there, the wise man [worships] the True Person, the Infallible One.
People who know the Vaikhānasa tradition call me Aniruddha;
but others, O King, the followers of the Pāñcarātra, understand me in this way.
O king of kings, they declare Vāsudeva, Saṃkarṣaṇa,
Pradyumna, and Aniruddha to be the fourfold form.
O Indra among kings, know that these and other forms, distinguished by various names, are not different from me; thus should the wise man worship me.

Thus, by these and other such statements, the *Śrī Pañcarātra*— which is recited as being equal to the various divisions of Vaiṣṇava scripture, which is not in contradiction with the Vedas, whose authority was established by the venerable Yāmunamuni, Vāsudeva Svāmī, and others, and which is accepted without distinction within the Vaiṣṇava tradition— [is shown to be authoritative].

Furthermore, this would result in the loss of authority for both the venerable *Pañcarātra* and *Vaikhānasa* scriptures; for these statements of mutual censure are intended solely to praise their own respective scriptures,
whereas these [other] statements are disparaging of one another.
I consider these to be the words of an authoritative person (*āptabhāṣita*) because they are observed in numerous, unconfused manuscript readings; nevertheless,

in passages such as "Those who offer the *agnihotra* before sunrise speak falsehood every morning," there is a censure of the *anudita-homa* (offering before sunrise) for the purpose of praising the *udita-homa* (offering after sunrise).
Like [passages of] censure and so forth, those [passages] marked as *ka*, *ca*,

and others should be understood as being intent on demonstrating the excellence (*prāśastya*) of the treatise under discussion— specifically, as being intent on excellence alone (*prāśastyamātraparatvena*), as indicated by *gha*, *cha*, *ja*, and *gha*. For censure does not function to censure that which is censured, but rather to praise something other than that which is censured.
The experts in logic maintain that this was intended as a praise.
Likewise, in passages such as "Śāṇḍilya, not finding firm grounding in the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches,
studied the Pañcarātra scripture," there is the risk of [being interpreted as] a censure of the Veda.
Anticipating the objection that this contradicts the Vedas, the commentators resolved the matter by showing that the passage is intended for the purpose of praising their own school;

they demonstrated this by citing the text beginning with "O Venerable Sir, I study the Ṛgveda," up to the point at the commencement of the knowledge of the Infinite (Bhūmavidyā): "Indeed, O Venerable Sir, I am merely a knower of the mantras, not a knower of the Self."
The statement regarding the attainment of self-knowledge through the study of all other Vedas has as its sole purpose the praise of the Bhūma-vidyā. Moreover:
"On one side are the four Vedas together, and on the other side is the Mahābhārata alone."
In ancient times, it was weighed against [the merit of] the assembled celestial rishis.
Because it possesses greater magnitude and greater weight than others,
and because of its vastness and gravity, it is called the *Mahābhārata*.
Statements such as these, which declare the Mahābhārata to be superior even to the Vedas,

are intended for the purpose of praising the Mahābhārata— which possesses the excellence of being a supplement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) that expands upon the meaning of the Vedas— and do not, however, express even a scent of depreciation toward the Vedas. Furthermore, in the *Bahvṛca-āmnāya*, the *Ṛgveda*...

"The *kumbyā* is a *yajus* of that same measure; *nigada* is useless speech; and *sāman* is that which is measured differently, as well as whatever else is sung (*geṣṇa*)"—this censure of the *yajus* and other Vedas is intended solely for the purpose of praising the *Ṛgveda*. Likewise here, although there are statements disparaging one another between the Śrī Vaikhānasa and Pañcarātra traditions, even if they are authoritative, they must be resolved as having an identical meaning according to what is intended by each.

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of universal confusion, and because there is the risk of over-extension if one were to accept the words of those whose speech is not to be trusted exactly as they are heard.
Indeed, it is stated in this very way in the *Kāraṇatantra* within the Śaiva Āgama:
It is said: "The statements in the *Kāraṇatantra* of the Śaiva scriptures also have the purpose of praising one's own system:
'A Śaiva should be authorized in both his own [tradition] and in another.'"
Those excellent twice-born householders who are devotees of Śiva perform everything [according to their tradition].
In the Yāmala, the Mātṛ-namamantra, the Kāpāla, the Pañcarātra,
as well as in the Buddhist, the Ārhata, the Lāguḍa, and even the Vaidika [traditions].
Moreover, in other paths as well,
the Śaivas perform everything— including the installation of that [Śiva’s] liṅga— in accordance with their respective scriptures.
Because the Śaiva [system] is primary here, and also due to its preeminent majesty, it possesses authority everywhere; others have no such authority within the Śiva-darśana.

Thus [it is said]. Because of the mention of the Vedic system alongside the Jaina, Yāmala, Buddhist, and other non-Vedic (bāhya) systems— which deal with objects unfit for sight, touch, and so forth— [the term "bāhya" applies] both to those who are unworthy of the Vedas and to the outsiders.

twice-born men who follow forbidden occupations, or Śūdras.

[Ka Kha Ga Ca Ja Jha: By the six [deities]. [Ka Ca: By Śiva and others.

If the consecration and other rites are performed out of delusion, there arises a fault consisting of the destruction of all merit.
Furthermore, for his pacification, one should perform the consecration of Hari according to the path taught in the Pañcarātra,
including a ritual bath with a thousand jars and a great festival preceded by the hoisting of the banner.
And because we observe the performance of specific expiations prescribed in the *Padma Purāṇa* and other texts,
this statement of praise from the Śaiva tradition—
“O mighty-armed Rudra, you indeed cause delusive scriptures to be composed”— [is merely figurative].
Having demonstrated that it requires little effort, show the fruit quickly.

If it is argued that, in such a manner, their lack of authority must be assumed— either because they were composed by one who is not the Lord (anīśvara), or because they are merely exaggerated rhetoric, or because they consist solely of praise for the Śaivas who are the intended audience of their own respective systems (*tantra*)— then, alas,
the same would apply to either one of these two distinct paths of the Śrī-Vaiṣṇavas when compared with the other, as perceived by those who have entered the other system (*tantra*).

Furthermore, because those who are distinguished by other tantras (*itaratantra-viśiṣṭaiḥ*) do not enter [the fold], and because there is no risk of mutual confusion (*paraspara-saṃkara-prasaṅga*), and because we observe the performance of penances prescribed in their respective tantras,
those statements regarding mutual disparagement and the entry into each other’s boundaries are interpolated and thus lack authority.

Alternatively, because they are intended as independent praises by way of hyperbole (ativāda), and since they must be interpreted as such, it is not appropriate for there to be a mutual inclusion [of one in the other], which would involve abandoning the traditional limits handed down through succession—
[as noted in manuscript Gha: "mutual inclusion is an error, not a benefit"].

Behold with an impartial vision; for those who fall into a partisan faction indeed fall away from the supreme boundary of Dharma. Therefore, [this applies] to the Vaikhānasa and Pañcarātra, to the four internal divisions of the Pañcarātra, and to the various specific sub-tantras within them.
It is established that their existence always occurs without mutual confusion.
Furthermore, there is the position that those statements concerning the entry into a superior doctrine by abandoning an inferior doctrine are interpolated.
In this regard, however, this must be briefly reflected upon: namely,

It has been stated that even by abandoning a previously established inferior doctrine (*pakṛṣṭasiddhānta*), entering into a superior doctrine (*utkṛṣṭasiddhānta*) is not a fault, but rather a merit; whereas a fault exists in abandoning a superior system (*tantra*) to enter an inferior system, as well as in the confusion of systems (*samānatantrasaṃkara*). It was said that a fault occurs when one abandons a superior system to enter an inferior system, or in the confusion of systems—this point also has its answer effectively provided. To illustrate:

In the twenty-second chapter of the *Śrīsāttvata*, following the description of the characteristics of the *samayiputraka-sādhaka* (the practitioner who is a son by initiation), there is a confusion regarding the characteristics of the *ācārya* (teacher) across various scriptures.
"and he who knows [it] by the power of the statement"—having said this, what follows is stated for the purpose of purifying the confusion of scriptures:
"In that regard, there are indeed three kinds of statements: the divine and those spoken by sages."
O lotus-eyed one, understand that distinction regarding human effort.
That which is purposeful, free from doubt, concise, clear, brief in syllables, and stable— that is indeed the word of the Supreme Lord, established by his command, and bestowing liberation.
It is indeed the praiser of all accomplishments, the promoter of them as well;
it is the delighter of all, hidden, and the syllable that brings about hidden certainty.
Know that the word of the Sage bestows the fruits of the fourfold aims of life;
it is not meaningless, incoherent, trivial, or mere bombast of words.
A statement that fails to carry out its intended purpose is known as human (pauruṣa);
it is to be rejected, for it is a mine of misfortunes and leads to hell.
Even if it is a human statement, if it restates a well-known fact, possesses a coherent meaning, and is distinguished [from falsehood], it should be accepted just like the words of the Sages.
Thus, here it is stated that there is a contradiction between the two statements spoken by the divine sage, because the first statement is unconvincing.

"Incoherent" refers to the contradiction between what precedes and what follows. Both of these [faults] are present in the statement regarding the adoption of a superior *saṃhitā* at the expense of a previously observed *saṃhitā*.

Certain individuals of audacious intellect, perceiving a contradiction with their own preceding and subsequent passages— which generally intend to prohibit all forms of syncretism— due to conflicts with the Śrīsāttvata, Pauṣkara, Nāradīya, Pādma, and other scriptures, [propound their views].

Having explained the divisions by means of the various names mentioned previously which are not far removed [from one another],
it has been stated that the system known as the Purāṇasiddhānta— which is the Tantrātantrasiddhānta that bestows liberation— is especially "glory-bestowing" (śrīkara).
This is the established doctrine of the Purāṇas, which is especially conducive to prosperity;
known by the name Śrīkara, it bestows the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
Thus [it is said]. All that precedes and follows this should be seen in detail in the *Sanmārgadīpikā*.

Although the phrase "bestowing the fruits of enjoyment and liberation" (*bhogamokṣaphalapradam*) is associated with a specific *saṃhitā* named *Śrīkara*, because that *saṃhitā* falls within the established doctrines of the Purāṇas, it is [treated] specifically [as such]. [The reading "viśeṣataḥ" appears in the Ka, Kha, and Ga manuscripts; "viśeṣaḥ" is the reading in the printed edition.]

Furthermore, by the use of the word "and" (*ca*) and by the inclusion of what is not explicitly stated, it is established that the entire system as perfected in other tantras possesses, in particular, the quality of bestowing glory (*śrīkaratva*) and the quality of granting liberation (*mokṣapradatva*). For kings and those residing in kingdoms generally desire glory; therefore, [this system is applicable] in common places for the sake of their prosperity.

The propriety of the established tenets of other *tantras* is even greater. Let those who are unattached indeed observe the boundaries of the established tenets of their own scriptures and so forth within their own homes and the like; however, the statement regarding the introduction of the tenets of others into the places where one's own *tantra* stands or in other *tantra* locations is a source of excellence, being the basis for an exceeding proximity to liberation (*apavarga*).

This should be considered as the final word. It is with reference to this very point that it is stated in the *Kālottara*: "For [the revelation] is self-manifested, divine, and bestows the most excellent fruit.
This is the position that the statements regarding the acceptance of the most excellent Siddhānta have as their scope the self-manifested (*svayam-vyakta*) sites.
Others, however, say that this refers specifically to objects situated in fixed locations; it is a statement regarding the adoption of a superior *saṃhitā* by abandoning an inferior *saṃhitā*.
For instance, as it is said in the *Kālottara*:
The scripture known as Pañcarātra is divided into many different branches;
it is proclaimed to be fourfold: first the Āgama-siddhānta, followed by that called Mantra, then Tantra, and finally Tantrāntara.

Having thus generally set forth the fourfold division, these treatises are all-encompassing, beginning with the statements: "The Nārāyaṇīya, the Maudgalya, and the Agni; the Nārāyaṇīya, the Audgalya, and that known as the Agnikāśyapa," and so forth.

By this [concluding] statement, having cited several *saṃhitās* from among the four [categories] beginning with the *Āgama-siddhānta*— as indicated by the letters *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *ca*— and using them as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those *saṃhitās* not explicitly mentioned,
[it is stated that] "this scripture called the *Pañcarātra* is the most excellent of all," thus [referring to] all four types.
Having established the *Pañcarātra-śāstra* as the most excellent of all,

there is also a designation of the Siddhāntas of the Āgamas and other systems by names such as "Self-manifested" (*svayaṃvyakta*) and so forth; and it is divided fourfold according to the distinctions of "Self-manifested" and the rest.
For the Siddhānta known as Āgama was indeed proclaimed by the Supreme Being as self-manifested.
That which is known as Mantrasiddhānta is proclaimed as divine;
indeed, that scripture known as Tantra is declared to be Saiddhāntika;
and that which is spoken of as another Tantra is declared to be Ārṣa.

Thus, having indicated other names for the very same scriptures, established doctrines, and so forth mentioned previously— which will be useful for what is to be said hereafter— by way of their forms as self-manifested divine siddhas:
While the *kautuka* was being worshipped with a self-manifested divine [image], [from "svayaṃvyaktena" onwards, two and a half verses are not found in the Kha and Ga manuscripts].
However, one should not perform the worship of the deity using two different tantras.
If it is worshipped out of delusion, the destruction of the site will certainly occur;
the death of the king, the kingdom, and the performer is likewise certain to happen.

Therefore, O best of the twice-born, worship should not be performed according to the path of one tantra or another; for that which is unspoken in the *Svayaṃvyakta*, the *Divya*, the *Siddha*, and the *Ārṣa* scriptures, O best of the twice-born, is found in the *Svayaṃvyakta* scripture.
Whatever is stated in this or another tantra should be adopted accordingly;
even when the teachers perform worship according to what is taught in various tantras.
Abandoning that [conventional] procedure, worship should be performed upon the images according to the path spoken by the Self-Manifested One (Svayambhū) and by means of the divine rite.
Since it is self-manifested, divine, and bestows the highest fruit,
one should worship it well according to the path taught in the supreme scriptures.

Thus, even though worship is performed according to both this tantra and other tantras, it is more appropriate to abandon those specific prescriptions and perform worship according to the supreme, self-manifested, and divine scripture, which bestows the most excellent fruit.

Regarding the statements concerning the acceptance of the supreme Siddhānta, it must be investigated whether they pertain to the Self-manifested (Svayambhū) site or to all sites. If [the term "all"] refers to all sites, then...
Otherwise, there would follow the undesirable consequence of having to condense numerous Saṃhitā texts, such as the *Tamasā-Sāttvata* and others, which have been accepted [as authoritative].
Furthermore, in this very work, later on— in the chapter defining the characteristics of the locations such as *svayamvyakta*—
after describing the characteristics of those respective locations, [the author proceeds] in the subsequent chapter determining the fourfold worship (*caturvidhapūjā*).
Having introduced the fourfold worship as being respectively Vedic, Tantric, Śrauta, and Mixed— each of which is itself fourfold—
the [text] provides the names based on the root scripture, the divine mantra, the engaged scripture, and their combination.
Immediately following the instruction,
it is said: "O best of the twice-born, one should worship the deity either in a self-manifested temple, using Vedic, Tantric, or Śrauta rites, or with a mixture of these."
In a place honored by sages and others, one should not perform any special rite without following the traditional succession, even for the sake of the prosperity of the king and the kingdom.

Thus, having established here that at the site of the Self-Manifested (Svayaṃvyakta) one may adopt specific offerings of cooked rice (caru) according to one's preference as an alternative, it is stated that in other sites worshipped by sages and others, one should not practice even a slight variation from the traditional sequence without following the lineage transmission; therefore, where...

In the manuscripts designated as Ka, Kha, and Ga, the following is not present: "In that which is self-manifested, the engagement in actions through conceptualization is possible" (the word *saṃbhavati* appears in Ka and Ga).
In that very context, there is the statement regarding the abandonment of a treatise with inferior results and the adoption of a treatise with superior results.

It must be understood according to the indicative mark (*liṅga*). From the indicative mark "the purifier [is placed] on the right ear," it is clearly determined that—just as there is a rule regarding location for the statement "during the day and at the twilights, with the sacred thread (*brahmasūtra*) worn over the ear"—it refers specifically to those locations which are self-manifested. This is also the case later in this very chapter on expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

The two verses beginning with "By those following the Vedic or Tantric paths" were recited again. It was also stated: "O God, one should worship the deity in a human abode by means of the Tantric path. And further:
"O twice-born one, whichever image was commenced according to which scripture in the past..."
Or else, he should worship that [deity] in a palace using that very same scripture.
He who performs a sacrifice by another path, disregarding that very scripture,
desires the destruction of the king, the kingdom, and the performer himself.
A wise person should never cause a confusion of the scriptures;
through the fault of confusing the scriptures, a great evil will certainly arise.

Thus it has been stated. For this reason as well, it is established that the statement regarding the abandonment of inferior scriptures and the adoption of superior ones must be placed in its own self-manifested locus, which was demonstrated by [the author] himself as being capable of various alternative interpretations of the meaning of diverse scriptures.
An investigation into the meaning of the words of those who are intent on discipline, concerning the specific status of the teacher and the student; and furthermore,
regarding this specific status, [of the teacher and the student].
A rule is established for the scripture and its qualified practitioners:
"In the self-manifested [temple] as well as in the divine one, according to the path taught in the divine scriptures,
together with the root Āgamas, it should always be performed by the mouths of the Bhāgavatas."
Worship should be performed by those who are self-restrained and devoted to the five-fold daily rites;
it should be carried out in a Vaiṣṇava temple by those who are exclusively followers of the Pāñcarātra.
When those who follow the lineage have entered by the path described in the words of the sages,
they should grasp the various networks of meanings not explicitly stated in the Siddhāntas, Āgamas,
and other scriptures by means of mutual correlation; one should not, however, extract [a meaning] from one scripture that contradicts another.

Thus, this too [refers to] the appropriateness of those with superior qualifications in a superior station adopting superior scriptures and so forth, and [the appropriateness] of those with inferior qualifications in an inferior station [adopting inferior ones].

Furthermore, it establishes the fitness for weapons, scriptures, and so forth; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that divine scriptures could never descend even into a Vaiṣṇava temple. For it is stated in the Pārameśvara-nirūpaṇa that even in a human dwelling, when established by primary qualified authorities, worship and other rites must be performed according to the divine scripture.

And because [this] is being demonstrated; here too, the avoidance of the confusion of established conclusions (*siddhāntasaṃkara*) has been established by the passage beginning with "the multitude of meanings not previously stated," and so forth.
Furthermore, in the *Pārameśvara*, in the chapter on the Determination of Self-Manifestation (*svayaṃvyaktanirṇayādhyāya*):

The performance of worship according to the divine scripture is possible everywhere, whether it be self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta), established by perfected beings (siddha), or installed by the wise (vibudha).
And by the Gandharvas and Vidyādharas, who have faces like those of sages, as well as mouths resembling the letters *kha*, *cha*, *ja*, and *jha*.
One skilled in the scriptures should worship the mantra-form established by the lowest of Rākṣasas according to the procedure taught in the divine scriptures.
Thus, this also demonstrates that the divine scripture exists in all places with an equal presence [or true existence], but it does not mean that one enters the divine by abandoning other scriptures.
Furthermore, that which was stated immediately prior—
wherever a deity has been installed by men according to the word of a sage,
O twice-born one, there too one should worship with those who possess knowledge and perceive reality.
By those who are devoted solely to Vāsudeva and who have abandoned other deities.

Thus, even though this point is established by the words of the mixed sages (which do not appear in the *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *ṅa* manuscripts), he says that worship alone is praised when performed with those who are devoted exclusively to Vāsudeva as taught in the *Vyāmiśrāgama*, and not, however, by abandoning the words of Manu— or rather, not by not abandoning them.

One performs worship according to the scripture that is superior to one's own authority but not in accordance with that authority; for it is appropriate even for those following a superior scripture to perform worship there according to the previously practiced scripture,
so that those established in the superior scripture may also [engage] in the duties of the inferior scripture for the sake of favoring the world.
Because it has already been demonstrated that the application [of the rules] for the sake of favoring others and so forth is established by other *saṃhitās* and the like;
and as for that which is stated immediately hereafter—

One should worship the Lord of the God of Gods according to the path prescribed in the divine scriptures, by those lords of men who are free from mixed doctrines, endowed with intense devotion, and proficient in the Niṣadva, Ākāra, and other [tantric] systems.
Thus, this too should be understood as concerning the subject of the places established by the divine scripture (*divyaśāstra*).
The statement regarding the adoption of the divine path preceded by the abandonment of the words of the sages has the purpose of praising the divine path.
However, this remains: as it was said—
"Wherever worship takes place according to the path taught in the words of the Sage,
if one wishes to perform that worship even there by means of the divine path..."
Having set aside the words of the Sage, if one should worship by way of the divine path,
there shall be the majesty of the deity's presence for a duration lasting until the end of the kalpa.
O Great-minded One, where worship and other rites are performed constantly by way of the divine path, one should never abandon that which is divine there.

If a Brahmin of deluded mind, out of ignorance, should either fail to perform worship and other rites according to the path taught in the words of the Sage, or should perform them [in a contrary manner], [he incurs sin].

O best of Brahmins, rituals along with their mantras and tantras, as well as spiritual accomplishments, will turn away from him; even in this very life they will quickly fail, and at the end of his body, his lineage shall perish.
Thus there is an additional reading in some manuscripts:
"The king goes to a terrible hell and the kingdom perishes;
therefore, with every effort, one should not abandon the divine path."

[Note: The portion from "asyāpi" up to "na tyajet" is not found in the Gha and Ṅga manuscripts. It is very clear that this passage also, by the previously stated reasoning, is intent upon praising the divine path (*divyamārga*).
This is evident from the presence of indicators such as the word "api" (also) therein, and by the concluding statement: "one should not abandon the divine path. In that very context...
And because the intended meaning rests there:
statements concerning the adoption of the divine path (divyamārga) have as their object the self-manifested (svayaṃvyakta) sites honored by the words of the sages;
