or else, according to the principle stated in the Kālottara, they refer to that which is self-manifested and suitable for the fourfold worship performed optionally.
Having restated that "worship exists there where it occurs according to the path taught in the words of the Sage," it is said that even in that case,

if there is a desire to worship by way of the divine path, worship by the divine path is not contradictory, provided one sets aside the words of the Sage; for nowhere here is there any [contradiction] regarding the place established by the words of the Sage.

The entry onto the divine path is now introduced; however, it is indeed honored by the words of the Sage. And that honor accorded by the words of the Sage occurs even in the case of a self-manifested [place], provided that it previously existed there—once its status as a self-manifested field has been determined through some means of valid cognition—even if one were to set aside the words of the Sage.
It is thus stated that one who is qualified for the divine scripture (*divya-śāstra*) should worship according to the procedure prescribed in the divine scripture.

By this, the classification of the scripture under names such as "divine" (*divya*) and so forth—and by extension, the detailed exposition taught in the chapter on determining the divine abodes (*divyādyāyatana-nirṇaya*)—is also refuted. For instance:
Furthermore, regarding the worship and other rites for the divine and other sense-bases that you have mentioned,
you should explain the scripture according to its divisions into the divine and so forth.

Thus questioned by Sanaka, Śāṇḍilya [the text reads "thus questioned by Sanaka" (ka kha ga)] spoke of the scripture which was proclaimed by Vāsudeva himself, the Blessed Lord; that is, the scripture directly composed by the Blessed Lord and set forth by Brahmā, Rudra, Indra, and others.

Know that the scripture which was spoken by the sages and composed by the gods headed by Brahmā and Rudra, as well as by the seers whose wealth is austerity, after they had declared it to be divine, is the one revealed by them.

Thus, having introduced the threefold nature of what was spoken by the sages (*munibhāṣita*)— as in the statement, "Know that this scripture composed by Brahmā and others is spoken by the sages, and it is to be understood as being of three kinds according to the distinction of *sāttvika* and so forth"— [the phrase "composed by Brahmā and others" is not seen in the Ka, Kha, Ga, and Jha manuscripts].

A scripture whose form consists solely of the binding together of meanings heard directly from the Blessed One is *sāttvika*. A scripture composed by Brahmā and his disciples— having compiled a portion heard from the Blessed One along with the remainder established through the power of their own yoga— is *rājasa*.

Having stated the threefold nature of that which was spoken by the sages— namely, that a treatise composed of meanings arising from mere conceptualizations of one's own yoga (ka kha ga jha) is *tāmasa*— [the text continues]: "That which is composed by humans, whether divine or spoken by the sages, shall be *pauruṣa*."
Having established that human speech— composed by mere mortals who are not yogis and whose authority is distinct from and lacks the possibility of being authoritative— is invalid,
he then explains that those [scriptures] designated as divine, sāttvika, rājasa, and tāmasa are indeed authoritative.
Having also divided the scriptures according to the specific rules of the *saṃhitās*, there are the divine scriptures such as the *Sāttvata*, *Pauṣkara*, and *Jayākhyā*, as well as the *Īśvara*,
*Bhāradvāja*, *Saumantava*, *Pārameśvara*, *Vaihāyasa*, *Citraśikhaṇḍi*, and *Jayottara* *saṃhitās*.
The *Ādi* and others are *sāttvika*; the *Sanatkumāra*, *Padmodbhava*, *Śātātapa*, *Tejodraviṇa*, *Māyāvaibhava*, and others are *rājasa*;
and the *Pañcapraśna*, *Śukrapraśna*, *Tattvasāgara*, and others are *tāmasa*.
Immediately after the instruction on the division of the *saṃhitās*, it is stated:
the classification of the *saṃhitās* according to distinctions such as divine (*divya*) and *sāttvika*;
and the statement regarding the adoption of superior scriptures in place of inferior ones.
Regarding the preeminence of sites that are self-manifested:
even where worship and other rites are performed by way of the *tāmasa* path,
there too, worship and so forth performed by the *rājasa* path alone shall grant accomplishment.
Even where worship and other rites are performed constantly by one of a rajasic nature,
there too, worship and other rites performed by one of a sattvic nature always bestow auspicious results.
However, where worship and other rites are performed daily according to the *sāttvika* method,
one should not perform the worship and so forth by way of the *rājasa* path.
Where worship and other rites have not been performed according to the *rājasa* path,
one should not perform worship and other rites there according to the *tāmasa* path.
Among the various types of rajasic actions, there shall be no mutual confusion.

Thus, among the three treatises spoken by the sages, which are designated according to their superior, middling, and inferior qualities— [the word "qualities" (guṇa) does not appear in the Ka, Kha, Jha, and Ga manuscripts]— it is said:

In a place where a scripture designated as having inferior qualities is being practiced, even by abandoning that [scripture], worship and so forth performed according to a scripture designated as having superior qualities bestows success. In a place where a scripture designated as having superior qualities is being practiced, [one should not act] with a scripture contrary to it.

Worship and the like should not be performed. [Indeed, for those designated by equal qualities; indeed, for those designated by qualities, and for those designated by equal qualities, it has been stated that no mutual confusion should be made. Here too, although it is indicated in general terms by the word "where," according to the previously stated principle—
By virtue of his sovereign majesty, it should be understood that [the Lord] has as his object all the specific fields manifested by themselves (*svayaṃvyakta*), but not everything everywhere;
or else, even when there is recognition of a scripture previously revealed and drawn forth, the divine [nature] is not to be abandoned.

Alternatively, in cases where the continuity of tradition has been interrupted due to long periods of time, the ravages of time, or other such factors, and people are thus bewildered as to what ought to be done— regarding those for whom the engagement with the scriptures was previously not extensive, yet who, during their state of ignorance, lacked any improper intention (abhisandhi)— this [teaching] is intended for all qualified persons.

It is stated that for the principal [deities], there is the fitness for the acquisition of the most excellent scriptures; furthermore, by some means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), there is the non-abandonment of the divine [nature] even when there is prior knowledge of the scriptures. And this [non-abandonment] is also indicated therein by the mark of the "exaggerated statement" (*ativāda*) through the word "also" (*api*). The status of the word "also" as a mark of an exaggerated statement is as follows:

This is well known from such applications as: "Even a Caṇḍāla who abides by his duty, the gods know him to be a Brāhmaṇa. For this very reason, an effort is made here once again to avoid confusion: "Having correctly understood the distinctions such as the divine and so forth, one should perform everything [accordingly]."
But he who performs worship and other rites without knowing [the distinctions] due to such confusion, [is at fault].
For he always causes confusion for the entire world, especially for his own lineage; therefore, O twice-born one, even in times of distress, [one must avoid him].
One who desires the welfare of others and is skilled in the scriptures should not cause confusion among the treatises.
Thus, the meaning is exactly as stated. Or rather, the acceptance of the preeminent scripture pertains to a specific qualified person; however, there is something more.
Wherever worship is performed according to the path taught in the words of the sages,
if one desires to perform that worship by means of the divine path,
one may abandon the words of the sages and worship by the divine path.
They maintain that such statements as these are restricted to specific qualified practitioners (*adhikāriviśeṣa*), because of the introductory context:

"But by those who are endowed with intense devotion, even though they are mixed [with other practices]. This refers to those who are detached from worldly, celestial, and mundane fruits, and who have undertaken the study of the scripture that is most proximate to liberation (*apavarga*).
And because it is logical: for those who are attached to the worldly fruits mentioned in their respective Tantras, there shall be acceptance [of those fruits] as before.
Thus, even the three scriptures beginning with the Sāttvika are indeed authoritative; and the Nāgara, Drāviḍa, and Vesara [or Drāvalavaiśasa] are likewise authoritative in their respective order.
Sattva, rajas, and tamas;
the Brahmin, the king, and the Vaiśya; Hari, Brahmā, and Hara—the primordial deity.
Thus, just as there is a mention of qualities such as *sattva* with the intention of expressing the superiority or mediocrity of the creation of celestial palaces (*vimāna*) and so forth,
here too, with that same intention, there is a mention of those qualities; this applies specifically to the subjects of authoritative treatises (*pramāṇabhūta-śāstra*).

For the distinction between the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* types has also been established in the *Bhagavad Gītā* through such statements as, "The *sāttvika* worship the gods, while the *rājasa* worship the *yakṣas* and *rakṣasas*," and so forth. However, in the case of human speech that lacks authority (*apramāṇa*), there is merely...

Because of the separate mention that "that which is performed by men is *pauruṣa*," in every *pauruṣa* statement, one should accept whatever is not contradictory; however, one should not perform the installation and so forth solely on the basis of such an injunction.
Thus, in this statement designated as "pauruṣa," the presence of contradictory portions [indicated by the variants ka, kha, ga, ca,
jha] has been shown here as the presence of both contradictory and non-contradictory portions; therefore, the designation of *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* is applied here.
It should be understood that this is intended according to the varying degrees of excellence in the attainment of specific fruits resulting from the predominance of *sattva*, *rajas*, or *tamas*.
The entire *Pañcarātra* is authoritative, for the authority of the Lord’s scripture has already been established in its entirety. Nor is there [any contradiction] here...
In those portions [of scripture] composed by persons such as Brahmā who are distinct from the Blessed Lord, the presence of defects in the author is possible; however,
in this scripture whose speaker is the Blessed Lord himself— since Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra—
even within the eternal Veda, he [the Lord] has [revealed it] to those sages according to their respective specific merits.
Because the authorship of the *saṃhitā* is presented as a qualification, just like the authorship of the *sūtra*, the *kāṇḍa*, and the *mantra*;
and just as there is a division of Vaiśampāyana’s *saṃhitā* within the Mahābhārata spoken by Vyāsa, so it is here as well—therefore, there is no difficulty whatsoever. Thus:

The entire Pañcarātra is authoritative. Its internal divisions into *saṃhitās* are established in four ways, just like the *Ṛgveda* and the others. Precisely as in those cases, it must be followed at all times by performing the practices according to one's specific qualification (*adhikāra*), while avoiding any confusion between different doctrines (*siddhānta*) and so forth. Such adherence—
For those who follow accordingly—[the sequence being *ga gha*, *a cha ja*;

and likewise in the following application, *ka jha*]—this is the means for attaining the supreme human goal known as the True Brahman or Vāsudeva, whether directly or through a lineage, according to one's qualification; thus it is the indication of attainment.
Success! For the sake of establishing the five-fold time (pañcakāla), this systematic exposition of the Śrī Pañcarātra Siddhānta has been composed by the scholar Veṅkaṭeśa.

With his four arms— expert in the initiation that destroys what is harmful, distinguished by various military arrays (*vyūha*), and skilled in the hundreds of their own scriptural traditions (*nigama*) as well as the doctrines of others— he manifested his vast majesty.
"May the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha protect us— those of us whose impurities have been stilled by practicing the complete dharma of the first age.
Thus [ends the work] of the illustrious Veṅkaṭanātha, the lion among poets and logicians, who is independent in all philosophical systems.

In the works of the Vedāntācārya, within the *Śrīpāñcarātrarakṣā*, the section titled "Establishment of the Siddhānta" (or "Establishment," according to the variants *gha*, *ṅ*, *ja*; or "Establishment of the System," according to *cha*).
The first chapter,
titled "Establishment of Daily Practice";
the second chapter.
Now, that which was first proposed—
the constant service to the Master as one's own eternal purpose— is established here without flaw.
This practice, which consists of both the universal and the particular, is heart-pleasing;
it is like the fragrant garland of the All-pervading Lord, composed of threads and clusters of flowers.
In this context, the service of the Blessed One through visiting him and so forth is common to all; first, for each individual day and night,
it is divided into five periods of time.

For all those who are steadfast in the dharma of the Blessed One, the service of the Blessed One— consisting of approaching, receiving, sacrificing, self-study, and yoga— is common to all, being accompanied by the fixed duties (niyatadharma) determined by one’s own caste, stage of life, birth, and qualities.

And although there is a distinction in the injunctions across the various recensions of the *Saṃhitās*, it is taught that in the various *Sūtras* this [dharma] exists in a form slightly different [from others], like the forty sacraments (*saṃskāras*) and so forth which share a common name of injunction;
therein, this is the duty (this is one’s own duty) for those who know the secret tradition (*rahasyāmnāya*).

The delusion of those who have not understood the *sāttvata* dharma is accidental; however, there is a settled rule (*vyavasthā*) that they follow the five-fold daily duty (*pāñcakālika-dharma*) according to the method prescribed in their own branch (*sva-śākhā*), while others do so according to the procedure taught in their respective *saṃhitās*. For even within these two groups, the distinction is taught solely on the basis of the specific qualification (*adhikāri-viśeṣa*) of the practitioner. As it has been said:

In the *Pādma*, Brahmā said: "I now wish to hear about that ritual procedure for propitiating [the deity], by means of which the rites beginning with plowing and ending with consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) are successfully accomplished."
O you who are affectionate toward your devotees, please tell me in its entirety: what is the procedure for propitiation, and what kind of person is qualified for it?
The Blessed Lord spoke regarding the primary eligibility of those who follow the single path (ekāyana), as opposed to others who attain it through initiation:
"Listen; I shall explain what you have asked in its entirety."
The first is the Ekāyana Veda, which establishes the true Brahman.
By that very [initiation], the Brahmins become consecrated and qualified for the primary ritual procedure;
for others, such as the Brāhmaṇas and the other castes, it is by means of initiation in due order.
The entitlement belongs even to those who follow the natural order (anuloma), and not to anyone else;
they are the secondary-qualified (anukalpa-adhikārin) in the ritual procedure for the worship of the Blessed One.
Among those born in the inverse order (pratiloma), the Sūta is praised as the foremost; he is also the foremost among the three born in the natural order (anuloma), beginning with the Kṣatriya.

And especially for a Sūta, the initiation is for one's own sake; [the teacher] should teach the initiation for the sake of others. Brahmins should perform the sacrifice for the sake of others according to both the primary and secondary rules.
The qualities of those who lack qualification are devoid of the purificatory rite of initiation (dīkṣā),
just as Brāhmaṇas and others [lack such status] without the initiatory sacrifice (dīkṣaṇīyeṣṭi).
Likewise, those who are born according to the prescribed rite of initiation become qualified for the ritual worship of the Blessed One as previously described.
And so forth. In this manner, it should also be understood in other *saṃhitās*.
In the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, there are five times (*pañca kālāḥ*) and the fivefold rites (*pāñcakālika-karmāṇi*);
these are here [to be followed] according to the path taught in their respective *siddhāntas* for the various followers of the *Pañcarātra*.

The fivefold practice beginning with *abhigamana* is common [to all]. Indeed, this division into five periods is taught even in the *Mantrasiddhānta* and other systems, as it is famously known as the "Three Jewels" (*ratnatraya*) because it has issued directly from the mouth of the Blessed One. As it has been said: [ka kha ga ca jha].
In the Jayākhyasaṃhitā among the Jayākhya, Sāttvata, and Pauṣkara [Tantras],
Nārada says: "O Lord, only one time is heard of in the world, and no other."
Five times have been mentioned by you; what is this? I have a doubt regarding this.
The Blessed One said: "O Nārada, indeed, for a single day of time,
from dawn until the end of night, there is a fivefold division."
Many times are not prescribed, as they must be performed according to the distinct nature of each ritual action.
Nārada,
tell me the characteristics of actions performed at a single time,
by knowing which I may immediately become one who has accomplished his purpose.
The Blessed One said: "O Brahmin, beginning from the *muhūrta* of Brahmā during the forenoon portion of the day,
one should perform worship with meditation, hymns of praise, and ritual actions, joined with body, speech, and mind."
One should approach the source of the world; that is known as "approaching" (abhigamana). Thereafter, having risen, one should perform the acquisition of flowers, fruits, and so forth.
The cause for the completion of the sacrifice to the Blessed One is the supreme *prahara*;
it is indeed known as the grasping of the gift (*dadupādāna*), resting upon the stages of action and time.
Then, O Brahmin, one should worship the Supreme Lord with an eight-limbed sacrifice; that period of more than one watch (prahara) is traditionally known as the time for sacrifice.
O best of sages, know that the portion of time consisting of hearing, reflection, exposition, and the recitation of texts is designated as *svādhyāya*.

When the end of the day has arrived, having performed worship, one should practice yoga; and at the end of the night, one should practice yoga as well, separated by periods of rest. This fifth division of time is known as Yoga, which bestows the grace of Brahman.
I have previously heard in its entirety from Nārada about that supreme sacrifice to the Blessed One.
Furthermore, I wish to know its constituent parts according to their specific divisions.
The Blessed Lord spoke of the eight limbs of sacrifice,
beginning with the internal sacrifice of the mind and ending with the self-offering.
That first limb of the sacrifice is the great *abhigamana* (approach) by name; and that *abhigamana* would be [as follows].
O Sage Nārada, know that whatever worship is performed with offerings such as water for the feet and flowers, and all external services, is designated as *bhoga* (enjoyment).
Worship is indeed performed with curd mixed with honey and clarified butter, or even with an animal sacrifice;
that is the third limb of the sacrifice, while the fourth is worship with food.
O Sage, that which is the giving of what has been offered according to the previously stated procedure is indeed called *saṃpradāna*; it is remembered as the fifth limb of sacrifice (*yāga*).
The sixth is the satiation of the fire, while the seventh is the sacrifice to the ancestors (pitṛyāga);
the eighth is known by the name Prāṇāgnihavana.
That is the eighth, the subsequent sacrifice;
I shall bestow that supreme state which belongs to those established therein, without delay.
Thus [it is said]. By the word "soon" (*acirāt*), the inherent excellence of this rite over other rites is expressed.
And Vyāsa and others record:
"No Vedic rite exists that is more meritorious than the propitiation of Viṣṇu."
Among all dharmas indeed, the Vaiṣṇava rule is the most excellent.

[Thus ends the section, according to Ka, Ca, and Jha. Excellence exists even in substances and other such things by virtue of their form alone, regardless of whether their effort is equal or unequal. As it is stated in the *Āśvamedhika* section of the *Śrī-Vaiṣṇava-dharma-śāstra*:
Of all flowers, the utpala is a thousand times more meritorious;
from that, O King, the lotus is likewise superior, and from the lotus, the hundred-petaled one.
Therefore, the thousand-petaled lotus is superior to that;
yet, by virtue of its qualities, the tulasī is even more excellent than the thousand-petaled lotus.
Then there is the *bakapuṣpa*, but the golden flower is superior to that;
O Pāṇḍava, there is nothing dearer to me than that golden blossom.
Regarding the procedure for the five times (*pañcakālavidhi*), there are the words of the *Padma[-purāṇa]*.

Thus, it is also established by others in the case of recitation, fire-offerings, gifts, and so forth. In the *Padma[-purāṇa]* as well, the service of the five times is described as most excellent (or most well-known).
O Blessed One, the excellence of those who know the ritual of the five times has been described here;
what are the five times, and what are the five rituals?
Tell me, who am desirous of knowledge, exactly as it is,
provided that what I have asked here is not an absolute secret.
The Blessed One said:
First is the undertaking of action; after that, the acquisition of materials;
then sacrifice; after that, self-study; and after that, yoga.
O Four-faced One, these five are their methods, and those times are likewise five in sequence; they consist of the entire collection of actions ending with the performance of auspicious deeds.
This exposition has been declared according to the sequence beginning with rising;
one should awaken during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, meditating upon the supreme Nārāyaṇa,
and having risen, one should remain on the bed reciting the Vaiṣṇava names.

This chapter and others are also to be understood as being composed by Kṛṣṇa. Thus, in other Saṃhitās as well, the rule for the five periods (pañcakāla-vidhi) should be observed here and there, both in brief and in detail. Furthermore:
Salutations to you, O knower of the five times, devoted to the five times;
you alone are the imperishable refuge for those whose minds are fixed solely on the five times.
In these and other passages, it is established that the five-fold dharma is to be known by the Lord alone, that it is most dear to the Lord,
and that those who are devoted to it attain the Lord without interruption— even through non-interruption [variant readings: *apyavyavadhānena*].

The five periods of time beginning with *saṃgava*, as mentioned by Bhoja, serve other purposes; for it is stated by King Bhoja in the *Prayogapaddhatiratnāvalī*: "In that regard, the periods of time beginning with *saṃgava* proceed day after day: *saṃgava*, *sama*, *viṣṇupriya*, *dharma*, and *virāga*—these are the five periods."
These have been taught by those who know the inner self (*adhyātmavid*). From sunrise, five *nāḍīs* are called *saṃgava*;
therefore, twice that measure is taught as *sama*. "To that extent [is] Viṣṇupriya," and so forth.
In this regard, this division of time is for the purpose of determining the specific flower and the specific deity to be worshipped; it is not...

This refers to the five duties beginning with *abhigamana*. For it was previously stated—[the portion from "starting with 'at the time of *saṃgava*' on that lunar day" up to "the demonstration has been made" does not exist in the manuscripts *ka*, *kha*, and *ga*]—"one should take the flowers indicated for that lunar day at the time of *saṃgava*; with lotuses or *karavīra* flowers, O beloved of Viṣṇu."

"One should worship the Blessed One with *kumuda* flowers for the sake of *dharma*, and with *bilva* leaves for the sake of *virāga*. Furthermore, later on, specific forms of the Blessed One to be worshipped at those respective times are shown:
therein, Vaikuṇṭha is pleased at the *saṅgava* period, Aniruddha at the *sama* period, and Śiṃśumāra, who is dear to Viṣṇu, at the *dharma* period.

[The times for the five acts] are as follows: [the time for] the submarine fire (vaḍabāmukha) is during passion; [the time for] Kapila is during dispassion. Thus, there are five specific times for the pleasure of the five [acts].
Therefore, the arrangement of the five acts beginning with *abhigamana* is obligatory (*nitya*) precisely according to the method stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* and other texts;
anything else is optional (*kāmya*), etc.

In the *Pāñcakālikadharma*, there is a distinction between the presence and absence of defects; thus, while the boundaries of daily conduct (*dinacaryā*) are established, there are also specific modes of worship for certain [occasions], such as the three times of worship (*traikālyārcana*),

as well as special worships on the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), solstices (*ayana*), eclipses (*uparāga*), the three [birth] constellations (*janmatraya*), the twelfth day (*dvādaśī*), and the *parvan* of the *Śravaṇā* constellation.

These [observances] should be undertaken according to one's capacity by including them within that [framework]. It is precisely with reference to one who is incapable [of full observance] that the performance of the rites is sometimes prescribed as being gathered together [into a single act]. And the state of having "five times with intervals" (*sacchidra-pañcakālatā*) applies only to one who is capable of only that much. "Having intervals" (*sacchidratva*) means being interspersed with other rites performed for different purposes.
One who knows the reality of the twelve syllables, understands the division of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha),
and knows the five times without interruption— he is remembered as a true Bhāgavata.
This, however, is a praise of Pūrṇa as one qualified for the [highest] level; it is not intended to establish that he alone is a Pañcakālika Bhāgavata. [As it is said:
"One who knows the division of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) and is devoted to the five times (pañcakāla)."
He who is devoted to the twelve-syllable mantra is indeed the best of the devotees of the Lord.
Thus, the statement of Śāṇḍilya is likewise;
the dharma of the five kalpas is indeed intended by the author of the Śrībhāṣya and others,
and similarly, the employment of the twelve-syllable mantra is also an indication of other all-pervading [mantras].
By the mere practice of the mantra taught in one's own *saṃhitā*—[the *niṣṭhā-mantra* (ka) "a cha ja jha";
*niṣṭhāmātreṇa* (kha, ga, ca)]—all [practitioners] attain the dharma of the five times as appropriate.
For this very reason, the disciples and grand-disciples of the commentators [attain it] by means of the venerable eight-syllabled [mantra].
Elaborating upon the method of practice (*samārādhana*), they taught the daily routine (*dinacaryā*) by means of a five-fold temporal division.
Thus, the daily routine beginning from the *brāhma-muhūrta* was set forth by Śrī Raṅganārāyaṇācārya, the lord of the Vaṅgivaṃśa, who was an immediate disciple of the author of the Bhāṣya.

After describing— in detail— the proclamation of Hari, world-weariness, the sattvic fortitude that serves as a support, and everything up to the final resolution [attained] immediately thereafter, it is stated next:
From this point forward, for as long as I live, I shall strive with a concentrated mind to perform worship at the feet of Śrī, again and again.
Having approached Hari in the morning, he afterwards acquired ritual materials;
then he worshipped the God, and thereafter he also recited the mantras.
Even while meditating on the supreme deity during the five prescribed times,
he always remains engaged in this manner according to the path of the five-fold ritual (pāñcakālika).
Worshipping Hari with devotion using auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings acquired by my own efforts, according to my capacity, I shall pass my days.
Thus it is said; and by the venerable Śrī Parāśara Bhaṭṭāraka:
"A person who is an ascetic (yati) should desire to attain the Lord after having crossed over the ocean of saṃsāra, which is mixed with the sufferings of conception, birth, and old age."
Having risen at dawn and recollected Hari, one should contemplate the Gaṅgā as having arisen from His feet; then, having bathed in the waters of that sacred ford, one should proceed.
Having performed all actions arising from faith and mindfulness as far as one’s ability allows as a means of propitiating the Supreme Self, one should offer libations while wearing the half-tilaka.

Having thus briefly demonstrated what was stated by the former teachers— beginning with the mantras established from Ādhāraśakti down to the end of the assembly (pāriṣadya)— and having prostrated to Hari, restrained his breath,
and bowed to his gurus, [he begins] the [recitation] of the venerable eight-syllabled mantra.

Having revealed the sages (*ṛṣi*), meters (*chandas*), deities (*devatā*), seeds (*bīja*), and powers (*śakti*), and in order to indicate that the mantra-installation (*mantranyāsa*)—though not mentioned by the author of the commentary (*bhāṣyakāra*)—is to be adopted according to the method taught by his disciples and others, he has briefly stated: "Then, having performed the mantra-installation, one should also contemplate the meaning of the mantra," beginning with the words "[by the ancients... (*pūrvaiḥ*).
[The portion ending with "svayam-eva-abhidhāya" is not present in the manuscripts Ka, Kha, Ga, and Jha;
however, because the contemplation of the meaning of the mantra (*mantrārthacintana*)—which had not been included in previous texts—is extremely useful, he himself has set it forth.
Thus, having himself explained [it], because it is so exceedingly useful... [mantrārtham atyantopayuktatayā Gha, Ja]. Thus.

Having reflected upon the meaning of the mantra, one should then— having condensed the meditation previously described by the ancients beginning with the words "that supreme person" (*param puruṣam*) and so forth— and having elaborated upon the meditation on the parts from the feet to the end of the hair not mentioned therein, proceed according to the sequence of the sixteen offerings.

And the propitiation has been prescribed. Among all other modes of service as well, these sixteen constitute the primary ones; everything else is performed only in connection with them. Furthermore, the adoption of either brevity or elaboration according to the requirements of place, time, and condition is sanctioned by the scriptures. Therefore:
Consistency with the previous [work] should also be observed here; for this very reason,
the Nārāyaṇamunis, who follow both [traditions], have also elaborated in due order the duties to be performed at each respective time according to the scheme of the five times (*pañcakāla*).
For thus do we describe the sequence of the ritual for serving the lotus-feet of the Blessed One, which must be performed constantly by those who are single-mindedly devoted.
Established in goodness during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, uttering "Hari,
Hari," he rises from that bed and sits there with a concentrated mind.
Having begun thus, and having approached the Lord, the Sovereign, through these two [verses] and their commentaries,
one who has accomplished his purpose should long entrust himself to His lotus feet.
This first chapter, titled "Approaching," concerns the sequence for the worship of Mādhava by the female servant of Nārāyaṇa.
Having thus concluded the section on *abhigamana* (approaching), [the text continues]:
"In the second part of the day, one intent on the propitiation of Kṛṣṇa should duly gather the materials for worship from the forest as prescribed by the scriptures."

Through these and other chapters, the materials for collection and so forth, which are to be accomplished during their respective time-fragments (*kālāṃśa*), have also been explained in detail according to sequence. Thus, for all those who are single-mindedly devoted to the Blessed One (*bhagavadekāntinaḥ*)— including those established in the fourfold *Pañcarātra*, and even among them, those for whom some pervasive mantra is primary— [the following applies].
In accordance with the various optional boundaries previously adopted by each individual, the *pañcakālika-dharma* (the five-fold daily ritual) has been attained.
The prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that those who have taken refuge (*prapanna*) must abandon this sequence of five times.

In this regard, those who rely solely on *prapatti*— which is immediate and the sole means for attaining liberation— in accordance with their own specific qualification, are now examined as to whether they should abandon or adopt this sequence of the five periods (*pañcakāla-krama*). This is discussed as being a subordinate limb (*aṅga*) within the treatises on *prapatti*.

Because there is an absence of such instruction, and because a qualified seeker who cannot endure delay is unable to wait for the completion of a hundred-year vow, it follows that the power of yoga— which is a constituent part of that vow— must itself be accepted as the means; thus, one should practice according to one's capacity in the form of the observances of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*).
Even though pleasing the Lord and obeying His command consist in the performance of the duties pertaining to one's caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*),
this must also be carried out according to the boundaries of daily conduct (*dinacaryā*) preceded by the divisions of time taught in the *dharmaśāstras* of Vyāsa, Dakṣa, and others.

The prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is that [the five-fold sequence] should be abandoned because it is established even through the practice of daily routine (*dinacaryā*), and otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of mutual obstruction among ritual acts. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is that those who have taken refuge (*prapanna*) must adopt the sequence of the five times (*pañcakālakrama*).
"But this [mantra] must indeed be enclosed by the *rathantara*. Let the investigation into the validity of the supporting evidence stand aside for now;

rather, let the traditional instruction of the authors of the Bhāṣya and others be considered first. Then, beginning with the words, "Now I shall describe the ritual procedure for the worship of the Lord for those who are exclusively devoted," [he continues].

In his ear, [the author] asks: "With reference to what kind of qualified practitioner (*adhikārin*) was this exposition of the extraordinary method of worship— preceded by specific rites such as ritual bathing and so forth— composed by the commentators, according to the path taught in the *Bhagavat-śāstra* and not mentioned in the *Dharma-śāstras* of Śaunaka, Vyāsa, Bodhāyana, and others?"
If it is argued that this has been understood by another qualified person capable of it, we say no; for up to the present day,

we observe its performance according to one's ability by his disciples, grand-disciples, and others who are devoted solely to *prapatti*, and they perform it with the understanding that it is a means (*sādhana*).

Because it is taught in that very same [text] through such statements as, "having become a supreme devotee (*paramaikāntin*) by having exclusive delight in service to the Lord due to the absence of the performance of those [other rites]," and because the term "supreme devotee" holds sovereign authority over a qualified person for whom there is no other means and no other purpose, [the author now describes] the procedure for the worship of the Lord for the supreme devotee.
In the phrase "I shall speak," there is a reference to what preceded; that very [preceding matter] is the refuge, as indicated by the words "having cut off all... and so forth.

Furthermore, since the manner of seeking refuge was previously described, the prose work concerning the complete subject of seeking refuge is understood to have been preceded by those two verses within that composition. And this—

The subject matter is within the capacity [of the qualified]. Therefore, it must be admitted— even by one who is unwilling— that the practice of worship is here compiled according to tradition, taking as its primary basis a certain *saṃhitā* that contains some portion of the established doctrine, specifically intended for such a person who has taken refuge [in the Lord] as a supreme *ekāntin*.

An exposition supporting that the *pañcakālaprakriyā* (the ritual procedure of the five times) is the system favored by the author of the *Śrībhāṣya*. And that worship consists of the offering of various seats and enjoyments in their proper sequence— namely, the *aupacārika* (offering of materials), *sāṃsparśika* (offering of touch), and *ābhyavahārika* (offering of food)— to be cast into the vessels for the *arghya* and other offerings.
It is observed that [the performance of worship] depends upon hundreds of materials such as various types of incense and flowers;

however, that which is acquired by oneself through righteous means is primary. For one who is incapable, the act of acquisition consists of instigating others, such as sons or disciples, to procure them. Furthermore, even with respect to materials already possessed, there is the act of taking them up for that specific purpose at the time of the rite.
Thus, prior to the propitiation itself, the acquisition of the proper materials is an indispensable prerequisite.

Therefore, by the very instruction regarding the sacrifice (*ijyā*), the acquisition of those things required for it—which have arrived at their own proper time—is also effectively taught by implication (*arthāt*). Furthermore, from that [instruction]:

Even the initial approach (*abhigamana*) previously mentioned ultimately culminates in the form of surrender (*prapatti*), as it involves reflecting upon the specific scriptures and particular mantras that enjoin it; this has already been established.

By that instruction, the act of approaching [the Lord] is also effectively taught by implication. For this very reason, the sages Nārāyaṇa, who understood his intention, said: "Having approached the Lord, the Sovereign, through the *Dvaya* and its commentaries..."
Having long cast oneself at his lotus-feet, one becomes a person of merit.
Thus, the approach (*abhigamana*) has been concluded (*nigamita*); and its detailed exposition consists precisely of the prose and other [metrical forms],
as well as the private recitation (*svādhyāya*) occurring immediately after the completion of the ritual worship up to the final oblation (*anuyāga*).

Through the hearing and recitation of the Vedas, Smṛtis, Itihāsas, Purāṇas, and mantras; through the chanting of mantras and virtuous discourse; and through hearing and teaching concerning the supreme self—according to one’s capacity—one kindles the knowledge that assists yoga, which arises subsequently from the study of the scriptures of the Blessed One, the Dharmaśāstras, and so forth.
It is established that [the teaching] is being imparted; thus, even that which is constant at that time is always spoken by the speaker together with the non-connection of the two meanings.

It is understood that the pair of statements mentioned in the prose is indeed taught because they occur at the appropriate occasion without obstructing other scriptural duties. For the "always-spoken" [teaching] does not apply during the time of sleep.
Because it is impossible to do so; because during the time of observing silence, it would contradict that injunction [it contradicts that in versions ka, kha, ga, and jha];

and because during the time of performing propitiation and other rites accomplished by means of other mantras and the like, it would be obstructed by those very same [mantras in version ka, kha, ga, and ca]. Therefore, its attainment occurs at the appropriate occasion.
In this way, yoga as well— consisting of one-pointedness in the pursuit of the two-fold purpose—
is practiced by one who has ceased all activities during the periods preceding and following the auspicious sleep, that is, during the first and last watches of the night.

Thus, as stated in passages such as these, [the goal] is to be attained through effort joined with the opportunity (or, according to variant readings: "to be attained through effort obtained by means of the opportunity," or "to be attained through effort joined with what is obtained by means of the opportunity").
Furthermore, in the *Śrīvaikuṇṭhagadya*, having established that one's devotion is solely fixed upon independent *prapatti* (surrender), and thereafter—

Having begun with the instruction that one should thus meditate every day for the sake of reviving the self, and having described the complete yoga of meditation upon the Blessed One who dwells upon the couch of the supreme state, as well as the specific points of contemplation,
one should place the glorious lotus-feet [the pair of lotus-feet] upon the head.
Having meditated thus, with all one's limbs submerged within the ocean of nectar, one should remain in bliss;

by this, a manifold yoga devoid of other purposes is prescribed as a daily duty. We shall demonstrate this in detail in its proper section. And having thus sought refuge in the obligatory [practice],...

With his mental faculty nourished by His grace, he contemplates that very Blessed One, the Lord of all lords, as his own master and well-wisher; and through meditation characterized by extreme affection, ceaselessness, and the clearest possible direct perception— [or through such contemplation...]
Since it has been stated that "he sat meditating" marks the commencement of the act of propitiation,

it is logical that at this juncture there should arise the most delicious form of meditation (*anudhyāna*), which— just like the act of propitiation itself— is characterized as service (*kaikarya*) performed for no other purpose. Therefore, by virtue of its primacy as having no other motive, [it is established].

It is understood that everything else established by the commentators— who taught the specific methods for complete propitiation— and by other treatises, is also authorized. For this very reason, his disciples, grand-disciples, and others have prescribed the service of the Lord precisely according to the division of the five periods (pañcakāla).

However, regarding the objections concerning the possibility of repetition in *prapatti* and so forth, they have established service to the Lord precisely through the division of time for the entrustment (*nikṣepa*). Furthermore, those objections concerning the possibility of repetition in *prapatti* and so forth have been refuted at the end of the *Nikṣeparakṣā*.
Regarding this, the claim that [the daily obligatory rites] should be abandoned because they are not taught as being auxiliary to *prapatti* is incorrect;

for by that same logic, it would follow that even the "perpetual worship" (*nitya-samārādhana*) mentioned by the Commentator (*Bhāṣyakāra*) must be abandoned. If it is granted that such worship is to be performed solely with the purpose of pleasing the Lord, then everything connected to it should likewise be accepted.

Therefore, let it be granted: for even those who advocate the rule of renouncing the nature of all dharmas as auxiliary to *prapatti* admit that for the surrendered soul (*prapanna*) who has become a servant to the Lord, the Master, the state of a servant is attained as his very nature. As for that which...

It was stated that there is no tolerance for delay until the completion of the hundred-year vow; that is indeed so. For we do not say that one who has already perfected the means (*niṣpannopāya*) must perform the hundred-year vow. Just as some people, while waiting for a boat to cross a river, pass the time with games like *līlā* or gambling, while others [do not].
In the case of gambling with a fixed stake (*paṇabandha*), both parties are equal in their observance of the rules of the game; therein,

those who play for sport do not wait for the arrival of a boat even when it comes at an indefinite time, as they interrupt their recreation and gambling, whereas those who have bound a stake delay until the completion of the gambling— so it is here as well.
This is the tradition of those who know the reality.
Regarding the power of the five-fold yoga (pāñcakālika-yoga), there is the removal of the contradiction with the practice of surrender (prapatti).
Furthermore, as for the claim that whatever else is joined with the power of yoga necessarily results in the acceptance of that [yoga] itself as the means—that too is weak.

This is because it is well known that masters such as Nātha Muni, Kurukeśvara, and others— who had previously been solely devoted to the means of *prapatti* (surrender) and who directly perceived the three principles (*tattva*) through the power of their own yoga—
subsequently experienced the taste of the bliss of the Lord attained through yoga by the grace of the Blessed One. Otherwise, [the following would not be possible].

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of having to accept that even the propitiation and other practices mentioned by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*)— which are preceded by such [theistic] contemplation— are themselves means [to liberation], simply because they are the most delicious when performed as service to the Master (*svāmikaikarya*). And if that [service] is indeed of the nature of service to the Master...
[The phrase "by way of being most delicious" does not appear in the Ka, Kha, Ga, Ca, or Jha manuscripts.

If it were to be adopted as its own purpose, then even in this meditative absorption (*samādhi*), this absorption—which consists of a mass of happiness for those impoverished of absorption—is equal; and it is also conducive to those who have taken refuge.
Regarding the etymological contemplation (*yaugikānusaṃdhāna*), it is stated in the *Śāṇḍilyasmṛti*:

"Such is this Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and such is this inner self (*pratyagātman*). [The manuscript reading *ka ca jha* corresponds to the *Śāṇḍilyasmṛti*; the variant *gha* reads *ayam īdṛśaḥ*.]
The continuous contemplation of that connection is proclaimed as *yoga*.
Yoga is the stabilization of the intellect in Brahman through the senses being brought under control,
whether those senses are engaged or disengaged in the extensive activities of the Blessed One.

Thus, this very connection— this very contemplation of the two-fold meaning— is what is intended. However, the contemplation of the Rāhu-mīmāṃsakas and the Kabandha-mīmāṃsakas, which is contrary to this, is outside the Veda.
The venerable Kṛṣṇa-muni said: "The view that the conscious self is indeed one alone,
and the view that action alone bears fruit— these two views arise from a lack of faith in the authority of the Vedas."
Being pleased, he pleases him; you are not merely a follower of a Brahmin.
Thus,

there is no conflict between the religion of the five times (*pāñcakālika-dharma*) and the rites prescribed in the *Smṛtis*. Furthermore, as for what was stated [elsewhere]— namely, that [the path] may also follow the way taught by Vyāsa, Dakṣa, and others—

The accomplishment of the daily routine (*dinacaryā*) consisting of the faithful observance of the duties appropriate to one's own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*); [for this reason, the reading "ataścaiva" appears everywhere, whereas in the restatement of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), it is seen as "anyathā"].
And for this reason, when both [types of duty] coincide, there arises the contingency of mutual obstruction among ritual acts; thus, in that regard—
This objection regarding mutual contradiction arises only for those who are ignorant of the history of the Śrauta and Smārta traditions.
For it has been resolved in this regard by the venerable sage Śrī Kṛṣṇa:
"There is a combination of the animal sacrifice, the iṣṭi, the dardhi-darvihomas, and those accompanied by Soma."
Just as many [causes] may have a single [effect], so too does this action [have multiple effects].
Thus it is said. Moreover, there is not even that much restriction here;

for in the *Vyāsa-smṛti*, even the "approaching" (*abhigamana*) and "conversing" (*saṃvādana*) are mentioned, and therein this pentad beginning with "approaching" is seen to be included. Vyāsa, moreover, states:
Having risen during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, one should contemplate righteousness (*dharma*) and worldly prosperity (*artha*);
thereafter, one should meditate upon the Lord with the mind, reflecting on the physical exhaustion resulting from those pursuits.
Having begun thus and instructed on the method for the morning bath and the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana),
[the text continues]: "Then, having returned home, the brahmin, having sipped water (ācamana) according to the rule,
shall duly kindle the fire."
Having thus prescribed the morning oblation with these and other words, he says immediately thereafter: "One should pay homage to the gods and others,
present offerings to them, give flowers and such to them, and likewise salute one's elders."
One should attend upon the teacher (and indeed teachers) and practice what is beneficial for him;
thereafter, the twice-born should diligently study the Vedas according to his ability.
The best of the twice-born should recite [the mantras], teach his disciples, retain them in memory, and reflect upon them; he should also examine the scriptures concerning dharma and other matters,
as well as the Vedic collections and especially the Vedāṅgas.

Thus. Here, according to the method stated by Dakṣa, in the case of Vedic study and other practices to be accomplished during the second half-watch, the unseen portion (*adṛṣṭāṃśa*)—that is, the portion whose purpose is unseen—is indicated by the words "recitation" (*japa*) and "hymn" (*stotra*) in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*. For someone who is emaciated by their practice, the unseen portion...

Kha; [Ka Ga Jha]: If there is a portion of the meaning already seen, it connects with the subsequent material through the contraction of the time for the *abhigamana* (approach). Here, the *abhigamana* is established by means of saluting the deity, offering oblations, and presenting flowers and other such items.

In this context, the salutation to the gods naturally results in the salutation to Viṣṇu alone, because the quality of being a god without qualification— and thus even the salutation to other gods— finds its ultimate rest in him alone. For this very reason, the Lord (Īśvara), who is described as the object of meditation at the outset in the words "one should meditate upon the Lord with the mind," is indeed Viṣṇu, the Lord of all, just like Jaya and the others.

Furthermore, "Īśvara," "Vikramī," and "Dhanvī" are recited among its names [in the *Nāmasaṃgraha*]; and because it is stated later [in the same work]: "There is no Vedic merit greater than the propitiation of Viṣṇu. This very point—

*Abhigamana*, consisting of acts such as salutation to Viṣṇu, is taught in various ways even in other scriptures. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "of the gods, etc.," the inclusion of the ancestors (*pitṛs*) and others is intended.
In the *Vyāsasmṛti*, this is referred to as *upādāna-saṃvādana*.
Having thus described what is to be done at the first period, he states the procurement— the gathering of the requisites for worship— which is to be accomplished during the second period:
"And one should also approach the Lord for the sake of accomplishing yoga and kṣema."
Then the twice-born man should provide for his family's needs according to the prescribed rules.
Thus it is said. And this approach to a worldly lord pertains to times of distress for one who lacks any other means of escape. For they remember:
"One should avoid entering cities," and so forth. And it is stated in the *Śrī Śāṇḍilya Smṛti*: [Note: This portion is not found in the manuscripts labeled śrī ka kha ga ca jha].
One should avoid from afar the dwellings of Buddhas, Rudras, and others, as well as cremation grounds, corpses, forests, and royal capitals.

Thus, the fivefold activity of time (*kālapañcakakṛtya*) has been explained therein [in the appropriate places, such as *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *cha*, *ja*, *jha*]; it is to be understood by all according to what is appropriate. And this very thing is prescribed in the scriptures of the Blessed One as being for the sake of the Blessed One (*bhagavadarthatvena*). Here too, the phrase "for the sake of the family" (*kuṭumbārthe*) indicates that it is not merely for that purpose alone.

What is intended [in the statement "for the sake of the family" (kuṭumbārthe) is that the exclusive purposefulness is not intended; this is because the notion of such exclusivity is prohibited everywhere]. And this was sung by the Blessed One himself— [it is sung (gīyate) in some versions].
This world is bound by action other than that performed for the sake of sacrifice;
therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment.
Thus, since even the maintenance of one's family— by means of the remnants of the sacrifice consisting of the worship of the Blessed Lord—
is itself merely the fulfillment of the command of the Blessed Lord, the Great Sage said "for the sake of the family" with that intention in mind.
One should reflect upon *dharma* and *artha*; thus, even the reflection on the objects of worldly endeavor mentioned at the outset is for the sake of *dharma*.

However, reflection on physical austerity (*kāyakleśa*) is for the purpose of seeking means that are free from affliction (*kleśa*). For Manu and others record: "One should accumulate wealth without causing affliction to the body."
Householders should always enjoy those sense-objects that come to them without effort.
And so forth.
In the *Vyāsasmṛti*, following the discussion on sacrificial offerings, he now states the duty for the third period of the day: "Then, at the time of midday, for the purpose of bathing..."

"One should fetch clay," and so forth. Regarding the performance of the bath, he describes the contemplation of the Lord as follows: "Having consecrated the water with auspicious mantras addressed to Varuṇa or containing the word 'water' (abliṅga), one should, with a pure disposition and without distraction, meditate upon the imperishable Viṣṇu."
The waters were produced from Nārāyaṇa, and they alone are his place of rest again;
therefore, at the time of bathing, a wise person should remember the god Nārāyaṇa.
Thus:
"In this regard, one should repeat the three-footed Sāvitrī, or the verse 'tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam,' or the Praṇava, or one should meditate upon Hari, the God."
And so it is said. Also, regarding the libation (tarpaṇa): "Having first uttered the syllable Oṃ, at the end of the name [and at the end of 'namaḥ'], one should say 'I offer libation.
One should satisfy the gods and the Brahman-sages with water mixed with unbroken rice grains."
Then, with devotion, one should offer water mixed with sesame seeds to the ancestors according to the procedure prescribed in the Sūtra.
Thus, it is prescribed here that one should contemplate [the deities] as being identical with the Blessed Lord by prefixing [their names] with the *praṇava* (Om).

This very point has also been shown by the Commentator regarding the daily rites (*nitya*): "having meditated upon the gods, sages, and ancestors as being identical with the Blessed Lord, and having gratified them. As for the rite to be performed during the third period of the day, which consists of direct sacrifice (*ijyā*), [it is as follows:]...
He states the very means of propitiation:
"There exists no Vedic rite that yields greater merit than the propitiation of Viṣṇu;
therefore, one should eternally propitiate Hari, who is without beginning, middle, or end."
By means of the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ" and the Puruṣa-sūkta—
no mantra equal to these two has been declared even within the four Vedas.
Then, with his mind fixed on Him and being tranquil, he should offer himself to Viṣṇu, whose splendor is stainless, by means of the mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ".

Thus, in this context, the praise beginning with "tad viṣṇoḥ" is not intended to disparage the praṇava and other elements prescribed by Yājñavalkya and others. This is because the supremacy of the worship of Viṣṇu is explicitly stated both generally and specifically throughout the preceding and subsequent texts.

It should be understood that the statement regarding the worship of other deities is intended for those persons of limited intelligence who are not awakened and who seek only small, perishable fruits. And it is sung: "The fruit of those of limited intelligence becomes finite. And it is said [in the subsequent portion]:
In the Mahābhārata:
"O fully awakened one, because Brahmā, Śitikaṇṭha (Śiva), and whatever other deities are remembered, do not yield limited fruit, they are not to be served [as ultimate goals]."
Thus it is said; and Bādarāyaṇa has declared: "One who takes refuge at the lotus feet of Viṣṇu should not bow to any other deity.
Due to the ripening of their past actions, everything up to the realm of Viriñca is inauspicious.
Thinking thus, Vāsudeva, the supreme refuge, [bestowed grace] upon the one who was dispassionate.
And thus:
"The worship prescribed in the Pañcarātra alone is the primary one for all,
and this worship of Viṣṇu is found among the scriptures of the Blessed One."
By means of those various pervasive mantras and so forth, it is elaborated in accordance with their respective jurisdictions.

It is established by the logic of adopting the *hautra* (priestly duties) prescribed in the *Hotṛ-śākhā*, that only that which is fully taught—even if not explicitly set forth in the specific scripture under one’s jurisdiction—possesses primacy. By this [it is meant that], in the absence of Vedic mantras...

Or [it may be performed] "according to what is proclaimed in the Pañcarātra"; for even the Smṛti, because mantras such as the Praṇava, the eight-syllabled, and the twelve-syllabled ones are studied after the Māyā [syllable] from the Atharvaṇa Rahasya,
includes them under the term "Vedic mantra," and thus [the rite may be performed] according to what is proclaimed in the Pañcarātra.
Thus, this portion should be applied as referring to other mantras whose roots are the Śruti texts on direct perception as condensed in the Tantras;
[it concerns] the obligatory nature of the propitiation of the Blessed Lord.

This worship of the Blessed Lord is constant, like the Vaiśvadeva and other such rites, according to the scriptural injunction: "One should constantly worship Hari. Śānaka said: "I shall now describe the supreme, constant worship of Viṣṇu."
"pra vaḥ pāntamandhaso dhiyā"—according to the rule for the half-verse, [the syllables *dhi*, *ṛ*, *ca*, *o*, *rdha*, *rca*, *kha*, *ga*, *dhi*, and *it* constitute the half-verse; *ka*, *jha*.]
Thus, according to another Sūtra:
"Having bathed daily and being pure, one should perform the libations to the gods, sages, and ancestors,
as well as the worship of the deities and the placing of sacrificial fuel."
Thus it is because of the general statement of Manu; and it is said in the *Anuśāsana-parvan*, in the dialogue between Śrī Puṇḍarīka and Nārada:
"Whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant, one who neglects the worship of Keśava does not attain the supreme goal."
Thus it is said. Similarly, in the case of Yājñavalkya and others—[as stated by Yogayājñavalkya]:
"Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and Rudra; Viṣṇu is the god, the sun;
therefore, I consider none other to be more worthy of worship than Janārdana."
Such things are stated. And regarding the transgression incurred by failing to perform the worship of such a deity, he himself says:
"He who, out of delusion or laziness, eats without having performed the worship of the deity, goes to the hells and is even born among swine."
Thus it is said. Furthermore, it is stated elsewhere that the food of a householder who lacks an image of the Blessed One (bhagavadarcāvatāra) in his home is not to be eaten:
"O Lord of the Earth, he in whose house an image of Keśava does not stand..."
One must not eat food that has no grain, for it is equal to what is unfit to be eaten.
Thus it is said. Immediately thereafter, elaborating upon the Prāṇāgnihotra preceded by the five great sacrifices (pañcamahāyajña), he speaks as follows:
"Then, one should offer the oblation of food into the breaths, conjoined with the Svāhā and the Praṇava."
Then, having offered to Apāna, immediately thereafter to Vyāna.
Then he should perform the offering for *udāna*, and the fifth for *samāna*;
having understood the true nature of these, the twice-born man should offer them into his own self.
One should eat the remaining food, accompanied by condiments, according to one's desire,
having meditated in the mind upon the deity as one's own self, indeed repeatedly recited.

Thus it is said. Here too, by the principle previously stated, the two words "deva" and "prajāpati" should be understood as referring to Viṣṇu. Meditating on Hari in his heart, one who is composed should offer food to Him.

In accordance with the statement of Vyāsa concerning the Prāṇāgnihotra found in the Karmakāṇḍa, as cited by the venerable Yāmuneya in such passages as these, it is understood from this very statement of Vyāsa that "meditation on the deity" (devadhyāna) is precisely that meditation on Hari residing within the heart. And such is...
The meal itself is designated elsewhere by the term "anuyāga" (concluding sacrifice).
[This phrase is not found in the Ka, Kha, and Jha manuscripts. Then, having instructed on everything else required for the meal as well, [he said:]
In the *Vyāsasmṛti*, regarding the recitation of the Veda after a meal: "Having thus eaten and being comfortably seated, one should facilitate the digestion of that food;
one should augment the Veda with the *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas*."

Thus he has described the study of scripture (*svādhyāya*) as to be accomplished during four periods of the day. Likewise, others also remember: "Having eaten and having approached the sun, one should always recite the Purāṇas," and so forth. Here, [the rule applies] to a specific qualified person who possesses complete knowledge and is independent of supplementary texts (*upabṛṃhaṇa*).

The recitation (*svādhyāya*) consisting of twelve, eight, or two six-syllabled [mantras], and so forth, is indeed the *svādhyāya*; such is the rule for that in various places. For this very reason, in the *Rahasya*, by means of the prohibition of other Vedāntas, the prescription of the *svādhyāya* consisting solely of the twelve [syllables] is established.
In the Vyāsasmṛti, yoga is also obtained by implication;
for immediately thereafter, after stating that which is performed during the fifth period— beginning with "Then one should perform the twilight worship" (tataḥ saṃdhyām upāsīta)— it continues.
Having kindled the fire according to the rules with mantras and having eaten the most excellent food,
he should sleep at night on a dry mat together with his servants and kinsmen.

In this passage, by the mention of eating at night (*rātribhojana*), the practice of yoga (*yoga*) following daytime eating—which was mentioned immediately after that—is understood to follow naturally; therefore, it is not explicitly stated. For instance, previously, immediately after the discussion on daytime eating, he said:
"One should perform the consecration of the breath (*prāṇānumantraṇa*) with the mantra beginning with 'In faith' (*śraddhāyām*)."
For it is said that one should thus unite one's own self with Brahman by means of the syllable.
Among all yogas, the yoga of the self (ātma-yoga) is remembered as the supreme;
he who performs it according to this rule attains the imperishable state.
Thus he concluded:
"In this manner, I have described in its entirety, day after day,
the entire range of duties for Brahmins which bestow the fruit of liberation."
The Brahmin who does not perform [his duties] out of atheism or laziness goes to terrible hells and is born into the womb of a crow.
There is no other path to liberation as easily accessible as the rule of the stages of life (āśrama);
therefore, one should perform actions for the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord.

Thus [it is said]. Here, Parameṣṭhin is indeed Viṣṇu, who is to be propitiated by all ritual acts (*sarvakarma*). That Viṣṇu alone is to be propitiated by all ritual acts, as [stated in the Gītā]: "The enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds..."
For I am indeed the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices;
by sacrifices you are eternally worshipped, O Acyuta who consists of all beings.
You alone are the consumer of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings, assuming the forms of both the ancestors and the gods.
This is well known from such passages as these. And he (Viṣṇu) is described here as being pleased by the rites performed by the Supreme Lord (Brahmā).

He is called *parameṣṭhin* because he "stands in the supreme discourse" (*parame vāde tiṣṭhati*). And he resides in the world named Vaikuṇṭha—which is composed of pure *sattva*, as stated in the verse "That highest step of Viṣṇu"—beyond darkness.

The Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) alone is present [in all times]. Thus, in the Dharmaśāstra of Vyāsa’s son, the worship of the Blessed One during the five periods of the day is prescribed as being integrated precisely with the Blessed One's obligatory duties; therefore, the abandonment of that worship by anyone is not tenable.
Even the division of the eight periods of time mentioned by Dakṣa is consistent with the five-fold ritual (pāñcakālika-karma);
as for that which was stated by Dakṣa regarding the daily duties according to the division of the eight periods of time, that too is indeed consistent with the present context:
"That which must be performed day after day by a twice-born man upon rising in the morning..."
I shall explain all of that, providing assistance to the twice-born.
From sunrise until sunset, a Brahmin should not remain inactive;
he should be engaged in obligatory rites, occasional rites, and other blameless optional rites.
If a twice-born man abandons his own duty and performs something else,
whether out of ignorance or greed, he becomes fallen through that renunciation.

Thus, having established that the performance of obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites, as well as optional rites (*kāmya*) that assist them, must be carried out without interruption at their proper times, the duties for the first portion of the day are now taught.
And likewise in the second, the third, the fourth, and the fifth.
In the sixth, seventh, and eighth parts respectively,
I shall explain in their entirety whatever duties are to be performed in these sections.

Having thus generally introduced the classification of duties according to the division of the eight periods of time, it is stated in the *Dakṣasmṛti* that the duties to be performed during the first and second periods are included within sexual intercourse:
"When the dawn has arrived, having performed purification as prescribed..."
Then one should perform the bath, preceded by the cleansing of the teeth.
By such statements as these, [it is shown that] one who neglects the twilight prayers (saṃdhyā) is perpetually impure and unfit for all ritual acts;
whatever other rite he may perform, he shall not partake of its fruit.
Having thus duly explained the rituals of bathing, sipping water (ācamana), and the twilight worship (saṃdhyāvandana) and so forth, [the text states]:
"But at the conclusion of the twilight rite, the fire-oblation (homa) is prescribed to be performed by oneself;
for the fruit that arises from performing the oblation oneself is not produced by anyone else."
An officiating priest, a son, a teacher, a brother, a sister's son, and a father-in-law—
whatever is offered by these very persons is indeed as if offered by oneself.
Having thus described the morning *homa*, he says immediately thereafter:
"Then, having performed the rites for the gods and beholding the Guru and auspicious sights,
the forenoon is especially recommended for all rites dedicated to the gods."
Rites for the gods should be performed in the forenoon, those for humans in the midday, and those for the ancestors in the afternoon; these duties should be carried out with diligence.

Thus [it is said]. Here, because the performance of rites for the gods (*devakārya*) is prescribed immediately after the morning oblations (*prātaḥsavana*), the approach to the Blessed One (*bhagavadabhigamana*)—which is enjoined for that same time—is also taught in a general sense. As for that which was stated immediately thereafter: "In the second part, however, the study of the Vedas (*vedābhyāsa*) is prescribed."
First, the acquisition of the Veda; then recitation, practice, and silent repetition;
and finally, its impartation to disciples—thus, indeed, the study of the Veda is fivefold.

Thus, that too is consistent; for the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* indeed prescribes recitation (*japa*), meditation (*dhyāna*), worship (*arcana*), and hymns (*stotra*) upon arrival during the first watch of the day.
And it speaks of the taking up [of materials] immediately thereafter:

The inclusion within the category of "acquisition" (upādāna) of the duties prescribed by Dakṣa for the third period of the day is declared to be the time for gathering sacrificial fuel, flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth;
likewise, in that third part of the day, one should accomplish the welfare of those who are to be supported.
Thus it is said. And this has been stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* with the words beginning "Then, of flowers, fruits, and so forth.
Here, the accomplishment of the welfare of those to be nourished should be understood—according to the logic previously stated—as being solely for the purpose of pleasing the Lord.
And regarding this, having introduced the morning bath [and other rites such as bathing], it says:
Prior to all ritual actions, there should be constant mindfulness of the Blessed One:
"While performing rituals such as bathing and the like, one should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa. (Variant readings: *dhyāyet* / *ka kha ga a jha*)
One attains the world of Brahmā and is not born here again.

Thus [and so it is said in the Gha manuscript]. And the Blessed Śaunaka has also taught: "One should constantly remember Hari alone, both before and after ritual acts. Here, because the word *karman* (action) is not restricted [to either seen or unseen results], it refers to all actions, whether visible or invisible.

The inclusion of all actions, whether their purpose is visible or invisible, is as follows: even in rites dedicated to other deities, Hari—who is their inner self—must be kept in mind; this is the intended meaning of the word "eva" (only).
By the word "nityam" (constantly), any suspicion that these are optional (*kāmya*) or occasional (*naimittika*) is dispelled. [This applies] at the time of action, which is naturally established.
Recollection (*smaraṇa*) is included by the word "and" (*ca*). Thus, it is established that in all scriptural rites, the constant contemplation of the Lord (*bhagavad-anusaṃdhāna*) is mandatory.

This very point is stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* among the nine principles (*nayāni*) as being unavoidable even in those rites prompted by worldly attachment (*rāga-prāpta*): [The text continues with the citation from the Jayākhyasaṃhitā.]
Though unattached to beds, seats, vehicles, and the like, and likewise unattached to food,
one should not abandon the meditative absorption that indeed yields the fruit of bliss.
Thus it is said. But to summarize everything:
"Having churned all the scriptures and having reflected upon them again and again, this one thing is well-established: Narayana alone should always be meditated upon."
Thus it is said.

And because this [practice] is eternal, because its fruit is bliss corresponding to its own nature, and because it is itself the goal, it is [the subject matter] even for those established in the independent *prapatti* scriptures—and indeed for those established in the scriptures [in general]. (ka kha ga ca ja)
It is difficult to abandon. And thus the self-evident nature of its being the primary purpose was stated by the sages Nārāyaṇa:
"The auspicious service of a servant toward his master, which conforms to his own nature and is endowed with devotion and faith—the wise know that to be true propitiation."
What indeed is not achievable by men devoted to the worship of the Blessed One?
This is especially so for Vaiṣṇavas; this itself is their very purpose.
Thus it is said; for even the interruption of the contemplation of the Blessed One is recorded in tradition as a loss of the supreme human goal:
"If one does not contemplate Vāsudeva for even a moment or a muhūrta, that is a loss, that is a great flaw, that is an error, and that is a derangement."

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that [ignorance] results in the loss of the human goal, provides an opening for enemies such as desire and anger, serves as the cause for the notion of a self in what is not the self, and is the cause of non-natural pleasure and pain.
Even when a single moment devoid of meditation has passed...
It is fitting for one who has been robbed by bandits to cry out loudly.
Thus it is said: even for those whose livelihoods are exhausted and who are intent on other matters—“Even with a mind occupied by other things, Viṣṇu should be served from time to time;
a cow, though bound to the post and wandering about, still eats mouthfuls of fodder.”

By such passages as these, service to the Blessed One is enjoined at the appropriate time through the *kṣut-kṣānti-kāraka* discipline (the practice of enduring hunger), with that alone being the sole purpose. Thus, in this context, for one who has perfected the means (*siddhopāya*) and for one who is still practicing the means (*upāya-sādhaka*),
service to the Blessed One is itself the primary goal, just like the taste of milk for one who is healthy and seeks health.
The inclusion of the fourth and fifth time-period duties mentioned by Dakṣa within the act of *ijyā* (sacrifice) is as follows:
having taught the various types of ritual bathing with the words, "In the fourth period, one should likewise fetch earth for the purpose of bathing," and so forth.
In the fifth part, however, a distribution according to what is appropriate is prescribed for the ancestors, the gods, human beings, and even insects.
Having thus made a distribution [of food] from that, the householder should eat what remains;
having eaten, however, he should sit comfortably and digest that food.
The duties pertaining to the sixth and seventh periods of time as stated by Dakṣa are included within *svādhyāya* (self-study).
However, the worldly conduct (*lokayātrā*) mentioned for the eighth period does not apply to those who are exclusively devoted to the Supreme (*paramaikāntinaḥ*).
Thus concludes the summary of the worship of the deities (*devatārcana*).

That which was stated as ending with the meal is also divided into two by means of internal sub-divisions; this very time is designated as "jyākāla" (the time of the bowstring) by treating these as one, and thus there is no contradiction. Here, the meaning indicated by the term *devasavibhāga* will later be referred to by the term *devatārcana*.
He specifically prescribed: "Sandhyā, bathing, recitation (japa), fire-offering (homa), self-study (svādhyāya), and worship of the deities.

Thus, it is stated that one should practice the sixth and seventh [periods] through the study of Itihāsas and Purāṇas; these two times are unified as the time for self-study (svādhyāya). Here, by measure, [there is a disparity between the three times...]. (ka kha ga)

Furthermore, a discrepancy in timing arises due to differences of opinion. Regarding the statement, "In the eighth [watch], however, one should attend to worldly affairs (lokayātrā), and thereafter, the external twilight (bahiḥsaṃdhyā)," this division of time for worldly affairs is not particularly relevant for one who has turned away from the world and is solely devoted to the Lord; therefore, it is not mentioned here. As was stated previously in the *Pūrvaśrava*...
In the text: "And upon hearing [the teacher's name], when the teacher’s teacher is present, one should behave as toward the teacher.

Toward teachers of knowledge and others who are not [one's own immediate teacher], [another kind of conduct is required]; toward teachers of knowledge and others who are not [one's own immediate teacher], it is constant."
The function [of the organs] is directed toward their own sources.
Thus it has been said by the knowers of Brahman:
"From this day forward, O people, you are 'you' and we are 'we.
You are devoted to wealth and pleasure; we are devoted to the acquisition of food."
There is no association between us and you;
we are the servants of Viṣṇu, while you are the servants of the senses.
Thus, in passages such as "fearing the multitude like a snake," the avoidance of those with discordant character and qualities is taught.

Furthermore, since it is taught by Kapila in the context of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) that living together with those of similar character is not a fault, this principle applies by implication (*kaimutya*) with equal force even to householders and others who seek liberation. And they declare:
The *Bahvṛca* says: "One who knows this (*idaṃvit*) should not eat together with one who does not know this (*anidaṃvit*), nor should he be a fellow-drinker (*sadharmā*). This is its elaboration:
"One who lacks knowledge (*āvidyaḥ*) is called a commoner (*prākṛta*); the one who possesses knowledge (*vaidyaḥ*) is called a Vaiṣṇava."
A physician should not perform any action whatsoever with ignorance—that is, without knowledge—regarding anything.
Thus it is said:
"Day by day, association with the virtuous is the source of dharma;
for association with the wicked is indeed the cause, the very womb, of the net of delusion."
Thus it is said:
"For whatever wise ascetics there may be who long for liberation,
