for them whose thirst has been severed, Hari indeed provides security and prosperity."
For those people who worship Me, thinking of no other,
and who are constantly devoted, I carry the burden of their acquisition and preservation.
Hari, the bestower of liberation, constantly grants physical health, wealth, and even incidental enjoyments to those who practice meditation.

"It is better to dwell within the cage of the flames of fire than to suffer the calamity of living among people who are indifferent to the thought of Śauri. By such statements as these, the world-renunciation of the knowers of Brahman is established.

For this very reason, it was stated previously that even approaching a worldly lord is restricted to times of distress. As for what was stated later— that in the *Dakṣasmṛti*, there is no contradiction between the study of the Vedas and yoga— this refers to the following.
One should spend the first and last watches of the night in the study of the Vedas;
for by sleeping during the middle two watches, one becomes fit for union with Brahman.
Thus, in this context, for one incapable of yoga, there is the practice of self-tasting (*svādhyāya*) which is subordinate to it; however, for one capable, there is yoga itself.
Therefore, there is no contradiction between these two scriptural injunctions that prescribe both [paths] as being for the same time. And at the end, Dakṣa has explained yoga in detail;
therein, this is declared to be the essence:
One should dissolve the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), which is entirely free from all desires and afflictions, into Brahman;
for this alone is true meditation and yoga—everything else is merely the prolixity of books.

Thus [it is said]. And Yājñavalkya says: "Having made the mind free from mental fluctuations (*vṛtti*), one should place the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*) in Brahman. "Free from mental fluctuations" means devoid of external mental activity. Therefore, although there is a sequential application in each of the two—Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) and yoga—at times such as evening (*pradoṣa*) and so forth, according to their respective parts, even though there is a difference in the application... [ka kha ga]

There is no contradiction; for according to the method established in the *Śārīraka* (Brahma-sūtras)—namely, "where there is one-pointedness, there [the rule applies], without distinction"—it is appropriate to practice yoga even at other times conducive to one-pointedness, even by suspending one's own duties such as the study of sacred texts (*svādhyāya*) and the like. This applies even during the divisions of the watches of the night and their halves, when one is engaged in the study of sacred texts and so forth.
As for the divisions of *nāḍikās* that are not too far from equal, nor deficient or excessive in their preceding or succeeding parts, these may be resolved as differences of opinion (*matabheda*).
In this manner, other *smṛtis* as well should be harmonized or reconciled.
Therefore, this is the conclusion regarding the necessity of performing [worship] at the five times;

because the service of the Blessed One through those various activities during the five times is ordained as being obligatory, one must also observe the command of the Blessed One according to the rules set forth by Vyāsa, Dakṣa, and others.

Because it has already been demonstrated that the fitness for grasping the most excellent and complete meaning of the scripture as taught in the authoritative treatises follows from the perfection of uninterrupted devotion to the Lord— and because this was also shown by the author of the Bhāṣya, his disciples, and others—

Since it has been taught that the worship of the Blessed One is to be performed in accordance with those who are solely devoted to *prapatti*, and since those qualified for it have practiced it up to the present day according to their capacity, the abandonment of what is not skillful (*anipuṇa*) is not to be disregarded. (The phrase "the abandonment of what is not skillful is not to be disregarded" does not appear in the manuscripts designated as ka, kha, ga, and jha.)

It is observed that by the maxim "as is the character of the master, so is the character of the subjects," one should not abandon the Dharma out of egoism, nor out of agitation, nor out of resentment,
nor for the sake of wealth, nor out of sectarianism, nor from the doctrine of causality, nor out of greed.
I would never, under any circumstances, abandon [the letters] ka, kha, ca, cha, and jha.

Thus speaking, the Blessed One, the delight of Vasudeva, [taught] the Śruti, because one must become equal in character to one’s master, because conduct that accords with the nature of pleasing the master is desired by all, and because such pleasing cannot be directly observed by seekers of liberation— as it cannot be by the eternal ones or the liberated— just as it is for those who have attained release.
"Smṛti is my very command"— according to this statement, and because one determines that He is pleased solely through the Śāstra,

one should rely upon some established limit among the various systems for propitiating the Supreme Self, which are divided according to the different Saṃhitās in the manner explained in passages such as "By whatever [means] he [worships Him]" (BhG 18.66).

Even those who are established in independent practice dwell with some indolence, according to their own capacity and the instructions they have received; yet all of them offer some small gift here while pronouncing blessings.
But here, those who have reached the end of the world become free from desire for blessings, for the sake of infinite victory.
He whose every undertaking here is free from the bond of desire for rewards,
and for whom everything is offered in renunciation— he is the true renouncer, and he is the wise one.

Now, O [O Ka Ca Jha], one should not entreat the Blessed One, for he said "No"; the Blessed One is to be taken as a refuge, but he is never to be entreated. Thus, because they have their own purpose—being free from the request for any other purpose through the manner impelled by *māyā* and so forth according to the secret [teaching]—in all five [cases]:

It is established that one should pass the time fruitfully, without interruption during the [prescribed] periods, through the performance of scriptural service (*śāstrīyakaiṅkarya*) consisting of propitiating the Blessed One,
until the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of the sacrifice known as the *nyāsavidyā*,
which is no different from the time of future liberation.
This is the essential point here: the purpose of practicing the fivefold daily ritual is that it preserves the auspicious thread, garments, and so forth, just as a bride does.
Thus he has entered upon the scriptural path of service to the Lord.
Just as a husband protects his wife by either restraining her from discarding or preserving the auspicious thread and so forth,
so too does he act for us in this case through restraint or enjoyment.
Thus,
having accepted all time here as being for the sake of the Lord’s service according to his command,
how could we, who hold that [service] as most venerable, ever disregard it during the fivefold sequence of its festivals?

Let our view, which distinguishes between the existent and the non-existent, not become an object of ridicule among those who, like fools, are deluded in their vain attempt to attain a hundred by abandoning twenty-five.
[This verse is found before the verse beginning with "kālaṃ sarvam" in the *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *jha* manuscripts;
in those, the reading is "uparundhan"].
Gradually obstructing the mass of internal darkness...

May he, the imperishable sun of the sky of reality, never rise before his time nor set behind it; may he, for the sake of pure beings whose own objects and natural qualities are obscured by the frost of worldly existence, remain present.

Thus ends the section titled "The Establishment of Daily Practice" within the *Śrīpāñcarātrarakṣā*, among the works of the venerable Vedāntācārya Śrī Veṅkaṭanātha, the lion among poets and logicians and the independent master of all philosophical systems.
The second chapter,
titled "The Eternal Exposition"; the third chapter.
He was a knower of the five supreme principles, devoted to the five times;
having conquered the afflictions of the five senses, he felt no fear from the five sources of danger.
Thus this verse is seen at the beginning of the third chapter in the ṅ, cha, and kośa manuscripts.
Now begins the transition to the sequence of daily duties (*nityakartavyakramasaṃkrama*). [In the *saṃcaya* manuscript, it appears as *ka kha jha*; in the *saṃcayakośa*, it reads *saṃ(kramaḥ)cayaḥ*.]
Along the river-path of the tradition beginning with Nātha, Yāmuna, Pūrṇa, and others.
Approaching [the Lord]. Regarding the limbs common to all ritual acts, it has been stated here by the venerable Yāmunācārya in the *Śrīmad-Gītārthasaṃgraha*:
"But the man of knowledge, the supreme exclusive devotee, whose life is dependent on the Supreme..."
She whose single consciousness experiences pleasure and pain solely through union with and separation from Him.

Through the practice of meditation on the Blessed One, through utterances, salutations, praises, and hymns of glory, he attained his true self, with the activities of his life-force, mind, intellect, and senses entirely directed toward Him.

One should perform everything from one's own duties up to the attainment of existence solely out of love, having abandoned the notion of means; indeed, one should fearlessly entrust that [agency] to the Divine.
Thus, this must not be forgotten from the time of awakening until dawn, while all ritual acts and duties are being performed;
it is that which has been declared in the *Samayācāraniyamādhyāya*, the *Śrīvaiṣṇava-dharmaśāstra*, and other texts for those who are supreme monotheists (*paramaikāntin*).

Furthermore, everything that must be specifically performed should be understood exactly as prescribed. In all undertakings of ritual action (*karmārambha*), one should recite the respective mantras taught in the scriptures of the Lord, as well as the additional phrases spoken by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*) such as "the Lord alone," and so forth. At the conclusion, one should recite with the mantras in the sequence beginning with "all [is] governed by me" (*sarvaṃ svaniyāmya*).
This is to be offered to the Blessed One. [The bracketed portion *na caitadakhilamupāsanādhikāryantaraṃ ka kha ga ca jha* is not part of the main text.

Nor should it be mistakenly thought—that is, maintained (*mantavyam kha ga*)—that this entire [work] concerns only those other qualified persons who employ means for worship; for if that were the case...

Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that prohibitions— such as those against consuming the *nirmālya* (remnants of offerings) from the Guru mentioned alongside [the prohibition of meat]—

would apply only to that specific context, thereby resulting in the non-application of such rules in cases like the *alepaka-vāda* (the doctrine of the "undefiled"). This has been explained at length in the previous section and in works such as the *Nikṣeparakṣā*.

Regarding the commencement of duties to be performed during the *brāhma-muhūrta*: therein, for one who is established in the daily observances (*nityānuṣṭhāna*) as taught by the Commentator (*bhāṣyakāra*), whatever is to be done upon the arrival of the *brāhma-muhūrta* and other such times,
that shall now be set forth in accordance with the *Saṃhitā* and other texts which constitute the root of the works of his disciples and grand-disciples.

It is summarized as follows: having rested at the proper time beforehand and enjoyed sleep, one should abandon sleep with vigilance when the final watch of the night has arrived; for it is remembered in such passages as, "But he who sleeps for two watches [of the night] possesses disciplined sleep and wakefulness," and so forth, in those yoga treatises.

Throughout the entire night, one should remain awake for the sake of unimpeded yoga and to avoid disturbances of the senses and other such occurrences that might arise during the period of sleep; this is what is being taught. [That is so in the versions marked ka, kha, ga, and jha.]

[The subject matter] concerns a specific type of person who has attained full health through a state of yoga that is independent of rest. Indeed, the operation of all scriptures—whether concerning obligatory, occasional, or optional matters—proceeds solely in accordance with the respective capacities of such individuals. For this very reason, it is the most preeminent among the means for accomplishing dharma.

Having stated that "Brahmā, remembering the body, [created] the Veda and the Upaveda of the Atharvans for the sake of activity," and thus [referring to] Āyurveda as the Upaveda of the Atharvaveda, [it is said]: "One should rise during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, examining what has been digested and what remains undigested. Having said this, sleeping again until the arrival of dawn is prescribed in the case of indigestion.

[The reading "īdṛśasarvapuruṣaśabdaḥ" is seen only in manuscript G. For it is stated that [this applies] to one who has awakened from a dream that was consistent with reality by means of embracing such a person. Therefore, for all human beings, the times for sleep and awakening are generally and ordinarily two watches (yāma) each.
The determination of the subject matter is taught by the words beginning with "lying down" (śayānaḥ) and so forth. Awakening during the *brāhma-muhūrta* and its fruit:
thus, having dispelled the darkness of sleep at the appropriate time, one becomes established in *sattva* and possesses a serene intellect.

By that [recollection], the object of meditation— which was previously contemplated, situated upon the variegated wall of the internal organ, and distinguished by various auspicious supports— though obscured by the darkness of sleep,
is revealed through the light of the lamp of sattvic knowledge, which is kindled by the essence (sattva) awakened at that moment.
Having observed correctly [it is observed],
then that very yoga of the latter part of the night is accomplished, which is explained as being to be performed among the Sāttvatas and others even before the *brāhmamuhūrta*.
Then, having risen at midnight, with sleep and fatigue overcome,
he should perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) using the very water contained in his water-pot (kamaṇḍalu);
having paid homage to his gurus and the deity, he should sit down upon a seat of antelope skin.
By such statements as these, this rule regarding the time for yoga is established for those devoted to this *saṃhitā*. [This rule regarding the time (is found in versions k, kha, ga, jha):

It is prescribed for times when there is no sound and during the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), due to the possibility of an excellence of one-pointed concentration (*aikāgrya*). Furthermore, it has been stated that there is no contradiction in the injunctions for these respective times, as they follow the specific capacities and other factors of the individual practitioner (*puruṣa*).
In this regard: having finished sleeping and performed the sipping of water (ācamana) and other rites, one should carry a Vaiṣṇava staff and a water-pot containing water.
The sacred thread, the Veda, and two auspicious golden earrings.

By the words "with water" (*idya*) and so forth, it is indicated that even for a yogi of the Blessed One, the carrying of a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) and other such practices taught by Manu and others are not set aside; thus, it is said "by one who has [water] situated in a water-pot.
This is because [the water] serves as the cause for the end of sleep and as an auxiliary to the subsequent ritual action.

And here, the ritual rinsing (ācamana) is performed according to the general rule (tantra). By the word "but" (tu), the specific rule taught in one's own scripture is indicated; furthermore, it implies that in the absence of water, one should touch the right ear. For they remember:
In the event of being unable to perform the proper sipping of water (ācamana), or when water is unavailable— or even when one is capable but no water is present—
and upon the aforementioned occasions, one should touch the right ear.
Thus [it is said]. Here, everything except for the fourfold mantra and so forth is common even to those established in other *saṃhitās*.

Regarding the phrase "on a seat of antelope skin" (*ajināsane*), the mention of the principal elements is "a cloth, an antelope skin, and kuśa grass on top," as sung [in the tradition]. Thereafter, one should remain or sit according to one's own preference.
By the phrase "by means of the lotus posture and so forth," mastery over the postures is prescribed.
As for the yoga of the latter part of the night,
it is described by the passage beginning with, "holding the body, head, and neck straight, motionless and steady," and so on.

The song required for the ten [stages] is also taught here in its entirety with specific detail— [beginning from "keeping the body, head, and neck straight" up to "it is taught"]— which is not seen elsewhere in the Gha and Ṅa manuscripts.
Keeping the body, head, and neck straight together with the chest.
The gaze should be directed toward the tip of the nose, characterized by slightly closed eyes.
The tongue should rest against the palate, and the row of teeth should remain slightly apart;
the two lips should be held slightly closed, and the two elbows should be kept [firmly] on the thighs.
One should place the two hands in the region between the thighs, below the navel,
in the manner of upper and lower, sequentially on the left and right.
Having thus firmly secured the motionless body with the yoga-band,
one should indeed contract that very [body] from the lower region upwards.
Having expanded [the mind] by means of that which is devoid of color, heart-like, and of unperceivable form— namely, the letters *gha*,
*ṅ*, *cha*— one should gradually withdraw the mind that has entered into the objects of the senses.
One should indeed cause [the mind] to be absorbed in the intellect, and that [intellect] one should place within its own domain;
having concentrated the self by means of the self together with the mantras, then in due order.
Thus, the justification for the cultivation of identity-in-yoga is that,
furthermore, the cultivation of identity-in-yoga is taught here in the state of yoga:

Then, having turned back with the intellect and with a mind non-different from that [object], one should contemplate Aniruddha, the Lord of Mantras, who abides in the state of waking, for a hundred times.
Through the power of reciting that mantra and by being bound to the state of identity with it,
his greatness arises along with full realization.
Through practice, at the end of a year, he becomes endowed with that non-duality;
then, having recited the Pradyumna mantra two hundred times, he should turn it back.
"Whoever this is, that am I; indeed, by means of this very non-duality, through such constant practice, the wise man becomes one whose doubts are severed."
And by its power, through that very time, it is born;
indeed, by this sequential yoga accompanied by recitation and meditation.
One should employ the entire multitude of mantras previously mentioned,
as long as the Blessed One remains manifest in the location characterized by the aforementioned features.
Though his form is dissolved and he is stainless, he is infinite; though a treasury of splendors, he is a mass of consciousness and bliss; though peaceful, he is incomparable and indeed undisturbed.
Having composed oneself by means of the self and having abandoned the act of recitation therein,
one should remain until, through the non-differentiation of the meditator and the object of meditation, one attains absorption in that [reality].
When, through practice, the yogi attains stability in a concentration free from all objects of perception, he then becomes one with Brahman, O Blessed One.

Thus, in this context, identity of essential nature and so forth is not intended; for, according to the method established in the *Śārīraka*, the relationship between the body and the embodied—the individual soul (*jīvātman*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—is non-contradictory, free from defects such as those concerning defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), in harmony with all the scriptures, and supported by favorable reasoning. Indeed, because He abides within that [body], they perceive Him as one.

Because what is intended is Viśiṣṭādvaita— which is well-established by hundreds of corroborative texts such as "The virtuous [are virtuous because they consist of That]," which is formulated in the Sūtra by Kāśakṛtsna as "because of the state of abiding" (sūtra 1.4.22), and which is consistent with the internal harmony of the preceding and following portions of the scripture.

By the passage beginning with "through the non-distinction of the meditator and the object of meditation," the state of non-conceptual samādhi is described. Furthermore, by the statement "then one attains Brahman," the fruit in the form of supreme identity is set forth. And regarding such statements as "one becomes Brahman itself," the Commentators have stated that the designation of identity is used when there is unity of nature.

It is just as in the case of the primary [identity], namely, "this is that very cow. Otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the Śruti and Smṛti texts: "He attains the stainless supreme equality" and "Having attained my own nature. Likewise, another Śruti says:
"As pure water poured into pure water becomes exactly like it, even so the self of the sage who knows becomes [one]."

"He becomes Gautama. Furthermore, the designation "he himself" is seen in the Śruti even in cases of identity, as in: "One who is contending should sacrifice a dwarf dedicated to Viṣṇu; having become Viṣṇu himself, he conquers these worlds. This being so, his greatness, together with that consciousness, arises as belonging to him.

Thus, there is consistency with the relevant textual passages beginning with these words. Furthermore, in the *Śārīraka* [Brahmasūtra], in the section on the fruit (*phalādhikaraṇa*), it is established by the sūtra "jagadvyāpāravarjam" that for the liberated one whose true nature has become manifest and who is endowed with the eight qualities, there is equality only in respect to experience, excluding the activity of governing the world.

"Because of the context, because of being non-proximate, and because of the indicative mark of similarity in experience alone. Therefore, what is intended here is precisely the contemplation of the specific identity, both in the state of the means and in the state of the fruit.
By this, after performing the placement of the sectarian marks (*lāñchana-nyāsa*) and so forth, and having formed the mudrā, one should contemplate the visualization (*dhyāna*). (ka kha)

"One should remember the God and contemplate, 'I am the God'"; thus even the opening verse of the *Samārādhanāgrantha* (or *Samārādhanagrantha*) is completed. Having bound the *mudrās* beginning with the *mūla-mudrā*, one should contemplate, "I am the God."
The passage beginning with *samārādhana* and ending with *bhāvayet* is absent from the Ka, Kha, Ga, Ca, and Jha manuscripts.

In such cases, the status as a rule of vision (*dṛṣṭividhi*) is very clear due to the presence of the particle *iti* and similar markers. For this very reason, it is stated that even by means of such a meditation, there is merely the subsequent production of fitness (*yogyatā*).
Through the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the mantras of the deities and by meditating on identity with the deity,
the practitioner becomes worthy of worship by making his limbs non-material (aprākṛta).
Thus it is said: otherwise, one should worship the Self in the form of the deity with water-offerings and incense;
by means of making the limbs non-ordinary, the practitioner becomes worthy of worship.
Thus [it is said]. Otherwise, one should worship the Self in the form of the deity with water-offerings and incense;
having meditated upon Nārāyaṇa within the heart, one should worship Him with enjoyments beginning with incense and ending with those [final offerings].

Regarding the nature of Yoga, how can the *Śāṇḍilya-smṛti* and Śrī Kṛṣṇa Muni be reconciled with what must immediately follow? For in the contemplation of identity of essence (*svarūpa-aikya-bhāvanā*), there could be no further meditation on Nārāyaṇa within the heart. Nor [is it possible] for one who is engaged in the remaining duties (*śeṣa-vṛtti*).
The contemplation of identity with its own essential nature (svarūpa) is not possible. Therefore, the position that this is an injunction for a meditative vision (dṛṣṭividhi) must be accepted here.

Alternatively, since another interpretation is possible, it is not appropriate to intend an injunction for a meditative vision; thus, the designation [of Brahman] as "all" follows from its being the body of all, its being dependent on them, and so forth. And with that intention...

The author of the Commentary will state [this] in the passage beginning with "svaniyāmya" (governed by oneself). Furthermore, it was established in the preceding section (*pūrvādhikāra*) by means of a statement from the *Śāṇḍilya-smṛti* that, in Yoga, there is simply the contemplation of the relationship between the Supreme Self and the individual self (*pratyagātman*), which possess distinct characteristics. And it has been stated in the *Sāttvata* [Purāṇa] in a scattered manner:

Having summarized this constantly at the end, [the author states]: "The notion that the identity of nature (svarūpaikyam) and so forth [of the individual soul with Brahman] is non-Vedic, and the view that the singular,
conscious [Self] alone is the agent which bears fruit— these two views arise from a lack of faith in the authority of the Vedas."
Being pleased, he pleases him; you are not merely a follower of the Brahmin.

permission for rest is granted in the midst of yoga practice;
in this way, when exhaustion is likely to arise from yoga performed according to the rules, [one may rest] during the Brāhma-muhūrta.
