(Variant readings: *samāsīta śayānaśca*; *samāste śayanasthaśca*; *samapte śayanasthaśca*).
And [the time for] *ca* and *cha* is until the end of the night.
Thus,
regarding the specific duties to be performed during the *brāhmamuhūrta* and the chanting of Hari's names therein—
[as found in versions *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *jha*]— concerning these specific duties beginning from the *brāhmamuhūrta*:
Only a mere indication of what must be done has been shown:
"When the Brāhma-muhūrta has arrived, having risen from bed and bathed, one should worship the Lord of the World and perform the offering of sacrificial fuel."

Thus, and so forth. This has been explained in detail in other *saṃhitās*. Here, one should rise while repeatedly chanting "Hari, Hari, Hari" and meditating upon Hari alone. Regarding this, the chanting of the word "Hari" seven times is prescribed by the venerable sage Gṛdhrasaras in the *Nityakramasaṃgraha* (or *Nityakarmasaṃgraha*).
And [this is] established [in scripture]. Regarding the recollection of the Blessed One preceded by the word "Hari" upon rising, it was stated by the venerable Śaunaka in the *Śrīviṣṇudharma*:
"While rising, think of Hari; while walking, think of Keśava."
While eating, contemplate Govinda; while sleeping, contemplate Mādhava.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, the remembrance of Hari at the beginning and end of all undertakings has been stated by him [the author] himself in his own sūtra:

"One should constantly remember Hari alone, both before and after the performance of ritual acts. And that Hari is to be remembered immediately after sleep, as he is the son of Dharma and the gods, being Nara, Nārāyaṇa, Hari, and likewise Kṛṣṇa.

According to the tradition, among the incarnations of the Blessed One that are to be remembered as being of the nature of the deities of the Dharma, he is the third; and he is the liberator of Gajendra—
rushing along after mounting Tārkṣya while the lordly elephant was crying out, seized by a crocodile.
May this Hari protect us from the accumulation of our sins— he whose ornaments, garments, and garlands are tossed about, whose voice is as deep as a thundercloud,
and who displays in his hands the discus, arrow, sword, the gesture of fearlessness, the conch, the bow, the mace, and the Kaumodakī.

Thus [it is said]. Indeed, He is meditated upon as the liberator of the lordly elephant (Gajendra) who was seized by the crocodile of darkness, and as the liberator of the multitude of living beings seized by the crocodile of insurmountable darkness in the form of deep sleep (suṣupti). With reference to Him alone, the three verses beginning with "I remember in the morning" (*prātaḥ smarāmi*), which are to be recited by the followers of the Purāṇas at dawn, [are composed].

It is recited by all. And in the description of its fruit, the Blessed One is indicated by the word "Hari": "He who, having risen in the morning, recites these three meritorious verses—to him Hari, the teacher of the three worlds, shall grant his own state."

Thus: [The word *hari* means "he who takes away" (*harati*) all that is undesirable—whether that which is evil in the form of its transformation (*vikāra*), or that which is evil in the form of its maturation (*vipāka*). He [takes away] Brahmā, Indra, Rudra, Yama, and Varuṇa as well.
Because he seizes [all things] by force, therefore he is called Hari.

By such passages as these, one should contemplate the absolute sovereignty (*niraṅkuśasvātantrya*) of that very [Lord], who performs the play of the arising, maintenance, and dissolution of the entire universe. Having thus arisen, the primary act is the rinsing of the mouth (*ācamana*) at the end of sleep, or alternatively, the touching of the right ear.

At that time, having prepared himself, sitting upon that very same bed, he should practice the application of yoga according to the sequence of the four stages mentioned in the Yoga-śāstra— namely, *yatamāna*, *vyatireka*, and *ekendriyavaśīkāra*— by means of the stage of *vyatireka-saṃjñā*, which constitutes the second state.

With his senses restrained and composed, for the sake of reflecting upon the specific states of the past and future and for examining what has been done and what remains to be done, he should observe that infinite time has passed in vain and attain supreme world-weariness (*nirveda*). The various forms of this world-weariness are to be understood from the specific details found in the respective *Saṃhitās*.
This has been summarized by the sages of the Nārāyaṇa lineage:
"Rising during the *brāhma-muhūrta*, established in goodness (*sattva*), uttering 'Hari,
Hari,' and remaining seated there with a concentrated mind."
Having seen that time has passed in vain, I am now disillusioned with this world.
Thus it has been stated in detail by the lords of the Vaṅgivaṃśa:
"When the Brāhma-muhūrta has arrived, having abandoned sleep with a tranquil mind, a Vaiṣṇava man should indeed utter: 'Hari, Hari!'"
Rising from that bed and sitting down with his senses restrained,
he felt terror and despondency in his heart, seeing that his life had passed away in vain.

With these and other verses ending with "To whom shall I describe this difficult-to-cross, wretched state?"—in twenty-one verses—[the author describes the world]. Although [it is said]: "A Brahmin, having examined the worlds acquired through karma, should attain detachment; there is nothing uncreated that can be gained by what is created. For the sake of realizing That, he..."

Regarding the instruction "one should approach the guru," although at the very time of the initial approach to the guru he had already treated the enjoyments of Hiranyagarbha and other such states as mere straw and had become fully possessed of world-weariness (*nirveda*), nevertheless, due to being bound by *prakṛti*— which is the substratum of the three *guṇas* characterized by various specific ripenings— he remained [in that state].
In order to avoid defects such as attachment to objects that have been esteemed, one must maintain that very same kind of detachment (*nirveda*).
Its necessity for constant maintenance was sung among the group of qualities beginning with humility (*amānitva*):
"the perception of the evils of birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering. Therefore, even for one who has perfected the means...

Just as in the case of Parāṅkuśa, Parakāla, and others, one must cultivate detachment from worldly existence by observing the continuous flow of adverse conditions— such as sleep and other states consisting primarily of *rajas* and *tamas*, which are most fit to be abandoned because they obstruct the experience of the Blessed One; therefore, on every day, at appropriate times, one must indeed practice world-weariness (*nirveda*).
Since it is thus established that one must rely upon *sāttvika* fortitude (*dhṛti*),

it is stated immediately thereafter to avoid the following consequence: namely, that due to despondency— which is the opposite of the non-despondency inherent in any one of the seven factors beginning with discrimination and renunciation— there would be a failure to accomplish the subsequent service.
Thus having become disillusioned, and thereafter having taken recourse to sattvic fortitude,
he restrained this disillusionment which causes the cessation of all activity.

By these and other such statements, there is first the pacification of remorse—which is like the desire to build a dam across water that has already flowed away—followed by the determination to perform service during future times as far as possible, which consists in relying upon *sāttvika* fortitude (*dhṛti*).
And the nature of *sāttvika* fortitude is as follows: [cedaṃ ka kha ga ṅ ca cha jha]...

The Blessed One sang: "That fortitude by which one sustains the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses through unwavering yoga— that fortitude, O Pārtha, is of the nature of goodness (sāttvikī)."
Thus,
this mode of sattvic fortitude is itself a mode of determination, comprised through the discernment of duties appropriate to that particular occasion.
From now on, for as long as I live, I shall strive with a concentrated mind to perform worship at the feet of Śrī, again and again.
Having approached Hari in the morning, he thereafter acquired ritual materials,
worshipped the God, and then likewise recited the mantras.
Even while meditating upon the Supreme Lord during the five prescribed times,
he should always abide in this manner according to the path of the five-fold ritual (pāñcakālika).
Worshipping Hari with devotion using auspicious perfumes, flowers, and other offerings acquired by my own efforts according to my capacity, I shall pass my days.

Thus [it is said]. Here, from this point forward, words such as "for as long as life lasts" (*yāvajjīvam*) and "always" (*sadā*) are naturally flowing on the very day the service (*kaiṅkarya*) begins; they continue throughout subsequent days as objects of detachment (*nirveda*), for the sake of accomplishing the increase of unconditioned service toward those internal obstacles which oppose devotion to the Lord.
For the sake of attaining the excellence characterized by the complete cessation of those specific defects designated by terms such as the eighteen *caṇḍālas* and the six *vṛṣalas*,
[one should practice] that which removes the wisdom of even the wise, [which is] exceedingly powerful... [in the *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *jha* manuscripts].

And this is for the purpose of avoiding the interruption of service (*kaṅkairyaviccheda*)— [the term *kaikarya* is glossed as *mūlabhūtapākṣika* with the variant readings *gha ṅ cha* and *ka kha ga ca jha*]— which might otherwise arise from the partiality (*pākṣika*) rooted in the sense objects, faculties, and so forth,
by one who is acting for the very first time in this manner.
While thus engaged, one must likewise act in accordance with one's heart's desire; for this very reason, even by the sages Nārāyaṇa it was said:
"The sequence of the method for the service of the Lord’s lotus feet..."
We declare that this must be constantly practiced by those who are single-mindedly devoted.
Thus, having introduced the subject of what must be performed daily, it is said:
"Seeing that time has passed in vain, I shall henceforth become disillusioned;
I shall propitiate, meditate upon, and worship Puruṣottama."
"I shall proclaim his praises, I shall bow to him, I shall contemplate him without ceasing,
and I shall go to him for refuge"— having thus resolved within my own mind.
Regarding the statement "the five-fold duties are themselves the primary purpose":

here, by the phrase "I shall pass my days there," it is shown that for the devoted monotheist (*paramaikāntin*) under discussion, it is impossible to pass the time in any other manner; thus, his service is uninterrupted.
The fact that it is its own purpose is revealed; for that very point was explicitly stated by the sages Nārāyaṇa:
"What indeed is not achievable by men devoted to the worship of the Lord?
This [devotion] is especially the purpose of the Vaiṣṇavas themselves."
Thus,
that which is remembered here as the contemplation of dharma and artha, as well as the contemplation of bodily exertion which serves as their means,
consists therein of dharma in the form of service (kaiṅkarya), and artha as that which is subordinate to it.

[The contemplation of bodily exertion as a remainder of dharma in the form of service (kaiṃkarya): For the sake of discerning between the heavy and the light [tasks] among those two, one should contemplate physical hardship. In that regard, one should not render the forenoon, midday, and afternoon fruitless, according to one's ability.

From the statements such as "among dharma, artha, and kāma, one should have dharma as the foremost," it follows that even the portion of activity directed toward kāma as a means— provided it is not contrary to dharma— is present among living beings as a form of kāma.

O bull among the Bharatas— having been thus addressed, the householder is entrusted to the side of service, as his desire for worldly objects is limited solely to the purpose of producing progeny and so forth according to the scriptures.
This is a prayer for the accomplishment of service free from obstacles.
[Regarding the meaning of *ka kha ga jha*]:

Out of fear that "this attainment of the great bliss of service (*aikarīya-mahānanda*), which possesses its own purpose as the sprout of liberation (*apavarga-aṅkura-bhūta*), will be obstructed by ten thousand obstacles even for men devoted to Govinda— how can this come to pass?"— so [it was said].
Immediately thereafter, the removal of obstacles is prayed for (or stated):
"My previous karmas—
countless, indestructible, beginningless, and impure— are opposed to this action."
Having prayed, "May the Lord, by his own grace, fulfill our desires even after destroying them," one should recite this mantra.

Thus, this prayer-mantra beginning with "This one desires to worship you," and so forth, should be learned from the presence of the teacher according to the prescribed rule and employed here daily. For such indeed is the proper application of all mantras. Otherwise, there is fruitlessness as well as the incurrence of faults both seen and unseen.
In various treatises it is recited:
"A mantra heard by chance, or through concealment or deception, or one seen on a leaf, shall be useless; on the contrary, it will bring about misfortune."
Thus [it is said]. Elsewhere, the reading of the fourth quarter of this very verse is: "one should mutter it if it causes harm.

Furthermore, the accomplishment of such unimpeded service is achieved through meditation on Hari preceded by surrender (*prapatti*) to the lineage of gurus, for the sake of attaining unimpeded service.
For those who have truly cultivated their selves, the Blessed One, by his mere will,
sprinkles them with nectar throughout the entire period until the conclusion of their vow.
Thinking, "In the manner described by the Śrīsāttvata and others, the temple of the Blessed One itself shall come into being," and for the sake of its accomplishment,
the meditation on Hari alone is first prescribed— having thus prayed with the words, "For its accomplishment, one should first recollect Hari," and so forth.
In this context, this meditation is intended to be preceded by taking refuge in the lineage of gurus;
for it is stated at that point in the *Nityāntara*: "Having first taken refuge in those gurus, and then in Hari.
And it is said in the *Śrīsāttvata* at the commencement of the yoga of the latter part of the night: "Having paid homage to the gurus and the Lord, one should sit upon a deerskin seat."

And so forth. In every undertaking of scriptural rites, the presentation of the lineage of gurus culminating in the Blessed Lord leads to the highest good (*niḥśreyasa*). And it is said in the *Rahasyāmnāyabrāhmaṇa*: "That lineage of teachers must be known, beginning from the Blessed Lord down to one's own teacher. Devotion to the divine and the guru alone [is the means].

It is heard in the Kaṭhavallī that the cause for the illumination of all the tantras is as follows: "For that great-souled one who has supreme devotion to the Divine, and who regards the Guru as he does the Divine, these meanings that have been declared truly shine forth."
Thus it is said; and it is also recorded by Āpastamba and others that "one should serve the teacher as if he were a god," and so forth. This refers to meditation (*dhyāna*) as a limb of yoga.
Thus, for the fulfillment of one's desires, having approached the Lord preceded by service to the Guru,

one should practice meditation— collecting from the Lord’s scriptures, their commentaries, the Nityagadya, the Stotra, and other sources, whatever has been stated in a scattered manner— as far as it can be understood, according to the principle set forth in the fourth chapter on the "Combination of Attributes" (*guṇopasaṃhāra*).

All common and uncommon characteristics regarding the form of the object of meditation and so forth are to be understood according to the specific details of their respective *saṃhitās* and other texts;
this includes the chanting of the names of the *vyūhas* and others, preceded by the *praṇava*.
Having thus meditated upon the Blessed One in his complete form,
one should then [recite] the fourfold names of the Vāsudeva and other manifestations (*vyūha*), the various names of the Keśava and other secondary manifestations,
the names of the ten incarnations (*avatāra*) beginning with the Fish, and whatever other distinct names have been learned.
One should recite aloud, with a voice that produces great joy, the names of the Goddesses and others arranged in hymns of praise.

One should mutter the mantra of the Blessed One as prescribed for that time, as well as the appropriate Vedic study [prescribed for that time]. One should also perform the kindling of the sacred fire as prescribed for that time.

One should perform, according to one's capacity, the recitation of the Lord’s mantras and the study of the Vedas as prompted by that specific time—namely, the appropriate recitation of the Lord’s mantras and the study of the Vedas as enjoined for that time (kha, ga; tatkālacoditaṃ samucitabhagavanmantrajapaṃ vedābhyāsaṃ ca gha, ca, jha; tatkāle coditaṃ ṅ, cha)—and therein, the chanting of the names beginning with Vāsudeva and ending with Kalki.
The *Pārameśvara* states that [the practice] consists of mantras preceded by the *praṇava*:
"Having fully awakened at dawn, one who remains upon the bed should rise and diligently perform the recitation of the sixteen names."
Oṃ, salutations to Vāsudeva; salutations to you, Saṃkarṣaṇa!
May there be salutations to you, Pradyumna; salutations to you, Aniruddha!
Gradually, O twice-born one, [from] Keśava up to Dāmodara: "Salutations again and again to Keśava, and salutations to Nārāyaṇa."
Salutation indeed to Mādhava, and then salutation to Govinda;
one should then offer salutation to Viṣṇu, and "Salutation to you, O Madhusūdana."
Salutations to Trivikrama, and then salutations to Vāmana;
salutations to Śrīdhara, and then salutations to you, Hṛṣīkeśa.
Salutations to Padmanābha, and salutations to Dāmodara;
now follows the glorification of the ten divine incarnations.
For the Lord, however, the sequence beginning with Ekaśṛṅga and the others has been prescribed;
"Salutations to You in the form of the Fish, and salutations thereafter to the Tortoise."
Salutations be to the primordial Varāha; salutations to you, the Nārasiṃha.
Salutations to the one in the form of Vāmana, and salutations to the three Rāmas as well.
"Obeisance to Kṛṣṇa, the Creator, whose weapons are the axe, the bowstring, and the plough;
O twice-born one, obeisance to you, O Viṣṇu Kalki—may all this be accompanied by the Praṇava."
One should pay homage to these manifestations of the all-pervading Lord Hari in their established order:
at dawn, and at the end of the yoga practice when the day comes to a close.
Then, with a voice raised even higher, which caused great delight, he uttered other hymns and mantras— indeed, all the manuscripts show "mantrāṇi" ending in the neuter gender.

Thus it is said. And this has been summarized by the lords of the Vaṅgi dynasty: "One desiring to perform a desired rite should recite its names, while self-restrained, together with the four names beginning with Vāsudeva."
One should devoutly recite the twelve names beginning with Keśava,
as well as the names of the ten incarnations beginning with Matsya and Kūrma; rising from bed while reciting these, one should always worship Hari.
Thus ends the sequence of rites to be performed prior to the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā), which,
when recited in a loud voice, removes all sins even for those who merely hear it.
With a mind gladdened by the chanting of Hari’s names which removes evil deeds,
he desired to go to worship the Blessed One— who, because He unites all beings when the twilight is near, is celebrated as "Sandhyā" (the Junction)— in His capacity as the Unifier.
O high-minded one, rising from his bed while uttering "Hari, where is Hari?",
he should place his left foot upon the ground, saying, "Salutation to the Mountain."

Thus, meditating upon Mahāvarāha as the supporter of the earth, one should place the left foot upon the ground with the mantra beginning with "namaḥ" and ending with "kṣitidhara," as recited in the *Pārameśvara* and other scriptures.
Then, regarding the mantra for the earth-supporter, it is said that the very same mantra applies to placing the left foot on the ground. In that regard:

They have explained it by means of the specific term: "One should place the left foot on the ground with the Śrīmad-Vārāha mantra, in order to dispel the suspicion that it might be another form such as the Tortoise (Kūrma) due to its similarity to supporting the earth. Furthermore, the treading upon the earth by the Great Boar (Mahāvarāha) and his consort is taught here along with the mantras in the Mahābhārata and other texts: "Homage be..."

"O Goddess Vasundharā, [I offer this] to you, Priyadattā. The glorification of the Earth as "Priyadattā" is remembered as a cause for non-depression, just like the glorification of Viṣṇu as "Brahmaṇyadeva":
"By singing 'Priyadattā on earth'—she who is indeed all-enduring—"
Chanting "O Viṣṇu, O God who is kind to Brahmins," one does not perish.
Thus it is said.

Then, performing the *padakrama* (the step-by-step recitation), one should meditate upon Viṣṇu as Trivikrama—the presiding deity of the organ of the feet—while reciting the *viṣṇukramaṇa* mantra. At the time of taking a step, one should recite: "In the stride, Viṣṇu; in strength, Hari."

Because it is stated that Viṣṇu is to be meditated upon, and because such meditation depends upon the appropriate scriptural means for its illumination, this concludes the sequence of duties to be performed prior to the *saṃdhyā* prayers.
[Now follows] the departure for bathing and the visualization of the sacred place (*deśa-dhyāna*).

Then, having gathered all the requisites for bathing—such as *darbha* grass, sesame seeds, and cloth—which serve both visible and invisible purposes, one should clear the exit path so that malevolent beings hidden in the darkness may flee. As it is stated in the *Pārameśvara*: "Having cleared the exit path outside," and so forth. Then...
As it is stated in the *Smṛti*: "Leaving the house, one should meditate upon Keśava; while walking, one should think of Keśava.

By the word *keśa*, the rays are meant—those rays which shine forth, as described in such passages as "the splendor born of the sun"; because he possesses those [rays], he is called Keśava. This is for the purpose of illuminating the path and so forth for one who is traveling.
In order to dispel the inner darkness such as delusion regarding the directions and so forth, [the Lord said]:
"Ka" is the name of Brahman; I am the Lord of all embodied beings.
Since we two have arisen from your body, therefore we possess the name of the place.
Thus, because he is the cause of the creation and protection of the universe— exemplified by Brahmā and Rudra—

and because his nature is the subduing of all the wicked— exemplified by the slaying of Keśin— and also for the sake of providing assistance during states of helplessness, one should contemplate him at that time.
Then, for the procedure of purification from the discharge of feces and urine,

he should go outside his own hermitage or dwelling toward the southwest direction; having traversed a distance measured by two bows and five arrows, and having set down his bathing requisites in a clean spot, he should proceed.

Having discharged urine and feces according to the aforementioned rules, one should perform purification (*śauca*)— which removes the odor and stains, is free from the pain of hemorrhoids and other ailments, and is governed by rules regarding the number, color, and size of the clay— appropriate to one's own caste, stage of life (*āśrama*), and condition, for the sake of an unseen merit (*adṛṣṭārtha*). In this regard:

When either urine or feces is discharged, purification is required for that one alone. When both are discharged sequentially, purification follows their respective order. When both are discharged simultaneously, the extraction of the rule is that purification of the feces must come first.

In that same *Pādma[-tantra]*— [in the sections marked ka, kha, ga, ca, jha]— after describing the manner of voiding excrement and urine with the passage beginning "the sacred thread [should be placed] at the level of the ear, and for the sake of knowledge, with grass and so forth," the rule for purification is stated immediately thereafter [in the sections marked ka, ca, jha]:
Then, having grasped the penis with the left hand,
one should rise from the water reservoir with a clod of earth in the right hand.
Having gone toward the northeast or the north, one should perform purification;
the anus with twelve applications of clay, and the penis with six.
Washing the left hand with water at various intervals,
one should wash both hands twelve times at the end of those [intervals].
Having washed the hands, shanks, waist, and thighs with water,
one should cleanse each part with four measures of clay.

Thus [it is said]. But the Grandfather spoke thus to Sanatkumāra: "Then, having risen before [the sun], one should go out toward the east, or toward the north, or toward the northeast—a direction suitable for the practice of purification."
Having gone to a place where there is abundant water, one should perform purification.
Thus they record that purity varies according to place and other factors:
"Place, time, as well as knowledge, the self, the substance, and the purpose of the substance."
Having understood the origin and the state [of the body], one should practice purification.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, the gradations of purity according to the division of day and so forth are recorded in the Smṛti: "Whatever purity is prescribed for the daytime, at night it shall be half of that;
on a journey, it is declared to be a quarter of that; and for one who is ill, it is according to his capacity."
Thus it is said. However, in the *Pārameśvara*, the number of clods of earth and other details are also stated according to the distinctions of seasons such as the rainy season:

"One who has not touched a sacred bathing place [should perform purification, etc., for the sake of purity]. (Note: The variant readings indicate that the phrase *śaucārtham* is preferred over *śaucādyam*).
One should untiringly perform purification that removes both odor and bodily smears.
Three applications of clay should be made to the penis, with one application of clay at intervals;
five should be applied to the left hand, and three to both hands for the sake of purification.
This is the purification after voiding urine; it is the same for excrement as well.
It is taught that the first application of earth should be the size of a handful.
The second and the third are proclaimed to be half of that [each];
above that, they are proclaimed to be the size of a cat's paw.
There should be five applications of clay for the anus, and likewise five for the intervening parts;
ten should be applied to the left hand, and seven to both hands together.
The purification of the feet is performed with three applications, and the purification of the calves with five;
then, O Brahmin, the wise man should apply seven applications of clay to the hips.
This is prescribed for devotees and those learned in the Vedas during the rainy season: to destroy the defects of sweat from one's own body and to alleviate the external mud.
Therefore, during the rains as described, there is indeed a single removal of impurity;
however, those devoted to ritual action must always perform it during autumn, summer, and spring.
From this [sequence: *eka-smāt ka kha ga ca jha*], each single letter is to be omitted [except for *gha*, which is to be preserved from the treasury (*kośa*) elsewhere];
however, the earth [is to be taken] by Brahmins learned in the Vedas (*śrotriya*) who abide in self-restraint during the winter and early spring [the sequence being: *vipra gha ṅ cha*].
One should perform purification on the path according to the requirements of place and time;
by thus removing all odor and residue, one becomes pure through the purity of the mind.
For the washing of the feet of the four classes of eminent twice-borns, earth equal to the size of a cat's paw is prescribed; then, three, two, and one [handfuls] respectively.
For those of the castes ending with the Śūdra, for the purification of the hips,
it is likewise seven [times] with both hands, and again three times.
The general method for washing the hands is declared to be common to all:
having placed both arms so that they fall between the knees, O best of the twice-born.
Having rendered the water held in the hollow of the hands perfectly pure and free from bubbles and other impurities, the Brāhmaṇa should then drink it while reciting the *Hṛdaya-mantra*.
The wise person should decrease the quantity of water by one measure for each of the three castes in succession; then, with hands already washed, he should sip water once more.
Thus, the methods for sipping water (ācamana) and cleansing the teeth (dantadhāvana),
as well as the various modes of performing ācamana, have been set forth in the Dharmaśāstras and the scriptures of the Blessed One.

In that regard, one should perform the ritual rinsing (*ācamana*) as prescribed in one's own scripture or otherwise according to one's realization— or according to one's capacity for realization— as the case may be. Immediately following the mention of the ritual rinsing, the method for cleansing the teeth and purifying the mouth is stated in the *Pārameśvara*:
Having thus washed according to the rule and sipped water, being self-restrained and pure,
he should then sit upon a seat facing either the east or the north.
One should perform the cleansing of the teeth with *arka* and other plants, including *apāmārga*, having taken them in the morning; they should have soft tips and be astringent, pungent, or bitter.
One should chew a tooth-stick that measures twelve finger-breadths in length, is free from crooks or knots, and does not injure the gums.
O Brahmin, when tooth-sticks are unavailable or during illness, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with water and the index finger twelve times.
They should be sixteen finger-breadths long, free from bends or knots,
and made either of gold and other precious metals, or likewise of kuśa grass, darbha grass, and so forth.
A Brahmin should perform the scraping of the tongue, as well as gargling and rinsing the mouth, and then perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana) with pure and clean water.
Thus it is said.
Regarding the phrase "by the *arka* and others" mentioned therein, it is explained in that very same place:
"The *arka*, *nyagrodha*, *khadira*, *karañja*, *kakubha*, and so forth."
And [he should offer] autumnal figs, holy figs, Plakṣa, and Darbha grass, as well as items made of bamboo.
One should collect mango sprouts, apāmārga, arjuna, dhātakī, and śamī, as well as other pure substances that are available among them.
Thus, here the mention of chewing even wood— which is otherwise not to be eaten—

is for the purpose of obtaining the preliminary and concluding acts such as sipping water (ācamana), just as in the case of eating food. In the Padma Purāṇa as well, the cleaning of the teeth is described in this same manner:
Having sipped water and turned toward the east, one should perform the cleansing of the teeth with a twig from the Nyagrodha,
Udumbara, Aśvattha, Plakṣa, Āmra, Arjuna, or Dhātakī trees.
O Lotus-seated One, palāśa, veṇu, khadira, śamī, and dāru are prescribed for cleansing;
these eleven are declared to be the best among all woods.
The tooth-cleansing stick should be twelve finger-breadths in length;
this is declared to be the rule for Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas respectively.

Thus: here, [in all cases where *gha*, *ṅ*, and *cha* are prohibited] there is the avoidance of all that is prohibited; and [in all cases where *gha*, *ṅ*, and *cha* are prescribed] there is the adoption of all that is prescribed.
The essential point is that when there is no other way, those [sounds] which are prescribed in some instances and prohibited in others may be employed. Thus.
This should be performed everywhere.

Having taken a tooth-stick with the characteristics as previously described and accompanied by the mantra, one should first perform the cleansing of the teeth with the lower row [of teeth] using a forward-moving motion, preceded by the Smārta mantra beginning with "āyurbalaṃ."

One should perform [the purification]. In the event of the non-availability of wood and so forth, one may use the leaves of those respective trees or grass; in the absence of even these, purification of the mouth is achieved with twelve mouthfuls of water. And thus it has been stated by the sages Nārāyaṇa:
"Having thoroughly purified the sacred site (tīrtha) and washed one's feet, and having sipped water while restraining speech..."

Having cleansed the teeth with grass or with substances perfected by the scriptures, such as *varta*, *arka*, *khadira*, and so forth, and having scraped the tongue, one should repeatedly perform gargling.
Thus they remember:
"In the absence of tooth-sticks, even on forbidden days,
purification of the mouth shall be achieved by twelve mouthfuls of water."
Thus it is said:
"On the first day of the lunar fortnight, on the new moon, on the sixth, and on the fourteenth and eighth days,
the contact of a toothbrush twig with the teeth burns one's family unto the seventh generation."
On the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth lunar days— these three junctions— one should avoid oil, meat, sexual intercourse, and the use of a tooth-stick.

By these and other such [statements], the prohibited days are to be understood. After cleaning the teeth, one should wash the tooth-stick, break it, and discard it in a clean place. This concludes the section on the holy bathing places (*tīrtha*).

In that regard, as for the going to a body of water mentioned prior to purification, what is intended there is a *tīrtha* that is *bhāgavata* (pertaining to the Lord) and *bhāgavatāśrita* (resorted to by devotees). As they say: "One should approach a pure and heart-gladdening *tīrtha* that is *bhāgavata*. Then, having resorted to such a *tīrtha*, one becomes pure.

And it is said that [this place] is "resorted to by the Bhāgavatas. They also remember: "Water, whether pure or impure, in the vicinity of Viṣṇu’s abode, is a sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā, which destroys even the greatest sins."
O Lord, O All-pervading One, those like you, who are devotees of the Blessed One and have themselves become sacred fords,
sanctify other sacred fords by means of the Wielder of the Mace residing within their own hearts.
O best of kings, for those who worship Vāsudeva, the source of the universe, there exists no sacred place (tīrtha) superior to them.
Know that to be a preeminent sacred ford (tīrtha), which destroys all sins, where the devotees of the Lord, pure in heart, perform their ablutions.
Thus it is said.
The procedure for bathing (snānavidhi) should be observed therein;
having thus gathered the requisites for bathing and reached the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should perform the rites up to the cleansing of the mouth.

One should perform the bath, which is the root of all ritual acts, preceded by immersion in sacred waters (*tīrtha*) and so forth, according to the sequence to be described hereafter. The obligatory nature (*nityatva*) and the efficacy (*prabhāva*) of the morning bath are established in various places, and authorities record the rules for bathing according to the distinctions of social classes (*varṇa*).
The Grandfather and others said:
"Immersion in water, that is bathing, is prescribed for all castes;
however, sprinkling with mantras is especially distinguished for the twice-born."

Thus it is said. In that regard, for one who is capable, the Varuṇa bath alone [is prescribed]. But for one who is incapable of that— "One should not perform the secondary baths after eating, nor when ill, nor at midnight."
Nor should one bathe after covering oneself with another's garment, nor in an unknown body of water.

Because of the prohibition of those [other baths] by such statements as these, there are other types of bathing. And among those, since the Smṛti declares that after the Vāruṇa bath, there is the ākaṇṭha (up-to-the-neck) bath, or, in case of inability, the aśiraska (headless) bath;
and for one who is unable even for that, there is the Kāpila bath; and for one who is unable even for that—
Among those [methods] taught in various scriptures— namely the earthly, fiery, windy, celestial,
[earthly-wind-mantrean, mantrean, and mental], as well as self-meditation (*ātma-dhyāna*), the five-limbed [rite], and that performed by another person preceded by touch— [the latter is... *aspr̥*...
In other types of baths that involve immersion (*avagāhana*) preceded by [the aforementioned rites], one should perform whatever is possible at that time. Regarding this, Kratu has said:
"Either purification followed by bathing should be undertaken, or the *brāhma* bath is desired."
For the elderly and the infirm, [this is achieved] by means of warm water or the limbs of yoga, such as the restraints (yamas) and so forth.
Thus [it is said]. Here, the intention is "according to one's qualification. And so it has been stated in the *Pārameśvara*:
"Without various [external] contacts, one should perform the five-limbed bath:
the face together with the two hands, and the feet up to the region of the hips."
In the event of defilement through contact with women and similar causes, one should perform a bath according to the prescribed rule.

Thus: for one unable to bathe in cold water, bathing in warm water is prescribed; and that only on days that are not prohibited and when the body is not afflicted [by illness]. In this manner, one should perform the bath according to one's capacity and other factors. And they have recorded the bath according to one's strength, either individually or combined:
One who has performed purification according to one's ability by means of these— divine, mental, vocal, aerial, terrestrial, fiery, and mental— or by all of them combined, or by some of them.

Thus [it is said]. Otherwise, one becomes unfit for action, according to the injunction: "All ritual acts [beginning with] bathing become fruitless. And Atri declares the obligatory nature of bathing, recitation, fire-offerings, and giving: "He who eats without having bathed consumes impurity; he who does not recite [mantras] consumes pus and blood."
One who has not offered oblations into the fire eats worms; one who does not give gifts consumes insects.
Thus,

having bathed in this manner and applied the *urdhva-puṇḍra*, one performs the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and the offering of water (*arghyadāna*), which are constituent parts of the ritual bath.
Having performed the libations (tarpaṇa) for the deities, sages, and ancestors who are of the nature of the Blessed Lord, and having sipped water (ācamana),

one should perform the sprinkling with mantras (mantraprokṣaṇa), the sipping of water with mantras (mantrācamana), the repeated sprinkling (punahprokṣaṇa), and the sprinkling of oneself (svātmapariṣecana) according to the method prescribed in one's own Sūtra and Saṃhitā. [The word "having performed" (kṛtvā) does not appear in any manuscript other than the *gha* codex.]

It is seen that one should offer water consecrated with the Gāyatrī as an arghya to the Supreme Self residing within the sun. Regarding this, the Grandfather spoke to Sanatkumāra that the casting of the handfuls of water should be done three times:
Taking water with both hands, being well-composed,
and consecrating the water with the Gāyatrī preceded by the Tāra and the Vyāhṛtis,
one should stand facing the sun and throw it upward three times during the two junctions of the day.

Thus it is said. Then, having circumambulated [the fire] clockwise for the purpose of shaking off evil—the expulsion of the demons known as Mandehas who were struck down by that water which had become vajra-like—one should invoke Keśava and the others, the lords of the months beginning with Mārgaśīrṣa, and Gāyatrī. (The reading *deśavādīn* is found only in manuscript *gha*).
One thousand and eight, one hundred and eight, or at least ten times, according to one's capacity—
the Gāyatrī mantra one thousand and eight times or one hundred and eight times.

One should recite the Gāyatrī one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times, or at least ten times according to one's capacity; as stated in the *Nikṣepacintāmaṇi*: "One should mutter the Gāyatrī one thousand and eight times, or one hundred and eight times, according to one's capacity."
Neither walking, nor laughing, nor looking toward the side;
nor stepping with one foot upon the other, nor likewise with the two hands.
These and others are the rules regarding the time for recitation.
O best of men, those who are my devotees, who have gone to me and are devoted to me, perform the recitation of the eight-syllabled mantra.
One should diligently honor those who sacrifice to me and observe my rules.
O Yudhiṣṭhira, for their purification, I indeed always preside over both twilights; thus, that vow of mine remains unbroken.

Therefore, this eight-syllabled mantra should be constantly recited by my devotees, free from impurity, during the periods of the twilight prayers for the sake of self-purification. [Note: In this context, the word *mantra* is seen in all manuscripts as ending in the neuter gender.]

Thus, the recitation of the eight-syllable mantra of Śīma as declared in the *Śrī-Vaiṣṇava-dharma-śāstra* should also be performed according to one's capacity during the occasion of the *saṃdhyā* (as indicated by a variant reading in some manuscripts: "it should be performed at the *saṃdhyā* itself"). This should be done six times through breath control (*prāṇāyāma*).

Bodhāyana and others remember that by means of the specific combination of the *praṇava* and the *vyāhṛtis*, ten recitations of the *gāyatrī* are equal to a thousand; thus, a gradation of results is recorded in tradition. Among these, the highest point is stated as "infinite [merit] in the presence of Viṣṇu. Furthermore, regarding the counting, there is an option between using the hands or a rosary (*akṣasūtra*) according to one's capacity.

[The state of being] an instrument. And it is stated in the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*: "One should perform recitation (japa) of two kinds: that which is placed on a rosary (*akṣasūtra*) and that which is placed in the hand. The meaning is: "placed on a rosary" or "placed in the hand. That very point is specified in the *Śrīsāttvata*: "By means of a crystal rosary, or by one's own finger-joints. In this regard:

The mention of "crystal" is an illustration for the category of rosaries (*akṣamālā*), since other scriptures record the preeminence of rosaries made of lotus seeds and so forth. However, there are various distinctions among rosaries made of gems, pearls, and other materials for the sake of specific fruits; likewise, specific rules regarding consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and so on are found in various places.

They are elaborated upon; and in the hand as well, there are various distinctions such as the conch-mudrā, the lotus-mudrā, and so forth [the conch-mudrās and lotus-mudrās]. In this regard, the essential point is as follows:
beginning from the base of the little finger and proceeding in a clockwise direction...
O Lord of Gods, one should recite it ten million times ending with the ring finger [O Goddess, with *gha*, *ṅ*, and *cha*].
Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the *Bodhāyanīya* regarding the procedure for the venerable eight-syllabled mantra (*aṣṭākṣara*), it is stated as follows:
"The sacrifice of recitation (*japayajña*) is proclaimed to be ten times more meritorious than the sacrifice of ritual action (*kriyāyāga*).
It should be known that if performed in a whisper (*upāṃśu*), it is a hundred times more meritorious than when performed aloud (*uccaiḥ*)."
The mental recitation is said to be a thousand times more effective than the whispered recitation.
Thus it is said. Furthermore, it is stated therein:
"If a guru or a Vaiṣṇava should arrive during the midst of one's recitation (japa), one should perform salutation and other forms of worship for him, and having obtained his permission,"
Then, having caused [the announcement] to be heard, he should, with a concentrated mind, perform the remainder of the recitation.
Since Viṣṇu’s feet are the source of everything and men take refuge there,
all actions indeed become fruitful when rooted in Him.

Thus, in the *Nāradīya* [Purāṇa], within the *Śrīmad-aṣṭākṣara-brahmavidyā*: "Every [mantra] is to be recited with the *praṇava*; even if recited without the *praṇava*, it is to be known as equal to a thousand [recitations]. For the *praṇava* is indeed the supreme syllable (*akṣara*)."
The recitation performed by one whose body bears the vertical *ūrdhvapuṇḍra* is said to be a thousand times more meritorious than that performed by one who is uncountable;
it is even a thousand times more meritorious than that performed by one who is countable.
Thus it has been said:
"In this way,
the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña) is ten times superior to the ritual sacrifice of prescribed rites (vidhiyajña)."

The whispered recitation (upāṃśu) is said to be a hundredfold [more effective] than the loud one, and the mental recitation (mānasa) is remembered as a thousandfold. The whispered recitation is superior to the loud recitation by ten times;
the tongue-recitation (jihvājapa) is a hundredfold, and the mental recitation is remembered as a thousandfold.
This and other such passages are also to be observed.
Regarding the worship of the Sun (sūryopasthāna):
thus, from sunrise onwards, one should face the eastern or northern direction, or the western or northern direction.
In accordance with such Smṛti texts, standing facing east or northeast,
having repeated the Gāyatrī as before, and having performed the three breath-controls (prāṇāyāma),
one should [proceed] preceded by the formal resolve (saṃkalpa) for the Sandhyā worship, using the mantra beginning with "On the highest peak" (uttame śikhare).

Having obtained permission with the Gāyatrī, and having worshipped the Blessed One residing within the solar orb with the mantras prescribed in his own Sūtra, he should perform a circumambulation and offer salutations to the fivefold Sandhyā and others as being identical with the Blessed One, reciting: "He who is this [person] in the human body..."

Having saluted and prostrated before the Supreme Self—who is situated within the heart and has been studied as "He who is in the sun is one"—[one should also perform] the salutation to the directions and so forth, which was previously taught by the teacher. (The variant readings *pūrvapūrvopadeśaka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *jha* refer to this.
One should also perform the salutation to the directions and so forth.

If there exists a lineage of successive instruction and practice from one's own predecessors, one should likewise prostrate while preceded by meditation upon the Lord as the Self. In this manner, the Grandfather (Brahmā) explained the method of attendance to Sanatkumāra:
With palms joined in reverence, he should daily worship the Sun, the Lord Bharga, whose orb is clearly manifest and who possesses a thousand rays;
then, having paid homage to him, he should worship the five deities of the twilight.
Having meditated upon the Supreme Self as his own self, the best of the twice-born worships the quarters with circumambulations and prostrations.

Thus [ends the section]. Then, having performed the libation for the Foundation Power (Ādhāraśakti) and the others, one should meditate upon the gods, sages, and ancestors— beginning with the Foundation Power and ending with their respective retinues— as being identical in essence with the Blessed Lord.

Having gratified [the deities] with their respective names preceded by the *praṇava*, one should wring out the bathing garment in a clean place on dry ground, perform the ritual sipping of water (*ācamana*), and then withdraw the invoked sacred waters and the mantras into one's own self.
In this regard, although there are three distinct types of twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*)— namely, the *ārṣī*, the *vaiṣṇavī*, and the *prājāpatyā*—

Although those various *saṃhitās* are indicated [in the text] as "ātmani ka ca jha," nevertheless, because those *saṃhitās* have for the most part been lost, their respective modes are difficult to discern; therefore, they are to be observed in the *Pārameśvara-paramasaṃhitā* and other such works.

Furthermore, because the lineage of instruction and practice for the various methods of performing the *saṃdhyopāsana* as seen in the *Pūrṇa* tradition has not been established, one must rely solely upon the *Saṃhitās* of the Bhagavat-śāstra [and the *Saṃhitās* and practices of one's own *Sūtra*— ka, kha, ga, ca, jha].

Because the performance of the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and conduct (*ācāra*) prescribed in one's own *sūtra* is permitted, and because there is no insistence on abandoning what was previously adopted, it is established that even when practicing according to one's own *sūtra*, it takes the form of propitiating the Blessed One; thus,
the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsti*) and other such rites are indeed those ordained by one's own *sūtra*.
It is proper to perform the twilight worship (*saṃdhyopasthāna*) and other rites. For it is stated in the *Nāradīya*:

"One should likewise perform the purificatory rites (*viśeṣaka*) and others prescribed by one's own *sūtra*, and so forth. And in the *Padma Purāṇa*, having performed purification, sipping water (*ācamana*), brushing the teeth, and bathing in due order, immediately thereafter—
The twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana) has been described:
having sipped water (ācamya), one should sprinkle one's body with darbha-grass water while reciting mantras,
and likewise with water consecrated by the Gāyatrī preceded by the syllable Om.
Having sprinkled water over himself, he should cast up a handful of water toward the sky,
desiring to fight the Rākṣasas during both twilights.
Those [waters], having become like vajras when impelled by them, destroy [the sins];
indeed, the atonement for violence is performed by circumambulating [the waters] clockwise.
Then, having entered, he should gratify the deity residing in his heart with the mantras prescribed in his own Vedic branch;
thereafter, he should salute his gurus, elders, and devotees of the Lord (bhāgavatas) in due order.
Thus it is said. For this very reason, the venerable Bhaṭṭārakas have stated:
"Having risen in the morning and recollected Hari, having meditated upon Gaṅgā as arising from His feet—and having plunged into the waters of the sacred ford—having thus immersed oneself therein..."

Having performed to the best of one's ability those rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti as a means of propitiating the Supreme Self, and having applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra), one should offer libations.

Thus it was said; and by his own gurus, the venerable Śrīvatsāṅka Miśra, who were instructing [the author] on the essence of *abhigamana* at the request of Vaṭuka Pūrṇa, it was stated at the outset: "Having risen in the morning, having offered oneself at the lotus-feet of one’s own guru, and having contemplated one's own self as fulfilled and overflowing with bliss..."
"Having performed his own duties such as bathing and so forth, seated in a pure place," and so on; and by the lords of the Vaṅga dynasty:
"Having applied the vertical mark (ūrdhvapuṇḍra) and having gratified the gods, sages, and ancestors with mantras."
With supreme devotion and self-restraint, he worshipped Acyuta, who is to be propitiated through one's own innermost core.
Having bowed to and remembered with the mind that which resides within the solar orb,
it is proclaimed as "Sandhyā" because of its nature as the unifier of all things.
Action prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti, appropriate to one’s own caste and stage of life,
performed without desire for fruit, and consisting of the worship of the Supreme Brahman.
Having attributed agency, enjoyership, and ownership to the Supreme Self,
and being endowed with obligatory, occasional, and optional rites;

Having properly completed the entire twilight ritual (saṃdhyā-karma) according to the rules, preceded by the ritual sipping of water (mantrācamana) and ending with the recitation of the Gāyatrī mantra.
Then, unwearied, having approached with his own ritual mantras Nārāyaṇa, who abides within the sun as the enjoyer of one's own karma;
And so forth.

Regarding the *saṃdhyā-arghya*, the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of its being the *arghya* for the Lord is intended here; that is, when casting the handful of water consecrated by the *gāyatrī* mantra, one should also contemplate it as having the nature of the *arghya* for the Lord.
It has been compiled by the Nārāyaṇa sages:

having sprinkled [the disciple] with the mantras beginning with "āpo hi," which are expressive of the Supreme Self, one performs the ritual rinsing of the mouth (ācamana) with those mantras that reveal Him.
Having offered the *arghya* to the Supreme Self residing within the sun,
one should mutter that Hari [the mantra] of Viṣṇu along with the *Sāvitrī*, which serves as its introductory formula.
Meditating and reciting [the mantra], he should worship that very Puruṣottama;
he should satisfy the gods, the ṛṣis, and the ancestors, who are of the nature of Nārāyaṇa.
Then, having wrung out that garment on the bank— starting from the foundational power (ādhāra-śakti) up to all the attendants— and remaining silent,
one should avoid conversation, looking, and other such interactions with heretics and the like.
Thus;
and they remember the fault in the neglect of the prescribed meditation:
"There is a fault in the neglect of *saṃdhyā*."
But those Brahmins who do not worship the morning twilight that has not yet come, nor the evening twilight that has not passed— how can they be considered true Brahmins?
Those Brahmins who do not constantly perform the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā) in the evening and the morning—
such persons a righteous king may, at his will, employ in menial tasks that are beneath their dignity.
Thus ends the sequence for the twilight rites (*saṃdhyā*). Now,
regarding the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), one should perform it after the sun has risen, in accordance with the direct Taittirīya Śruti and other authorities.
Either after the midday meal, or before the meal [as in variants *ka*, *kha*, *jha*], or at some other appropriate occasion;
one should perform prostrations toward the temple of the Blessed One located near a sacred bathing place (*tīrtha*).

Immediately after bathing at the sacred ford (tīrtha), one should pay obeisance to the temple of Viṣṇu situated near that ford according to the method described in the Mahābhārata. A mere indication of what must be done upon entering the temple of the Blessed Lord is shown in the Śrīsāttvata:
A temple of the God of gods, a Pāñcarātrika preceptor,
an Aśvattha tree, a Vaṭa tree, a cow, a virtuous assembly, and the house of one's guru.
From a distance one should perform circumambulation,
and from nearby one should prostrate like a staff toward the image of the Lord in the four directions.
One should not enter the temple of the Blessed One while mounted on a vehicle or wearing sandals, nor with distracted mind; one should not lie down there.
Thus it is said.

In that regard, one should perform circumambulations and prostrations in pairs; for there is a prohibition against odd numbers, as indicated by the statement: "The counting of one, three, five, seven, and so forth is indeed uneven. Furthermore, both upon entering and exiting, one should perform a salutation to Viṣvaksena.
Having thus performed the ritual, one should bow to Viṣvaksena and the respective door-keepers, and having obtained their permission, enter each respective place.
One should move like a wheel, not letting the body sway, and should not show the back.
The wise one should exit by the rear part in the presence of the deity.

Thus it is said. Having entered, one should prostrate with the eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga*)—as far as possible given the particular place and time—by means of any one of these: the *mastaka-sampuṭa*, *prahva-aṅga*, *pañcāṅga-daṇḍa*, and so forth.
Among these, the eight-limbed prostration (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*) is as follows:
The modes of prostration on the ground according to the Nyaya system, together with mind, intellect, and ego,
consist of four limbs like those of a tortoise, with the head as the fifth.

Thus the author of the commentary will cite what was stated by the Sāttvata: "The group of five beginning with the *mastiṣka* is recited in the venerable Vaikhānasa scripture—'That is the *mastiṣka-praṇāma*; one should place the *añjali* upon the head.'"
That is the *saṃpuṭa* salutation; one should offer the joined palms at the heart.
Prahlāda should form the *saṃpuṭa* gesture;
that is the salutation with a bowed body, touching the ground with the toes of the feet, the knees, and the head.
One should pay homage with palms joined; this is declared to be the five-limbed prostration (pañcāṅga).
One should lie upon the ground like a staff, stretching out both feet and hands.
That is the prostration with the staff-like limbs; thus one should perform the salutations.

Thus it is said. In the *Saṃkarṣaṇasaṃhitā*, within the section on the prostration of well-performed deeds (*sukṛtapraṇāmaprakaraṇa*), the prostration is described as follows: "Placing the two hands, which extend upward from the tips of the pair of feet—[the feet] whose knees and shanks are joined [together]—upon the ground, one should mentally recollect Vāsudeva."
Thus it is said. And in this manner, the eight-limbed prostration (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*) is remembered:
"With the chest, with the head, with speech, and with the mind, as well as with the two cheeks, the two feet, the two hands, and the two knees—this is called the eight-limbed prostration."

Thus [it is said]. And in the *Rahasyāmnāyabrāhmaṇa*, within the section on salutation (*namaskāra-prakaraṇa*), after teaching the nature and other characteristics of the complete salutation through such statements as "one must bow with both knees, both hands, and the head," its fruit is also declared: "Bowing with all the instruments of action, one bows completely; bowing completely..."
"He becomes a performer of what is appropriate; as one who performs what is appropriate, he attains the Blessed One.
Thus, the twelve-limbed prostration and so forth are to be observed in their respective contexts. However, bowing with only one hand is prohibited by the *Śrī Bhāgavata*:
Those who know the Dharma understand that for one who bows to the Supreme Person with only a single hand, the cutting off of that hand is the just punishment.

Thus it is said. For even the state of having joined palms does not belong to this [deity], because of the lexicographical reading: "The two young women are the *añjali*, and the man is the *añjali*. However, for those such as the fly-whisk bearers, since their other hands are occupied, the joining of one hand alone is not permitted.

Therefore, there is no contradiction with such statements as "the punishment for showing contempt and so forth is the amputation of a hand," or "even a single salutation made with joined palms [is sufficient]," provided that the capacity [for full prostration] exists; for they maintain that even for one who bows with both hands, there is a deficiency [if the proper form is not observed]. As it is said: [text fragment]... provided that the capacity exists. Even for one bowing with both hands, they declare a deficiency [in the rite]. As for example: [text fragment]... provided that the capacity exists. Even for one bowing with both hands, they declare a deficiency. For this person bows only with his hands and arms, not with his knees nor his head; he bows with a single type of knowledge—the knowledge of specific tactile sensations—and thus he is deficient regarding the specific objects of touch. Other forms of knowledge belong to ritual action. By bowing with only one part, he bows deficiently; by bowing deficiently, he becomes one who fails to accomplish what is required.

"One who acts improperly does not reach the Blessed One. Regarding the mention of the name of the Ācārya (in the variants *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ṅa*, *ca*, *cha*, *jha*) and the mention of the name of the Blessed One (*gha*), one should perform such acts as joining the palms of the hands in each respective instance. And this practice has been demonstrated.
In the *Saṃbhava-parvan*, during the introduction of Vyāsa, Bhīṣma spoke with palms joined in reverence after the Great Sage had been extolled;
this is the manner of service to the Blessed One.

Having thus bowed down according to rank and risen, he stood to the right of the Blessed One; having approached the Blessed One for refuge through the lineage of gurus, his entire body was suffused with the joy of beholding that purifying and enchanting sight.
One should recite hymns that are outpourings of joy, which are pleasing through praise and capable of enchanting by their sweetness.
Furthermore, the greatness of beholding the Lord’s incarnate icons (arcāvatāra) is thus stated in the Śrīpauṣkara— [the word *māhātmya* does not appear elsewhere except in the *Gha* manuscript]:
Thus it is said. However, elsewhere, even for great sins, it is prescribed as an expiation:
"One should gaze at the form of Hari from the pedestal up to [the top].
For one who beholds Puruṣottama from the pedestal (ā-pīṭha) to the crown of the head (mauli), [this is the purification].
Even great sins perish quickly; how much more so, then, minor offenses?
And so forth. Regarding the power of praising and proclaiming [the virtues of the Lord]:
"This is considered by me to be the most excellent of all dharmas:
that a person should always worship the Lotus-Eyed One with devotion through hymns of praise."
O King, in the Kali age, which is a reservoir of defects, there is indeed one great virtue for those who chant the name of Keśava:
by the mere chanting of Kṛṣṇa’s name, one is released from bondage and goes to the supreme state.
This is to be understood from such passages as these.
Regarding the procedure for accepting the grace of the Blessed One (*bhagavatprasāda*),
here [it refers to] whatever has been obtained through the grace of the Blessed One, such as the water from the feet of Tulasī (*tulasīpādodaka*) and so forth.
Preceded by prostration, with cheeks blooming with joy, one should honor him with a bow of the head and partake [of the offering] as is appropriate.
Regarding this, the learned recite in such works as *The Determination of Ācamana* composed by King Pratāpa:
[āmrekṣu-khaṇḍa-gha-ṅ-cha]—in the chewing of mangoes, sugarcane stalks, and betel leaves...
In the drinking of Soma and in the drinking of water from the feet of Viṣṇu, neither the beginning nor the end rinsing (ācamana) is prescribed.

Thus it is said. And the *Atharvaṇa-śruti*, which is the source of that [tradition], has been compiled by the sage Nārāyaṇa: "The Blessed One is the purifier; Vāsudeva is the purifier; His feet are the purifier; the water from His feet is the purifier. Drinking it or sipping it is not [required] as it is with the *soma*."

Thus, considering himself to have achieved his purpose through service to the Blessed One, he should sit down in a secluded place with the permission of the Blessed One and worship by means of recitation (*japa*) and other practices.
Furthermore, regarding the mantra of the Blessed One, he should avoid those transgressions (*apacāra*) prescribed in the various scriptures. Thus it is said in the *Śrī-Vārāha*:
In the Purāṇa, thirty-two offenses are enumerated. Regarding these thirty-two offenses,
Śrī Dharaṇī said:
O God of gods, Lord of the universe, I have heard everything from you;
now tell me, O Lord of the lords of gods, Mādhava, who are affectionate toward your devotees, those by whom one becomes unworthy of entering your abode.
The Blessed One said:
O Vasundharā, I shall declare the transgressions; listen to that.
Those men who, within my dwellings, cause the cessation of songs, instrumental music, dances, and other meritorious narratives and stories through their harshness;
O Vasudhā, those sinners go to twenty-one hells;
thereafter, O highly fortunate one, they take birth in the womb of a donkey.
O Goddess, for seven births there,
that man who bows to me after covering his body with a cloth shall indeed undergo the state of a sow.
O beautiful lady, a fool who, wrapped in a black woolen blanket, bows down to me shall be born with leprosy for three lifetimes.
He goes to birth in the womb of a Caṇḍāla for nine or five births on earth,
with all his limbs smeared with oil and his feet hidden by sandals.
O auspicious upholder of beings, whatever man enters my house shall go for three births into the womb of household guardians (or the womb of household nets), O auspicious one.
Listen now to the fruit of the sin of whoever should throw nails, hair, body hair, or likewise bones into my houses.
Having resorted to the womb of a bee, being covered with claws and hair,
he remains in that very state for seven births and twenty-one hells.
Whoever chews betel leaf and throws it into my temple shall go to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings.
Released from that, O illustrious lady, Śunaka remains for three more births; he dwells [in those states] indeed, there is no doubt.
O beautiful one, that sinful man who spits within my temple shall fall into the terrible hell called Krimibhakṣya.
Having become a *śloṣmātaka* tree, he is born for five lifetimes;
yet, that man who goes into the midst of a cremation ground and worships me, [attains liberation].
A person is instantly liberated from the merit accumulated over seven lifetimes; O auspicious one, having entered the womb of a jackal (or a swan), they shall dwell there for three births.
O Goddess of auspicious countenance, whoever voids urine in my temple shall indeed fall headfirst into the hell known as Mūtragarta.
Therefore, O lady of beautiful hips, once liberated from that, he will take refuge under a nimba or bimba tree and be born as a sow for eight lifetimes.
Any man who voids excrement in my temple goes in succession to twenty-one terrible hells.
Released from that, O highly fortunate lady, he is born as a worm in excrement;
so too is the man who follows a corpse out of his own desire.
If one desires to propitiate me, he goes to the lowest state;
O Mountain, he enters the womb of a crow for births upon this earth.
O Vasundharā, having thus performed the maintenance of a clay vessel, one must not enter a temple; hear now the fruit for one who has entered.
O lady of excellent hips, having taken birth nine and five times in the womb of a Cāṇḍāla,
he will then become a cruel and harsh hunter.
O highly fortunate lady, having partaken of the śrāddha, a man who then worships me attains the state of a sparrow and subsequently enters the body of a monitor lizard.
O Vasundharā, he who out of delusion steps upon the shadow of the vimāna,
yet intentionally performs a circumambulation while standing there;
He might stand in a desolate forest, surrounded by many thorns,
devoid of fruits and flowers, becoming a mere empty tree in the wilderness.
He who voids excrement or urine even near a temple shall remain in the terrible Raurava hell for ten million years.
Released even from that, O fair-browed one, the man attains the state of a village pig;
for a hundred births he is born in a village as a pig that dwells in excrement.
Those who engage in incoherent chatter in my presence,
even they, having become partridges, are born for five lifetimes.
Those who carry away a lamp that has been lit from another's house shall remain blind for fifteen births.
O fair-faced one, listen to the fruit of the sin of those who depart from my temple while the discourse is being recited, without having first taken [the sacred water].
Those lowest of men who lie in their homes with their feet stretched out shall indeed become deaf and mute for five births.
Listen now to the fruit of their sin for spitting phlegm and leaving food remnants:
they shall indeed become hollow trees in a waterless and most dreadful forest.
They will be born for seven lifetimes and thereafter attain the state of a caṇḍāla;
for three lifetimes they will be both impoverished and foolish.
Those who worship me with flowers intended for another purpose shall indeed go to the state of frogs in my own great abode.
Indeed, those deluded men who, having gone to the temple of another deity, depart for home without having bathed, fall into the state of a Śūdra for two births.
O Earth, hear now the fruit of that sin of mine alone:
having gone from house to house, I myself became a beggar, tormented by hunger.
Even if he does not obtain alms there,
that ignorant man is born poor for four lifetimes, and at the end of those lives as well.
He who regards me as equal to other gods attains the womb of a Caṇḍāla for fifteen births; he is the lowest of men.
The man who smells the fragrance of flowers intended as offerings goes to birth in the womb of a Caṇḍāla for fourteen lifetimes.
O auspicious Earth, he shall become afflicted with foul-smelling leprosy for three births; of this there is no doubt.

One should not perform a ritual bath merely after touching outcastes or those who have fallen from their caste, even if they are staying near a shrine of Viṣṇu or have come there for the purpose of serving Viṣṇu.
If one bathes during the festival of Vāsudeva out of fear of physical contact [with others],
his ancestors dwelling in heaven fall instantly into hell.
One should drink the water from the feet of Viṣṇu, especially that of the Vaiṣṇavas;
in that case, one should not perform the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), just as a superior twice-born man does not do so when drinking soma.
"Alternatively, there are thirty-two types of transgressions.

Thus, in the *Śrī-Vārāha Purāṇa*, within the *Dharaṇīpraśna* section, in the chapter titled "The Thirty-two Transgressions" (the forty-fifth), a compendium of both those mentioned and those not mentioned should be performed. In this regard, there is this one method:
Likewise, thirty-two offenses against Viṣṇu have been proclaimed;
among them, traveling to the house of the Lord by means of vehicles or even on sandals.
Not attending festivals and other celebrations of the deity, not bowing before him,
bowing with only one hand, and performing circumambulation in front of him [are all prohibited].
One should not perform the salutation of the Blessed One and other such acts while in a state of impurity from food remnants or ritual defilement;
nor should one stretch out one's feet before him, nor sit in the cross-legged posture (paryaṅka).
Sleeping, eating, idle chatter, speaking loudly, vain talk, weeping, and so forth, as well as quarreling;
Inflicting punishment or showing favor toward women, speaking with suggestive intent, uttering vulgar speech, and the emission of downward-voiding wind.
Covering oneself with a blanket, disparaging others, praising others,
using figurative expressions when one has the capacity [to speak directly], and eating what has not been offered.
Not offering fruits and other items that have grown at that particular time,
and giving away what remains after it has been assigned for use as condiments and the like.
Turning one's back on one's seat, saluting others,
remaining silent toward the guru, praising oneself, and likewise reviling the deities.
Thus it is said.
In this manner, other procedural variations should also be understood from their respective contexts. Likewise:
"If a Vaiṣṇava man should touch wine even through negligence..."
O Earth, I do not tolerate even a hundred such transgressions.
One should not engage in eating, sleeping, idle chatter, or especially the recitation of sacred texts (svādhyāya), nor should one sit upon a seat within the temple of Keśava.
He who regards the form of Viṣṇu as being merely iron,
and he who perceives a human nature in his guru— both of these fall into hell.

Other such transgressions mentioned previously should also be observed. Thus, being vigilant in the temple of the Blessed One and having avoided all transgressions, one should exit after prostrating as before and obtaining permission from Viṣvaksena and the others. [This concludes] the approach for the commencement of the sacrifice.
Then, having returned to the hermitage house and other dwellings presided over by his own deity, with hands and feet thoroughly washed and having performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana),

he should inspect the house with vessels made of gold, silver, copper, or similar materials— using either water previously fetched and kept in a water-jar (maṇika) or [freshly drawn] water— and, according to the procedure of his own *sūtra*, offer oblations into his fire, which is of the nature of the Lord.
Having come to the temple, one should bow from afar. And regarding the approach here, it has been shown by Vaṅgīśvara as follows:
"Then, having taken up a water-pot and filled it with pure water..."
For the purpose of propitiating Hari, he remained silent with his mind fully restrained.
Avoiding with effort the sight of heretics and the like while meditating on the god Nārāyaṇa along the way, he should take refuge at the sacrificial ground.
Then, having washed his feet and performed the ritual sipping of water (ācamana), being well-composed, whether he be a student, a householder, a forest-dweller, or a silent sage;
Endowed with faith, one should perform [the rite] according to the rules appropriate for one's own caste and stage of life,
using materials such as sacrificial fuel and clarified butter, and with mantras as prescribed.
Having offered oblations into the fires during the Agnihotra and other rites, even while passing over the prescribed time,
he performs his own duty solely through the act of worshipping another.
When one's own mind has been made stainless, pure, and well-established,
one attains the authority for the Lord’s meditation, worship, recitation, and other such practices.
Having emerged from the fire-sanctuary and gone to his own sacrificial hall,
he should worship the Supreme Self in accordance with the requirements of place, time, and other factors.
Whether with leaves, flowers, or fruits, according to the method prescribed for the time of worship— or even with a mere añjali offered in whatever manner— [one should perform the rite].

Thus [it is said]. Here, because the qualification for meditation, worship, and so forth is prescribed for one whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has been purified by action in the form of service to others (*parārādhana*), the view of certain false-seers (*kudṛṣṭi*) is refuted. And it was stated by Parakālasūri in the midst of presenting the views of false-seers:

O Lord of the Vṛṣabha mountain, some desire to attain you through acts such as praise, recitation, gazing upon your form, meditation, service, remembrance, narration, and worship— rites that are far removed from the Vedas.
Whose lotus feet are to be reached by those who have attained perfection on the path of the Vedas.
Thus [the word *iti* is seen only in the lexicon].
And this has been summarized by the sages Nārāyaṇa: "One should avoid conversation, looking, and so forth with heretics and the like."
Having returned home, washed his feet, sipped water, and restrained his speech;
Having obtained permission from the gatekeepers, he entered the abode of Hari;
and having approached the Lord of Gods with profound joy and composure,
he placed his mind, intellect, and ego upon the surface of the earth.
Like a tortoise, [he should withdraw] his four limbs and his head as the fifth right there.
Bowing with the eight-limbed prostration as prescribed in the divine scriptures,
one should bow to the lotus-eyed Lord, humbled by the path of devotion.
Having approached the Lord, the Sovereign, through these two [verses] and their commentaries,
and having long surrendered oneself at His lotus feet, one becomes a person of fulfilled purpose.
Thus it is said. And here,
when the *brāhma-muhūrta* has arrived, having risen from bed and bathed,
one should worship the Lord of the World and perform the offering of fuel-sticks (*samid-dāna*).
[gha] ||

Thus much has been stated by the Sāttvata; this applies equally to all [the word "of all" does not appear in the Gha, Ṅa, Cha, and Kośa manuscripts]. However, the remainder [the word "only" does not appear in the Gha, Ṅa, Cha, and Kośa manuscripts] pertains only to those established in their respective *saṃhitās*. Likewise, in other *saṃhitās*, there is also the performance of rites at different times.
This is what should be grasped. In the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā*, however, the approach (*abhigamana*) prescribed in all the *saṃhitās* is stated in summary:

"O Brahmin, beginning from the *muhūrta* after Brahmā [i.e., dawn], during the first portion of the day, one should perform [worship] with recitation, meditation, adoration, and hymns, joined with action, speech, and mind."
One should approach the source of the world; that is known as "approaching" (abhigamana).
Thus it is said;
and in the Padma Purāṇa, this has been shown by delimiting the actions from beginning to end:
"O Four-faced One, whatever collection of actions exists ending with virtuous conduct,"
This procedure has been described according to the sequence beginning with rising.
Thus it is said.
And the duty to be performed immediately after the worship of the *saṃdhyā* is explained as follows: "Having saluted the gurus, the elders, and likewise the *bhāgavatas*, in due order..."
Having entered his own hermitage and approached the god according to the prescribed rite, he [performed worship].
One should worship until the conclusion of the recitation and fire-offerings, and one should also give mouthfuls of food to the cows,
as well as ointments, unguents, garlands, garments, and ornaments.
Equipped with lac-dye, betel for cleansing the mouth, and other auspicious items, he should perform the act of approaching [the teacher].

Thus, by this, that which is intended by the Smṛti—namely, "having then performed the rites for the gods, one should observe the teacher and auspicious things"—is also explained. And here, the full text as found in the Ka, Kha, Ga, A, and Jha manuscripts is adopted: "Endowed with other auspicious things, he should perform the act of approaching."

In this way, one should perform the salutation to the deities and others as taught by Vyāsa and others, the offering of oblations, the presentation of flowers and other items, the respectful greeting of elders, and service to the guru.
