[Six: The performance of secondary suffixes (*taddhita*), the study of the Vedas, silent recitation (*japa*), formal recitation (*adhyayana*), memorization, reflection upon their meaning, the study of treatises on dharma, the investigation of Vedic injunctions (*nigama*), the examination of the Vedāṅgas, and so forth—these duties to be performed during the first period [of the day] are to be carried out according to the procedure purified by the previous qualification. Thus has *abhigamana* been explained.
Thus concludes the section on approach (*abhigamana*).
Now we shall explain grasping (*upādāna*); and it is summarized as follows:
Then, when the second part of the day had arrived, the lords of the Vaṅga dynasty, in accordance with the Dharma,
collected all the materials for worship as prescribed by their own scriptural mantras.

Thus it has been explained by the sages Nārāyaṇa: "O you who are intent upon the worship of Kṛṣṇa, [offer] substances suitable for use as sacrificial materials and those unsuitable for them in two portions."
One should acquire those substances prescribed by the scriptures which are intended for the purpose of ārādhanā.
Abundant, pure, produced in sacred lands, not terrifying, and not forbidden— these are indeed the things collected by the Vaiṣṇavas.
Fragrant, pleasing, and facing [the deity], flowers; garments— starting from these up to those fit for the enjoyment of the gods— as well as wealth, grain, and unguents such as sandalwood.
[Chandanānyanulepanam ṅ ca cha] || Sandalwood and ointment. Ṅ and Cha.
Other excellent items, such as roots and fruits,
were washed many times— those very things fit for the enjoyment of the gods.
In particular, there were substances such as curd,
milk, and ghee, along with excellent side dishes and lentils, mung beans, and so forth.
Having respectfully taken all other items such as betel-leaf and the like,
and having prepared them appropriately, one should then proceed with the worship.
Thus it is said;
and as stated in the Śrīsāttvata:
"Having risen in the morning, one should indeed gather [the materials] oneself from one's own garden."
For the purpose of worship, one should always diligently prepare the flowers and other offerings with the Astra-mantra.
Or he may go to the forest, for there he may acquire [wealth] without hindrance;
it may come from trees that bear no thorns, or even from those that grow with thorns.
All flowers, beginning with white ones, that are pleasing to the heart, fragrant, suitable for ritual action, and acceptable may be used;
however, those with a pungent odor, those unsuitable for ritual action, and likewise those that are unknown [as being fit] should not be used.
Those born at crossroads, in the abodes of Śiva, in cremation grounds, or in the midst of forests;
those wounded by lightning strikes and the like; and those infested with worms and insects.
Leaves, flowers, fruits, and so forth— certain fragrant white and red lotuses included— should be avoided with great effort.
Indeed, pure items must always be employed in the ritual worship;
likewise, sprouts and leaves that have fallen upon the ground are also suitable.
While those flowers that bloom according to the seasons are prescribed for daily worship,
it is not beneficial to perform worship in the home with flowers produced from the *karavīra*.

Especially for one who possesses desire and is endowed with the attainment of supernatural powers (siddhi), there is no fault otherwise; however, there is fault [if it occurs] through those who are insane and the like.
For those who have been killed instantly, the rite is prescribed; for those who are not yet withered, it is performed according to the sequence.
For them, once they have been sprinkled with water, the offering must be made; it should not be done otherwise.
Through the observation of the mantra-practitioners, [all things] quickly attain faultlessness;
the hearts of those whose souls are devoted to the mantra become purified by devotion.
Thus,
since this has been instructed through the determination of restrictive rules (*niyamapariccheda*), it should be understood as being beyond contradiction.
Furthermore, with reference to one who possesses the capacity, the natural inclination toward spontaneous engagement and so forth is taught here.

Because another alternative is also permitted elsewhere; for here, in the worship of the Vaiśeṣikas and similar practices, the word "morning" (prātaḥ) sometimes has its primary meaning, otherwise there would be a conflict with the rule regarding approaching [the teacher] in the morning, and because in all other scriptures the acquisition of wealth is prescribed specifically for the second period of the day. By the word "morning,"...

Due to the force of proximity, the appropriate time for that is indicated in order to establish an excess of speed, just as in the case of the scriptural injunction: "Twice-born men shall eat in the evening and in the morning. For this very reason, the rising mentioned here does not occur immediately after sleep; rather, it occurs [after the gathering of flowers, kuśa grass, and so forth].

"One should perform the gathering of flowers, fruits, and so forth after rising"—this statement from the *Jayākhyasaṃhitā* refers to the rising from one's seat in the presence of the deity following the preliminary rite of *abhigamana*. Furthermore, the rules regarding flowers mentioned in the *Śrīvaiṣṇavadharmaśāstra* were shown in the preceding section as a relevant digression. In the *Pādma-purāṇa*, however, the procurement of various diverse materials is described as follows:
[The acquisition of the two is explained: ka kha ga jha] One should take up the means of worship exactly as they were before, in their proper manner. [ka jha;
kha ga ca read "yathāpūjā"] One should take up the means of worship exactly as they were before, in their proper manner.
Flowers, fruits, roots, and various medicinal herbs as well.
And curds and other items suitable for the sacrificial oblation, rice grains (and so forth), molasses and the like,
as well as bathing materials, garments, and delicious waters.

Having brought darbha grass, leaves (*parṇa*), and fuel sticks according to one's capacity and wealth— whether obtained through begging or otherwise— one should cause them to be placed in the place of worship.
Having thus brought it to the stage of appropriation, one should thereafter perform the worship.
Thus, in this Saṃhitā, as well as in other Saṃhitās, such as the section on flowers (puṣpaprakaraṇa) and the section on cooked oblations (haviṣpākaprakaraṇa), etc. [variants:
haviḥprakaraṇa, etc. (ka kha ga ca jha).

The entire classification of substances into those to be abandoned and those to be adopted should be observed. Here, regarding what is called "begging" (*yāñcayā*), this lowest-of-the-low category is [not seen in the Gha, Ṅa, Cha, and Kośa manuscripts];
that which is produced by one's own effort is said to be "praiseworthy" (*śasta*) or "middling" (*madhyama*), while that which is wild (*vanya*) is called "inferior."
But that which is purchased by barter is inferior, while that which is borrowed from another is the lowest of the low.
Thus, because that which was stated in the section on flowers applies without distinction to all substances,
Bhojarāja has likewise described the classification of flowers into *rājasa*, *tāmasa*, and so forth, as well as those to be avoided and those not to be avoided among flowers.

He compiled the classification of what flowers, sprouts, leaves, roots, and incenses are to be offered and what are not to be offered—and in the Gha manuscript alone, the letter *ca* is seen—[as follows]: "Now, flowers are of three kinds: *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa*.
White ones are *sāttvika*; red ones are *rājasa*; black ones are *tāmasa*. [Regarding white ones...]

There are two kinds of white: *valarkṣa* and *aruṇa*. Red is *tapākusuma* (the color of the hibiscus flower) and so forth; *aruṇa* is the color of the *kiṃśuka* (butea monosperma) flower and so forth. Yellow is of two kinds:
yellow and green. Black is of two kinds: blue (*nīla*) and dark (*śyāmala*).

"And *śyāma*": blue, such as the *tāpiñcha* and so forth; and blackish-blue (*kṛṣṇaśyāma*), such as the *viṣṇukrāntā* and so forth. Their fruit is distinguished: those of the *sāttvika* type yield full fruits, while those of the *rājasa* type yield half-fruits; therefore, they are half-fruited.
[The fruits] beginning with *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *jha* are from royal sources and are characterized by darkness (*tāmasa*).
These—whether produced in one's own garden (*svārāmotpanna*), wild, purchased, obtained through acceptance, or requested—are [to be used]. [According to some versions, they may also be unrequested.]
Six kinds of flowers are to be accepted: among them, those grown in one's own garden are the best; those from the forest are middling;
those purchased for a price are inferior; and those obtained by begging are the lowest of the low. (In the *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, and *jha* manuscripts, "begged" is the lowest of the low.)

[There is no fruit for the donor] in a flower received as a gift; there may or may not be anything for the one who performed the act [of growing it]. Therefore, one should not worship with flowers obtained through acceptance.
[These include: *karavīra*, the two types of *padma*, *ketakī*, *jāti*, *mallikā*, and *utpala*.
Tintriṇā, three [gha], tagara, campaka, śvetārka, kuṭaja, bakula,
[ka kha ga ṅ ca cha jha], kandalī, tulasī, tamāla, vanamāla [vanamālī gha ṅ cha],
maruvaka, śamī, sinduvāra, palāśa, sahadevī, phaṇijjaka, and puṃnāga.
Vaṃśa, puṃnāga, kṣudrapuṃnāga, mālatī, śvetakumuda, kandala, padma, mahāpuṣpa, nāga, sadābhadrā, priyaṅgu, bilva, vanamallikā, the two types of agasti,
the two types of atasī, vaiṣṇavī, karṇikāra, and the two types of aśoka.

The flowers are *kuṭaja*, *sthālī*, the two types of *agasti*, *vaiṣṇavī*, *karṇikāra*, *aśoka*, *kuṭaja* [as well as those beginning with *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *jha*], *kāraṇḍa*, the two types of *nandyāvarta*, *kṣudraketakī*, and so forth.

These are to be gathered according to the specific lunar days (*tithi*), the planetary positions (*grahaṇa*), the solstices (*ayana*), the transits (*saṃkrānti*), the *vyatīpāta* yoga, the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), and other such distinctions.
Furthermore, due to specific times such as *saṃgava* and others, the fruits become complete. In that regard, the flowers for the lunar days (*tithi*) dedicated to Viṣṇu are:
*vaiṣṇavī*, *kandala*, *padma*, *lakṣmī*, *sinduvāra*, *droṇa*, *priyaṅgu*, *mālatī*, *pāṭala*, *ketakī*, *jāti*, *mallikā*, and *mahājāti*.

One should take the leaves of the *palāśa* and *aśvattha* trees according to the sequence of the lunar days (*tithis*), and flowers for the other days. One should worship the Blessed One with *nandyāvartaka* flowers during the sun’s passage into a new zodiac sign (*saṃkrānti*); with *upanandyāvartaka* flowers during the solstices (*ayana*); with *tulasī* during the equinoxes (*viṣuva*); with *phaṇijjaka* during the *vyatīpāta* yoga; and with flower-nectars during an eclipse.

One should worship with *mandāraka* flowers, *makaranda* nectar, and *ghamaranda* nectar. At the time of *saṅgava*, one should take the specific flower prescribed for that particular lunar day (*tithi*). One should worship the Blessed One with lotuses during *sama*, with water-lilies (*kumuda*) during *dharma*, with *karavīra* flowers during *viṣṇupriya*, and with *bilva* leaves during *virāga*.

In this regard, the time-periods beginning with *saṃgava* proceed day after day. *Saṃgava*, *sama*, *viṣṇupriya*, *dharma*, and *virāga*—these five time-periods have been taught by those who know the Self (*ātmavid*). From sunrise, for five *nāḍīs* (a *nāḍī* being twenty-four minutes), the period is called *saṃgava*. Therefore...

It is taught that [the time] is equal to twice that measure. By that much one is dear to Viṣṇu; by that much there is dharma; by that much there is detachment (*virāga*). In that regard, having become the preceding and following [periods], the *saṃgava* and other [intervals] arise from the two channels.

The *muhūrtas* have been described. Among them, at *saṅgava*, there is the pleasure (*prīti*) of Vaikuṇṭha; at *sama*, that of Aniruddha; at *viṣṇupriya*, that of Śiṃśumāra; at *dharma*, that of the submarine fire (*vaḍavāmukhāgni*); and at *virāga*, that of Kapila. Thus, these are the five specific times for the pleasure of the five [deities]. Worship with flowers gathered during the day is the primary practice.

At night, with *rātripuṣpa* flowers. Even when these have been prepared, they are defective if they are budding, withered, stale, remnants of a meal, smelled, faded, untouched by insects, eaten by insects, inhabited by insects, or if they have blossomed in an inauspicious place or during an inauspicious time.
One should not take them up directly.
Having washed one's hands, one should take the flowers in a vessel. Covering them, one should place them in a place that is neither in the sun nor in the heat, so that they do not wither.
A garland (*mālā*) is superior to the offering of single flowers; a wreath (*srak*) is superior to a garland. A garland has a single strand, while a wreath has many strands.
In that regard, one should not tie the flowers with threads, for they would become like discarded offerings (*nirmālya*).
One should never criticize things dedicated to the deity, but should always offer praise. [This applies to] what is dedicated to the deity...

A human being should not take what belongs to the gods, thinking "it is for me. Whatever flower is yellow in color, whether born of water or born of land, that may be gathered in times of distress. Even if not specifically mentioned elsewhere, one should especially avoid those things that ought to be avoided.
The *karāṇḍa* (or *koraṇḍa*), black-colored trees, *kapittha*, *girikarṇikā*, mango, *vibhītaka*, *śirīṣa*, *madayantī*, *nirguṇḍī*, *sinduvāra*, *kiṃśuka*, *śalmalī*,
*japā*, *arka*, *kanaka*, *unmatta*, *kārañja*, poisonous trees, *bandhūka*, *mādhavī*, *nīpa*, *arjuna*, and *pāṭali*.

One should especially avoid these among trees and creepers: *ciñcā*, *kośātakī*, *alābu*, and *śigru* (the word *viśeṣeṇa*—meaning "especially"—is seen only in manuscript G). Likewise, one should avoid the sprouts of barley, mung beans, *priyaṅgu*, flat beans, hemp, *dūrvā* grass, *bhūtṛṇa* grass, and black gram.

One should take [these]. The sprouts of other trees are like discarded offerings (*nirmālya*). One should take only the leaves of the *apāmārga*, *sadābhadra*, *tulasī*, *bilva*, *aśvattha*, *palāśa*, *dhātakī*, *tamāla*, *gandhapūrṇa*, *kṛṣṇā*, *brāhmī*, and *śamī* trees. As for lotuses, one should take only their buds.
One should take it. For water-born flowers such as the *padma* and *utpala*, there is a state of being stale (*paryuṣitatva*) after two days have passed.

Of all roots, the root of *uśīra* alone is distinguished. One should burn incense made of *devadāru* mixed with *candana* and *agaru*—starting from "on smokeless embers" up to "mixed with black *agaru*."
[The portion up to *ṅ cha kośayoḥ* is not seen. It is recommended that [the incense] arise from smokeless charcoal;

one should offer incense consisting of *sāla* and *sarja* resin mixed with black aloe-wood (*kṛṣṇāgaru*), or another [incense] provided it is free from animal parts. In the vessel, [one should use] cow’s ghee or divine [ghee]. [The word *divyena* appears in manuscript *gha*.]

There should be no lamp made with oil, even if it is provided with a wick and lit by a pleasant breeze. The wick or thread should be made of *dukūla*, *kṣauma*, or cotton; it should be new cloth, perfumed with fragrant incense.
One should offer ornaments made of gold and jewels, but not those that are defective or have been previously worn.

"An ornament should not be worn by human beings"— this is the essence extracted from a consideration of various *Saṃhitās*. All other matters as well should be seen in detail within those respective *Saṃhitās*.
In the *Śrī Śāṇḍilya-smṛti*, a distinction is made between substances that are to be avoided and those that are not, extending even to wooden items.
In the *Śrī Viṣṇu-smṛti* and other texts, among fragrant substances derived from living beings,
musk and deer musk are accepted for use as unguents (*aṅgarāga*) during worship (*arcā*).
One should also adopt such practices as wearing white garments and avoiding red flowers other than the *padma* and *kalhāra*.

Furthermore, the purification of one's essential nature— beginning with approaching the Lord for the sake of *yoga-kṣema* (acquisition and preservation)— which was established in the preceding section, must not be forgotten.
The rules regarding acceptance and the acquisition of materials for ritual offerings are thus summarized in various places,
as stated in the venerable Śāṇḍilyasmṛti:
One should never accept even a single kākiṇī from an unchaste woman, a eunuch, an outcast, or an enemy, even when it is offered, even in times of distress.
Thus [and so forth]. And it is said in the *Śrīsāttvata*:
"One should not accept even a small amount of wealth from a thief, an outcast, a fierce man, a eunuch, or one possessed by deceit, greed, and pride."
One may accept it from one who is not a devotee by way of formal courtesy.
Thus it is said; and it is also recorded in the Smṛti, O Lord of the Earth: "In whose house an image of Keśava does not stand..."
One must never eat his food, for it is equal to that which is unfit to be eaten.

Thus [it is said]. In this regard, neither cooked nor uncooked food should be accepted in a house devoid of the constant duty (*nityadharma*) consisting of the worship of Keśava; for the word "food" (*anna*) is employed in both cases, otherwise there would be the specific qualification "cooked food" (*pakvānna*).

Because the practical application [of other rules] is untenable. Furthermore, the detailed expansion of the merits and defects regarding acceptance (*pratigraha*) should be studied in the *Dharmaśāstras*.
Regarding all acts of acceptance occurring in both times of distress and non-distress, the venerable Śaunaka records a specific mantra taught by Yama:
Those by whom it was said while giving gifts, "May Acyuta be pleased," and likewise those who were the recipients, do not come within my domain.
Thus, by means of other mantras such as *bala* and so forth, there is the acceptance [of offerings] and so on for those devoted to each respective deity.

Although the general acceptance of all flowers and other items is taught by means of the *astra-mantra*, nevertheless, specific mantras for *tulasī* are taught in their respective ritual manuals (*kalpas*), such as: "O *tulasī*, you are born from nectar (*amṛta*)."
The rules regarding the means of receiving gifts (*pratigraha*) are as follows:
likewise, even by means of teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and so forth— which are permitted for the sake of livelihood— one must act in accordance with the scriptures.
One should procure appropriate articles for worship through those employed for that purpose.

However, one who already possesses a complete supply of goods acquired previously should not engage in receiving gifts and the like. This is because of the Smṛti injunction: "In times of distress, there is the next [allowable] mode of livelihood"; thus, even when obtaining a livelihood among those permitted, one should desist from it and not make it a constant practice.

One may engage in agriculture or trade performed by oneself, as well as usury and similar activities, provided there is no other possible means of livelihood. Furthermore, even the aforementioned restrictions regarding the Nandana forest, the ears [of grain], and so forth— as stated in passages such as "constantly glorifying Me, striving with firm vows"— are permitted for the purpose of providing flowers, fruits, and other materials for worship.

It falls within the category of "appropriation" (*upādāna*). In this regard, wandering mendicants (*parivrājaka*) must not personally perform tasks such as gathering flowers; for it is stated in the *Yatidharmasamuccaya* that since an expiation is prescribed for the plucking of fruits and flowers, these should be performed with water or with items brought by others. This is the rule.

And the *Vṛddhavasiṣṭha-smṛti* is cited therein: "Having granted safety to all living beings—fish and others in the water, and beasts, deer, reptiles, and so forth on land—one should avoid taking flowers, roots, and fruits; cutting [trees]; honey; meat; speaking untruths; and giving [unlawful gifts]."

However, in the case of others—namely, taking what has not been given, whether produced by oneself or by another, from other gardens and so forth—one may also incur the status of a thief; this is to be understood in various contexts. Furthermore, Manu and others have recorded rules regarding property, houses, wives, and so forth.
One who enjoys his vehicles, beds, seats, wells, gardens, and houses when they have not been given shall incur one-fourth of the sin.
Taking what is not given, violence contrary to the rules, and adultery with another's wife— this is remembered as the threefold bodily [action].
By such statements as these, [it is shown that] here, in the undertaking of all scriptural substances— which serve as the means for propitiation either directly or indirectly—
within one's own capacity, and which are devoid of excessive exertion and physical hardship that would obstruct meditation and the like;

One should proceed according to the proper method; this is the summary of the requisites. For there is the taking up of internal qualities of a previously established substance, as well as the avoidance of excessive exertion (the word *hi* does not appear in the Ga, Ca, and Cha manuscripts).
Among the eight qualities enumerated as necessarily required for those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), Gautama recites:

"Compassion toward all beings, forbearance, freedom from envy, purity, lack of exertion, auspiciousness, non-miserliness, and lack of longing. (Note: The portion from "beginning with 'great effort'" up to "he recites" is omitted in the Kha manuscript.)
"He who possesses these forty sacraments but does not have the eight qualities of the self does not attain union with or residence in the same world as Brahman;
however, he who possesses even a portion of the sacraments and the eight qualities of the self indeed attains union with and residence in the same world as Brahman. This being so—

Just as with the acquisition of external wealth, the primary means for the cultivation of qualities such as self-control, tranquility, and humility— through the service of a true teacher, virtuous conversation, and other causes for the increase of knowledge— is by engaging in them according to what is right (*nyāyataḥ*).
[The word *pravṛttaiḥ* is found only in the Gha, Ṅa, and Cha manuscripts.]

Even the correct acquisition [of offerings] must be included within the category of material requisites (*upādāna*) at the time of procurement— even for one who already possesses previously established and complete external implements for worship— just as the absence of external objects of perception is [included] in the absence of qualities.

Because of the association with despicable qualities designated as the "eighteen outcastes" (caṇḍāla) and the "six vṛṣalas" mentioned in the Mahābhārata and other texts, there would follow the consequence that they are unfit for the sacrificial rites to be performed immediately thereafter. For this very reason, there is a strict insistence on that [exclusion]— [for this very reason, there is a strict adherence to the Śruti (as found in versions kha, ga, ca)].

"Nothing is done elsewhere than what has been heard, and one takes delight in that very thing and finds curiosity therein. Therefore, one should acquire all external and internal requisites for propitiation (*samārādhana*) as is appropriate. Thus has "acquisition" (*upādāna*) been explained.
Thus, with the left leg extended in the posture of worship (*ijyā*), he drew back his right foot, which removes the misfortunes of those who take refuge in him.
Placing one arm upon his knee and the other upon the coils of the serpent,
and subsequently holding the conch and the discus with both arms for the subduing of adversaries;
May the divine Lord of Vaikuṇṭha— who is adorned with goddesses, ornaments, and the like, who resembles a fresh rain-cloud, and who is supreme— grant protection to us and to the worlds.

Now, we shall explain the worship consisting of ritual offerings and the enjoyment [of results], which concerns the nature of the deity to be meditated upon according to the Mantra-siddhānta, by means of a commentary on the *Nitya-grantha* composed by the Bhāṣyakāra:
"In the Mantra-siddhānta, however, there is a distinction of retinues... [and the subordinate elements].
There is an option between two alternative forms [of the ritual].

Among these, first, while demonstrating the connection between what has been performed and what is about to be performed for a particular qualified practitioner, one should recollect the time obtained through the mantra at the commencement of the rite.
One should apply oneself solely to sacrifice; that is the source of all ritual actions.
Thus, having offered praise, he shows the primary portion of the daily duties (*ahorātrakṛtya*) which constitute the essence of the work he intends to compose—
the explanation of the word "atha" as it occurs in the *Nityagrantha*.

It has been established in the Bhāṣya and other works that since the word *atha* can signify "immediate succession" (*anantarya*) as established by its well-known excellence, it is untenable to adopt any other meaning for it. Thus, following the proper exposition of surrender (*prapatti*) in the prose passages beginning with "[I shall speak]" (in manuscripts *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, *jha*), thereafter—
Or, immediately after the attainment of the specific qualification for that ultimate goal,
having contemplated the expansion of His true nature, form, qualities, manifestations, pastimes, and instruments, [one meditates upon Him].

From the statement "one should go for refuge to the All-encompassing One" (*akhila*) and so forth, and according to what will be explained hereafter, it is understood that the author intends to indicate that the prose work concerning such a taking of refuge has already occurred previously. Furthermore, in that [work], there is the phrase "the support of the entire world" (*akhilajagadādhāra*).
The intended meaning is the series of verses beginning with these words, because no other passage is seen to function as the instrument (*karaṇa*) of *prapatti*;
furthermore, the true nature, form, qualities, and manifestations (*vibhūti*) [of the Lord] are elaborated upon precisely in prose, and therein [it is said]:
"Having no other refuge, I take refuge in the pair of Your lotus feet."

Because it is stated explicitly in the text. Therefore, as has been explained, this alone is the meaning of the word *atha* here [the word *atra* does not appear in the Ka, Kha, Ga, and Jha manuscripts].
This is the meaning of the term *paramaikāntin*.

It is both supreme (*parama*) and absolute (*ekānta*), hence "supreme-absolute" (*paramaikānta*). One who possesses this is a "supreme-absolute devotee" (*paramaikāntī*). "Absolute" (*ekānta*) refers to a singular certainty regarding both that which is to be attained (*prāpya*) and the means of attainment (*prāpaka*). These two together constitute "supreme-absolute" (*paramaikānta*).
Alternatively, the compound may be analyzed as "one who is both supreme and absolute" (*paramaś cāsau ekāntī ca*).

In that regard as well, supremacy [of the path] arises from the conjunction of being the exclusive means (*ananya-upāyatva*) and having no other purpose (*ananya-prayojanatva*). Furthermore, being the exclusive means extends up to the state of having no other deity. As it has been said:
"I have indeed heard that my devotees are of four kinds."
Among them, those who are single-minded are the best, for they have no other deity.
Thus [it is said]. And "having no other purpose" extends to the point of being independent of even the bliss of self-realization. This too has been stated:
"But those three types of devotees who remain are considered to be seekers of fruits;
all of them are subject to falling away, whereas the awakened one partakes in liberation."

Thus, by this same logic, the intention that [the bliss of experiencing the Lord] also results in the bliss of experiencing the Blessed One has been refuted; for even the bliss of the liberated is dependent upon another independent being, like the pleasure of a world-ruler tasting milk from the mouth of a parrot in his inner apartments.

This is because it has been established for the sake of one's own spiritual delight. Furthermore, it was demonstrated in the previous section that such supreme single-minded devotion (*paramaikāntitva*) is possible even for those established in the systems of Mantra-siddhānta and others. Indeed, even today, this is observed to be possible for those who hear the three prose texts (*gadyatraya*) and other works exactly as they are from a true teacher.

For in that state, through the definitive determination of what is higher and lower exactly as it is, and by uprooting anything else, such qualities as being devoted to no other deity are established. And the Blessed One himself described that very state: [The Blessed One himself said: (Note: The word *ca* is not seen in the Gha manuscripts.)
Those who are devoted to no other deity, who are dear to my devotees,
and who have come to me alone for refuge— they are proclaimed as my true devotees.

Thus, through the ascertainment of the nature of the Lord—who is the unsurpassed object of enjoyment—and by turning away from other objects, the state of having no other purpose is also established therein; that state in which the Lord becomes exceedingly near, like a friend or kinsman, and is fit to be served according to one's own will. As it was said by the venerable Śaunaka:
For those who have turned their faces away from Govinda and whose minds are attached to sense objects,
that supreme Brahman remains far, far away.
Those men who have fixed their minds on Govinda through absorption in Him,
and who have renounced the objects of the senses— it should be understood that [the fruit of their practice] exists in His presence.
Thus,
for those who are exclusively devoted to the Supreme Lord, the avoidance of other deities is the rule;
likewise, for those who have renounced limited objects, the renunciation of limited other deities constitutes the discipline.
Desiring the success of their actions, people here worship the deities;
for in the world of men, success born of action is quickly attained.
O Awakened One, because Brahmā, Śitikaṇṭha, and whatever other deities are remembered do not yield limited fruit, they are not served by those who have awakened.
Thus, by means of the presence or absence of attachment to limited fruits—
and by means of the establishment of connection or non-connection with a deity— it is said: "He who is attached to the Supreme Self is detached from the non-Supreme Self."
Being completely liberated from all cravings, he is worthy to consume almsfood.

Thus, for the renunciant (pravrajita) who has been established [in this teaching] as one detached from all objects other than the Supreme Self, there is the avoidance of other deities; likewise, for the enlightened (pratibuddha) qualified person even within the other three stages of life (āśrama). Furthermore, the abandonment by renunciants of the worship of other deities is recorded in the Smṛti. Atri says:

One should perform the worship of Viṣṇu and of the deities who are identical with Him throughout the three periods of the day, consisting of salutations, offerings, and so forth; one should not do so for anyone else.
Thus [it is said]:
"The Lord is the Blessed Viṣṇu, the Supreme Self, the Great Unborn;
the sole ruler of the moving and the unmoving, the supreme goal of ascetics."
Thus it is said. Furthermore, he himself stated:
"If one who has taken refuge in another symbol of Viṣṇu meditates upon or worships that other, even after hundreds of millions of kalpas, no higher goal is found for him."
Thus it is said. In this way, the avoidance of other deities by all those who have awakened has already been shown. By this [it is meant]:
"If one does not perform a salutation upon seeing an image of a deity or an ascetic carrying the triple staff (tridaṇḍin), one becomes pure through fasting."

Such passages as these should be understood as referring to those other than the awakened (the unenlightened). Even for the awakened, this [prohibition] finds its scope in images of the Lord and His retinue that are suitable for one's own salutation. However, in the case of persisting in what is forbidden, there is unworthiness for worship.
Thus, by the word "exclusively devoted to the Supreme" (paremaikāntin), the specific qualified person is described:
"Neither one who violates another's wife nor one who steals another's property should touch me, disregarding [this rule]; and having touched me, he becomes fallen."

All such [factors] that cause one to become unworthy should be examined in their respective places; and they have been summarized by the lords of the Vaṅgivaṃśa dynasty through the common application of all substances suitable for worship:
Apart from not being an object of prohibition, there is no other quality that serves as a cause for the Supreme Lord’s pleasure regarding the objects used in His own worship.

Thus [it is said]. For even the worshipper possesses the status of being an object of worship (*arcanāṅgavastutva*) without distinction. And just as in the case of excellent species—such as tulasī leaves, lotus flowers, mango fruits, and the water of the Gaṅgā—they become subjects of prohibition due to various causes of defilement, so too it is with the worshipper, because of some cause of defilement from whatever source.

It becomes an object of prohibition due to its unfitness for expiation; otherwise, there would be the consequence of contradicting such scriptural passages as, "Not one who has not desisted from evil conduct [attains this]," and because expiatory rites are prescribed even for images and other objects touched by things that are sources of defilement. For even in the case of a knower of Brahman, there are statements regarding the non-clinging of future sins.
Furthermore, it is established in the Bhāṣya and other works that [the rule regarding meat] concerns objects such as those obtained through negligence (*prāmādikaviṣaya*).

This meaning is also proven by such Sūtras as "And there is permission for all food in case of danger to life, because that is seen [in scripture]," and so forth. Moreover, in this context, a figurative treatment (*upacāra*) like that applied to a king is prescribed.

And just as the conduct of service toward a king consists primarily in the avoidance of transgressions, so it is here as well. And just as in the case of a virtuous king, even those servants who have committed offenses become faultless through a mere apology, so it is here too;
thus there is the attainment of that [result]. This also is summarized:
Whether through ignorance or knowledge, even when offenses have occurred, there is only one prayer: "Forgive me; may you accept my atonement."
Thus [it is said]. As for what was stated immediately prior:
"Because of unfitness for worship and the like, no one fails to commit an offense;
therefore, by one who has not disregarded the consideration of the faults of every agent,"
By the grace of this deity alone, everyone is worthy of performing that rite.

Thus, even this indicates the fitness for requesting forgiveness; otherwise, the injunction to offer the prayer "forgive me" would be untenable (the reading *prārthanānupapatteḥ* is found in the Ka, Kha, Ga, Jha, and Kośa manuscripts). Nor does this imply that one who has committed an offense [is thereby absolved].
One should be fearless, according to the maxim: "It is better to avoid touching mud from afar than to wash it off.
Faults are those which bring about a state of unfitness for action.
And here, the Blessed One spoke thus regarding the faults that cause unfitness for action:
"Listen, O beautiful one, to the definitive determination of food according to its true nature."
O Vasundharā, listen now to that which is food and that which is non-food.
O Mādhavī, whatever person eats this food for the sake of my yoga—
even if that person has committed an inauspicious deed— becomes established in dharma.

One should always consume food that is suitable for work; for all types of rice and *śāli* grains are indeed suitable for this purpose. Furthermore, from that [food], the maintenance of life proceeds, which is the basis for the engagement in all activities.
I shall declare those things which are unfit for action and by which I am currently displeased:
my devotees must never eat the food of a king.
But by eating the king’s food, a great offense would be committed;
therefore, my dear, one should not commit the thirty-two offenses.
Regarding the foods, drinks, and edibles that I have prescribed:
whoever approaches me without having chewed a tooth-stick (dantakāṣṭha) [is at fault].
But a knower of dharma does not commit a second offense;
for that man who, having engaged in sexual union, touches me, [commits a grave transgression].
O Vasundharā, O Goddess, I shall consider this my third offense:
that one who, having seen a corpse, approaches me.
But the fourth offense, O Earth, I do not forgive:
he who approaches me after having touched— or seen— a woman in her courses.
But seeing this fifth offense, I truly cannot forgive it:
that you have performed the funeral rites for a corpse without even having inquired whether it was actually dead.
O Vasundharā, I do not forgive this sixth offense:
that at the time of the ritual for my worship, the pitiless one releases a wind.
And this is my seventh offense, O Goddess, which does not please me:
that someone voids excrement at the very time of my worship.
This is my eighth offense, which I do not approve of here:
that someone speaks aloud during the time of my worship.
Furthermore, O Vasundharā, I cannot endure a ninth offense:
that anyone who beholds me while clothed in blue garments.
O Goddess, this tenth offense does not please me:
that someone, having put on but a single garment, should approach me.
The eleventh offense, however, is that which causes me displeasure:
when a laborer, being angry, performs his tasks.
And I shall reckon this as the twelfth offense, O Vasundharā:
he who would offer me flowers that are unfit for ritual use.
But I shall not mention the thirteenth offense, O Vasundharā:
he who approaches [his teacher] wearing a garment dyed with safflower.
O Vasundharā, O Goddess, I do not forgive the fourteenth offense:
whoever should ever touch me while I am in the dark.
O Vasundharā, I shall assign fifteen offenses to him who causes my rituals to be performed with black cloth.
I consider that to be the sixteenth offense, without a doubt:
he who, while shaking his garment, would direct it toward me.
I consider him who, having eaten the meat of a boar, partakes [of it], to have committed the seventeenth offense; of this there is no doubt.
O Mādhavī, he confesses his nineteenth offense:
"He who approaches me while eating the web-footed [or web-killer] crane."
O Vasundharā, O Mādhavī, I shall reckon this as my twentieth offense:
that he who, out of delusion, touches a lamp after having already touched you.
O Vasundharā, I shall reckon that as the twenty-first offense:
he who, having gone to a cremation ground, approaches me.
I shall inflict upon him the twenty-second offense;
having eaten oil-cake, he must then approach me— or rather, according to another reading, "approach the treasury."
O Mādhavī, that man who looks upon me while disregarding my immersion [in the water] would incur the offense of the thirty-three [gods] against me.
O Vasundharā, O proud lady, I consider that person who performs a prostration with only one hand to have committed twenty-four offenses.
O Earth, I do not forgive that fifth offense:
he who approaches me solely for the purpose of acquiring wealth from others.
O Earth, I do not forgive that twenty-seventh offense:
those who eat here without having first given away nine-tenths of the rice.
O Vasundharā, I reckon that as the twenty-eighth offense:
he who desires to give me incense without first offering a flower.
O Vasundharā, I acknowledge this as the twenty-ninth offense:
that mortal who approaches me while wearing his shoes.
O Earth, I shall consider this a grave offense:
that he who awakens me by striking the kettle-drum.
O Vasundharā, I shall designate the thirty-first offense:
when one who is afflicted by undigested humors approaches me,
one should know that to be a great offense, the thirty-second and most supreme here.

Thus, for one who avoids these and other causes of unworthiness, and who, when such a lapse occurs, performs the appropriate expiation with remorse, there exists the qualification for worship in this [path].
There is also a specific qualification based on birth and so forth.
Thus, a specific distinction of eligibility based on birth and other factors is also heard in the scriptures. As it is stated in the Śrīsāttvata:
"For those who have perfected the eightfold yoga and whose minds are devoted to the heart-rite (hṛdyāga)..."
The authority of yogins would reside in one who lies within the heart.
For those Brahmins who know the Vedas and have been liberated from the mixed scriptures,
there is authority in the mantra consisting of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha).
Nor is it otherwise.
For the three castes beginning with the Kṣatriyas who have truly taken refuge,
there is indeed no entitlement to the ritual procedure of the fourfold manifestation (cāturvyūha) without the mantra.
But for the discerning, when the mantra-wheel is active and characterized by sovereign power,
they have completely cast off the sense of "mine" and their minds are devoted to their own spiritual duties.

When the sequence of initiation has been obtained, there is indeed the qualification for the four classes of devotees to properly [engage] with the Supreme Lord through action, speech, and mind, provided their conduct is established.
Thus, for those who have correctly understood it, this single procedure for Samānakarṇa, established as it is and preceded by the mantra, is now set forth in three sections.

Thus it is said. Furthermore, in the case of the *jayā* and other [types of initiation], one should observe the distinctions such as those between the *āpta* (the authoritative teacher) and others. Ultimately, for all of them, the attainment of the Blessed One is the same.
This applies even to those devotees (*bhāgavata*) who are incomplete [in their practice].
Thus [ends] the section on sacrifice and Vedic study;
now we shall explain the section on what is to be tasted, when the fourth mealtime has arrived.

The treatises of the great sages— such as Manu, Parāśara, Pārāśarya, Śuka, Śaunaka, and others— who had mastered all the Vedas and their meanings, who clarified the sense of Vedic passages as they themselves understood them, and who had directly realized the true nature of both the higher and lower principles through the power of their own yoga.

[In place of the phrase "the compositions of the great sages," the word "supplements to the Vedas" (vedopabṛṃhaṇāni) is seen in the Kha, Ga, Ca, and Jha manuscripts. One should practice through hearing, reflection, recitation, and so forth.
This very duty for that time was stated by Vyāsa: "One should supplement the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas."

"According to Dakṣa, however, one should practice the sixth and seventh [limbs] by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Likewise, one should observe such statements as: "Having eaten and performed the *upasthāna* rite, one should always recite the Purāṇas. [This is seen in the Jha manuscripts: "One should practice through hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), recitation (*japa*), and so forth. This very point was stated by Vyāsa:

Regarding the duties for that time: "One should augment the Veda with the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Dakṣa, however, states: "One should study the sixth and seventh [Vedas] by means of the Itihāsas and Purāṇas. Furthermore, one should observe such injunctions as: "Having eaten and having attended upon [the deity], one should always recite the Purāṇas."

For one who has no need for supplementary elaboration (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), it is appropriate to perform the recitation (*japa*) of those portions of the Veda that are to be so elaborated. Even therein, it is stated in the *Śrī-Śāṇḍilya-smṛti* and other texts that only those portions which directly propound the Blessed Lord are to be recited; this applies especially to those who delight in concise summaries and are devoted to the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*).
This is the instruction for the recitation of the mantra that is the essence of all and is all-pervasive.
It is stated everywhere that even at the time of recitation and so forth, one must avoid silence toward the guru and others. And thus said Audhāyana:
"During the study of the Veda, one should show honor to the guru and others."
If a guru or a Vaiṣṇava should arrive during the course of the japa,
one should perform hospitality such as conversation and worship for him, and having obtained his permission, [proceed].
Having caused [the text] to be recited, one should then perform the remainder of the recitation with a concentrated mind;
for all beings originate from Him, and men have their refuge in the feet of Viṣṇu.
For indeed, it is by virtue of that root that all ritual actions become fruitful.
Thus [it is said]. In that regard, the observances (*niyama*), such as silence and reflection on the meaning of mantras, are to be adopted here and there.

Furthermore, discussion with disciples, teachers, and fellow students who seek the highest good, who are free from malice, and who are devoid of passion—this "dialogue" (*saṃvāda*), which consists of mutual instruction, is also included because it is not different in its fruit, namely the ascertainment of reality (*tattva-nirṇaya*).

It should be practiced at the very time of one's own study (*svādhyāya*), just like the *itihāsas*, *purāṇas*, and so forth. And they record in their tradition: "During the recitation performed during the first watch of the night—which falls within the period of approaching the deity—one should mutter (*japet*), teach disciples, retain [the texts], and reflect upon them (*vicārayet*).

Furthermore, reflection (*vicāra*), practice (*abhyasana*), and muttering (*japa*) [are synonyms]. [Note: In lexicons other than the *Amara-kośa*, the particle *ca* does not appear after these terms. It has been said:

And immediately after the procedure for the secondary sacrifice (*anuyāga*), having sipped water again according to the *Śrīsāttvata*, it is said: "Being purified once more, one should go to the house of the Lord," having placed [the senses] upon the ground together with mind, intellect, and ego.
Like a tortoise, one should withdraw the four limbs and the fifth, the head, just as it does there.
Having thus performed the prostration with eight limbs (*aṣṭāṅga-praṇāma*) and having paid homage with the eight limbs, one should then sit down before the Lord Hari.
One should study the scriptures and investigate the meaning of their statements through such investigation.

Thus, here [are included] the hearing, reflection, recitation, chanting, and so forth, as well as debates and discussions, concerning the histories (itihāsa), purāṇas, hymns (stotra), the Upaniṣads (nigamānta), the two [Vedānta] systems, the all-pervading mantras, and other such texts which please the Blessed One and delight one's own mind.
Harshness, falsehood, slander, and idle chatter— these four types of verbal conduct act as the oil for the lamp of wisdom born of yoga.

Furthermore, all activities that serve as obstacles to the arising of various verbal evils demonstrated by such passages as "ityādi" become *svādhyāya* (Vedic study), either collectively or individually, as the case may be.
The essence of *svādhyāya* is this: one should practice the recitation of the scriptures in a manner conducive to tranquility (*śama*) and other virtues. For it has been said:
In the Mahābhārata:
That which has been heard, but which leads neither to dispassion, nor to dharma, nor to peace—
even if well-composed in words, it is merely the cawing of a crow.

Thus, there is no liberation for one who is devoted solely to the science of grammar, and so forth; furthermore, when the sun is turning red at the evening twilight, one should perform the evening twilight worship (*sāyaṃsaṃdhyopāsana*) and the evening fire-oblation (*sāyaṃhoma*), according to the sūtras.

Furthermore, according to one's capacity, there is the approach to the Blessed One (bhagavadabhigamana) [as found in versions ka, kha, ga, ca, jha], followed by eating preceded by the approach to the Blessed One and the offering of oblations (havirnivedana). If the meal is interrupted due to some cause, there is the recitation of the *prāṇāgnihotra* mantras. Thereafter, there is the study of sacred texts (*svādhyāya*) and yoga appropriate for the night.
The sequence: In this regard, the authorities are as follows:
"One should approach the Blessed One at both twilights;
one should not consume any food, even that which is purifying, without first offering it to Hari."
Twice-born men must eat their meal in the evening and in the morning as enjoined by the Vedas;
they should not eat in between, for this rule is equal in importance to the Agnihotra sacrifice.
If his meal is interrupted, he should recite the mantras of the Prāṇāgnihotra;
he should spend the first and last watches of the night in the study of the Vedas,
applying himself during those preceding and following periods of the night.

And so forth. Regarding the recitation of the Veda (*svādhyāya*) during the first watch of the night, which is to be performed by one who has no other purpose and is authorized to do so: on the thirteenth lunar day, at the time known as *pradoṣa* (the first part of the night), it must be avoided. As it has been summarized:
In the *Kālavidhāna*:

"The practice of silence (*maunācaraṇa*) [is prescribed] during the great twilight (*mahāpradoṣa*), at the two equinoxes and solstices, on the fifteenth, first, and eighth lunar days, and on the lunar day presided over by Kali."
And at the onset of night, the Creator has declared that men should not perform the act of Vedic study for the Lord of Love.
Thus it is said. And this is recorded in the *Smṛtyarṇava*:

"One who has performed the twilight prayers on the thirteenth day, yet fails to remember [the Lord] on that thirteenth day, does not attain his own welfare. (Variant readings: *saṃsmaran* for *asmaran*; *trayodaśyāṃ ca smaran* for *trayodaśyāṃ asmaran*).
One should observe silence during the half of the night conjoined with one-eighth part of the day.

Thus, since silence is prescribed for the time known as *pradoṣa* during states other than those fixed for the *sāvitrī-homa* and so forth, even the recitation (*japa*) of mantras and the like must be avoided. As it is stated in the *Kṛṣṇamantrakalpa*:

Only the recitation of one's own Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) is prohibited; however, the recitation of mantras (*mantrajapa*) and so forth is prescribed. And the necessity of the eight-syllable mantra recitation was stated by Bodhāyana:
"In this manner, having begun with the Guru, one should perform the practice of the mantra."
The wise man should daily recite the eight-syllable mantra eight thousand times.
"Without having recited the eight-syllable mantra, I shall not eat anything;
I shall recite it for as long as I live"—having thus resolved, one should thereafter recite it day after day.

For one whose recitation of the eight-syllabled mantra is constant— whether performed as a regular obligation (*nitya*), on specific occasions (*naimittika*), or for the sake of a desired goal (*kāmya*)— the daily worship of the deity is prescribed as a constant duty (*nitya-devārcanā*).

Thus it is said. Furthermore, at the time of the injunction for silence (*mauna*), there is no interruption of the Lord’s dharma; for at that time, the very performance of silence according to the rule is itself the nature of service to the Lord, whether it pertains to the sphere of engagement (*pravṛtti*) or the sphere of cessation (*nivṛtti*).

The command of the Blessed One must always be followed; thus, there is the accomplishment of flawless practice (*acchidrānuṣṭhāna*). Although it is prohibited for one who does not perform that specific ritual to see Lord Hari and so forth during the evening twilight (*pradoṣa*), and this was indeed observed by the Paramaikāntins such as the Commentator (Śrī Śaṅkarācārya) and others, nevertheless—[regarding the worship in one's own home]...
In this context, the word *sva-* is not seen in the Gha, Ṅa, Cha, and Ka manuscripts.

Regarding the phrase "because of its being performed for that" (*tatkriyatvāt*)—referring to the worship of one's own personal deity (*svagṛhārcā*)—the reading found in many manuscripts is *tadanujñā tatkriyatvāt* (with permission for that, because of its being performed for that);
however, in the Ka and Jha manuscripts, only *tatkriyātvāt* occurs. And it has been stated thus:
In the *Bodhāyanīya-purāṇasārasamuccaya*:

"The Lord situated in the assembly hall (*āsthāna*) should always be served; He situated in the celestial chariot (*vimāna*) may be served according to the time; however, in one's own home, the Lord should be served at all times, except during midnight."
Thus, even at midnight, if a specific occasion such as an eclipse occurs,
the service of the Blessed One, recitation (*japa*), and so forth— preceded by ritual bathing and other rites— are enjoined as mandatory; therefore, there is no contradiction.

According to the view of some, the performance of *svādhyāya* (Vedic study) and *yoga* should be carried out by collecting [the relevant passages] even before the *anuyāga*. Furthermore, these two— *svādhyāya* and *yoga*— are taught as being collected together prior to the daily *anuyāga* in certain specific *saṃhitās*, as compiled by Nārāyaṇa Muni:
Having bowed again to the Lord of Gods during the fourth part of the day,
he performed his own prescribed recitation over the mantras consisting of twelve, eight, and six syllables, and so forth.
One should especially recite the mantra one thousand and eight times,
or one hundred and eight times, or at least ten times according to one's capacity.

Having paid homage to the Guru and the others, as well as the seed-syllables (*bīja*), powers (*śakti*), and so forth, and having prostrated before the Lord, the Master of Mantras, he gazes [at Him] from the feet upward. [Note: The phrase "āpādādavalokayan" (gazing from the feet upward) is absent in the Kha and Ga manuscripts, extending from that point up to "svadhāma nītvā deveśam" (having led the Lord of Gods to His own abode).]
Having recited [the mantra] for a very long time and having established himself in yoga, he should bow to Hari;

then, having led the Lord of Gods to his own abode [with the thought "to his own abode" (svadhāma) in the mind, according to the Ka-kosha], he should remain prostrate before Him along with His retinue.
There, having worshipped with the *arghya* and other offerings, and having performed protection by means of the lords of the *astra* mantras,
and having prostrated again and again, and then having arranged the fire-oblation (*homa*) and so forth,
and having performed the subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*), the person becomes one who has accomplished his purpose.
Thus it is said.
This very sequence has been explained in detail by his gurus, the lords of the Vaṅgi dynasty. For instance:
"The fourth part of the day that has arrived is declared for the purpose of Vedic study."
Having informed that Viṣṇu and having obtained his permission as well, [he proceeded].
Having withdrawn the mind from all external objects along with the senses,
reciting the eight-syllable mantra preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma), being self-restrained,
and having already become concentrated through your supreme devotion.

Having performed the ritual placements (nyāsa) as prescribed upon the fingers of the hands and the body, one should likewise assign the gurus, the mantra, the ṛṣi, the meter (chandas), and the deity in their proper order.
One should bow with the head to Śakti and Bīja, thus showing due respect; first, one should bow to the God.
This salutation with the head is offered to all the Gurus [and those who came before].
Now, salutations even to those gurus who bestow the knowledge of the mantra;
salutations to you, the King of Mantras; salutations to you, whose essence is the eight-syllabled [mantra].
Salutations to you, O support of consciousness, who are designated as the Supreme Brahman;
abiding within the heart, you restrain all individual selves.
Salutation to Hari, the inner controller of the eight-syllabled mantra,
the Seer; salutation to her who presides over the number of syllables in the great eight-syllabled mantra (or, who distinguishes those numbers).
And I bow my head to the goddess Gāyatrī,
in whom the power of the mantra resides, who grants the desired object to those who take refuge in her.
I bow down to that Śakti, whose foot is for Nārāyaṇa; I prostrate before her.
The seed-syllable arising from the letter *A* denotes Vāsudeva.

I bow with my head to that *praṇava*, the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and source of this [mantra]. [In the Ka, Kha, Ga, Ca, and Jha manuscripts, the following is read prior to the verse beginning with "The power of the mantra" (*mantra-śaktiḥ*): "Also to the deity of the mantra... I bow to the deity of the mantra as well.
The supreme, imperishable Self.
I bow my head to Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman, Hari;
and having thus prostrated before the gurus and others, I worship them with perfumes and other offerings.
Constantly gazing at the image of the Blessed One from its base upward,
one should recite the eight-syllable mantra while reflecting upon its meaning.
Eagerly reciting either one thousand and eight times, or a hundred, or ten,
at the conclusion of the recitation, he should meditate in his mind upon Acyuta according to the described form.
Having thus mentally formed a union with [the Lord] together with His consort, His retinue, His gatekeepers, and the lords of the Gaṇas, he remained for a very long time with a joyful mind.
Then, rising from that yoga and prostrating like a staff,
he praised him with many hymns and also performed circumambulations.

Having stood before the God of Gods and placed his own joined palms upon his head— [following this, the half-verse "jitanta" is seen as an addition in the printed *Kārikā*: "with the mantra *jitanta*, one should go for refuge to that God"]— one should take refuge in that deity.
Then, when he has granted fearlessness to that person who has sought refuge in him and is pleased with him, [the following occurs].
He shall be fearless toward all beings, with a mind at peace, once that action— which is both difficult to attain and hard to perform— has been completed.
Having offered the *arghya* as before and having offered oneself with the mantra of self-offering—
whether as a servant, a disciple, a son, or one's own self.
With reverence, one should offer one's own self along with one's own water to the Supreme Self,
and deposit one's own agency within that very Supreme Self.
One should ask forgiveness for one's own offenses, whether committed intentionally or unintentionally,
and for those that are innumerable, unbearable, or being committed day and night.
O All-pervading Lord, whether through ignorance, or through incapacity, or even through some offense committed out of a wicked disposition, you ought to forgive me with compassion.
Whatever unwholesome deed has been committed by me, whether through ignorance or knowledge, let all of that be forgiven; and accept me as your servant.
O Supreme Person, forgive all these transgressions committed by me day after day under the pretext of ritual service.
Thus entreated with bowed heads by the Supreme Self, who was gracious,
who forgave every transgression, and who showered the nectar of compassion;
By him who possesses a multitude of infinite qualities, such as affection, magnanimity, and virtuous conduct.
By his own supreme compassion, he who is a refuge for the refugeless,
having summoned him with a wondrous voice sweet with a smiling glance, said:
He himself placed that pair of feet upon his own head,
carrying them while all his impurities were destroyed by the touch of those feet.
Having sat for a very long time before him with supreme joy,
he then rose and bowed down to him again and again.
Having reminded [the deity] of his own abode and having bowed down for its departure,
one should then offer a pair of sandals and bring the Lord there,
together with his consort, his retinue, and the lords of the various classes of gatekeepers.
Then, he prepared a bed with a suitable arrangement, provided with an excellent pillow, and well-adorned.
When the Supreme Self had ascended the couch of infinite splendor,
the two goddesses likewise sat down on either side of the Lord, each according to her respective place.
When the commanders of the army and the others were all seated according to their respective positions,
then the guest-offering, water for the feet, water for sipping, betel, and so forth, were presented as was appropriate.
Having offered [the gift] to the Lord, who is joined by the Goddess and accompanied by his attendants,
he prostrated himself like a staff upon the ground again and again before Hari.
Then, desiring to perform the daily ritual beginning with the secondary sacrifice (anuyāga),
he was granted permission by the other [deity] to go outside himself.
Nirganduka, having entrusted the Lord to the gatekeepers and others,
as well as to Caṇḍa and the other guardians of the harem, departed with a heavy heart.
He likewise [worshipped] Kumuda and the other lords of the Gaṇas, as well as the weapons such as the discus,
and especially Garuḍa, as well as Śeṣa and the consumer of Śeṣa (Ananta).
Having prostrated, one should cause the Lord to be remembered with affection, reverence, and trepidation—
treating him as if depositing one's very life or entrusting him with a great treasure.
As if intending to deposit his own eye, as if entrusting it to the Destroyer at the end of the aeon—
may all of you, together with your hosts, remain armored in every direction.
"And remain attentive;
I entrust to you my Lord, my Guru, my father, and my mother."
Protect Hari, Śrī, and the Earth from all sides;
always manifest yourselves to me in whatever forms have been assigned to you.
"Having gone for refuge to you, O you whose wealth has departed, I am departing.
Having thus informed them, he should afterwards pray to Hari with these words.
Indeed, O Lord, you alone sustain and support the entire world, including both the mobile and the immobile,
from Brahmā down to the smallest plant.
And at the end, you will withdraw [all things] by means of your own respective forms as you desire;
by whom, O God, are you protected, or by whom are you harmed?
May you yourself protect you— the gods, the fierce ones, and even the guardians—
as well as me, my own, and this entire household without exception.
O Madhusūdana, having fulfilled my own resolve by your mere will,
I, trusting in you, have entrusted this [world] to you, O granter of the needs of those who seek them.
"Having requested thus, 'When you have arrived at the proper time, you should give everything to me,' and having prostrated before him like a staff,"

Having reported all— the fire-oblation, the rites for the ancestors, the animal sacrifice, the subsequent offerings, and so forth— he, being commissioned by him with the desire to perform them, [proceeded].
Gazing at him alone with eyes whose lashes were moist with affection,
he went forth very slowly with his hands joined in reverence upon his head.
Having bolted the pair of doors, performed the protection rite, and paid obeisance,
one should perform the ritual action according to the rules, beginning with the fire-oblation and ending with the secondary sacrifice.

Thus, because self-study (*svādhyāya*) and yoga are taught here as being combined within the midst of the eightfold sacrifice (*aṣṭāṅgayajana*), it is explained in the secret traditions (*rahasyāmnāya*) and elsewhere— and is not contradicted here— that when one is unable to perform them in their proper sequence due to differences in place, time, or state, even the sacrifices and other rites may be combined at another appropriate time.
It has been indicated that the integration of self-study (*svādhyāya*) and yoga in their proper measure at the appropriate times occurs everywhere;
thus, self-study has already been shown and explained. This concludes the section on self-study.
Yoga:

Now we shall explain yoga. In that regard, a specific type of yoga for which no other purpose need be undertaken has already been shown previously, as stated in the Śrī-Śāṇḍilya-smṛti, beginning with the words, "This Supreme Self is such... and so forth.
Furthermore, the lack of contradiction among the methods of yoga taught in the *Śrīsāttvata* and other scriptures has been thoroughly established.
Regarding this, the Blessed Lord Parāśara spoke as follows: [In that regard, the Blessed Lord Parāśara spoke thus—ka kha ga jha].
The union of that distinguished movement of the mind, which depends upon one's own effort, with Brahman is designated as yoga.

Thus it is said. This alone is the yoga for one who has no other purpose; however, other minor yogas taught in the Yoga-śāstras are indeed intended for the sake of various supernatural attainments (*siddhi*). Even for one who has no other purpose, there exist differences in the procedures (*prakriyā*) due to the various types of *nyāsa* and *vidyā* mentioned here and there, as well as the different systems described in the respective *Saṃhitās* concerning the objects of one's own steadfastness.

Although the forms, qualities, vibhūtis, and so forth to be connected [with Him] are manifold, nevertheless, they reside in the Supreme Brahman, the glorious Puruṣottama— the Lord of all— whose essential nature is defined by the pentad beginning with bliss which characterizes His own being, and who is qualified by the specific forms and other attributes revealed by the various Vidyās.
The nature of yoga as the uninterrupted flow of mental activity is common to all; for this very reason,
Śāṇḍilya declared that among the four distinct duties of the stages of life (āśrama) which have been observed, yoga alone is equal in its application to meditative absorption (samādhi).

Thus, the statement from the Mahābhārata is well-concordant; the words are also concordant. The subjects to be contemplated in yoga are exactly as they have been described for contemplation in the Nityagadyastotra and other works composed by the Bhāṣyakāra and others.
This should be reflected upon by those firmly established in that tradition. In the *Śrīvaikuṇṭhagadya*, however, [the word "tu" (but/however) is read as an insertion in manuscript *gha*;

in manuscripts *ka* and *kha*, it is read as "śabdaḥ"]. Having prescribed surrender (*prapatti*) alone as the means to liberation for one who has no other recourse, [it is taught that this is like a hungry and healthy person eating milk-rice; in manuscript *ka* and *kha*, it reads "like eating milk-rice"].

Furthermore, the specific distinctions of meditative yoga (*dhyānayoga*) and the specific distinctions of the subsequent contemplations (*anusaṃdhāna*) connected therewith have been elaborated precisely as being for one's own purpose. For instance,

beginning with the passage "the distinction of the nature, maintenance, and activity of the threefold sentient and non-sentient [worlds] which are under His control," [it is explained] by way of His sovereignty (*svāmitva*).

Having stated the firm resolve toward the Refuge— which consists of both the goal to be attained and the means of attainment— by means of the passage ending with "accepting [him] as a friend and as a teacher," [the text] next describes the desire for the specific human goal (puruṣārtha) with the words: "having as his sole desire perpetual and ultimate service."

Having established that there is no other purpose [for his life], and considering that for the sake of attaining Him there is no means other than taking refuge at His two lotus feet even in a thousand crores of kalpas,
he thus declares the contemplation of having no other means (*ananyopāyatā*) with the words beginning "of that very Blessed One" (*tasyaiva bhagavataḥ*).

Having described the attributes suitable for being a refuge by the words ending with "of the glorious one of great majesty," one should take refuge in the pair of lotus feet with a total disposition directed toward them, which alone revives those who have no other self;
thus, the very act of choosing refuge is the means to liberation. [And as the means to liberation...]

Having performed this, one should then daily reflect in this manner for the sake of sustaining one's own life; thus, for one who is established solely in independent *prapatti*, it is according to the principle of eating and so forth for the purpose of preserving life. (Note: "For the purpose of preserving life" is the reading found in the Gha manuscript, whereas elsewhere the text reads "for the purpose of daily [preserving life]").

Having performed a specific recollection for the sake of reviving herself, and having extensively described the attainment of the supreme state within, she— on a great divine yogic seat upon the serpent Ananta,
filling the universe with her own radiance while in the divine world of glorious sovereignty and other splendors— [remained].

[He saw] the Blessed One seated together with Śrī, who was like unto himself in her virtue, beauty, qualities, and grace, and who was commanding all the attendants—including those who ate the remnants of his meals—to perform various services appropriate to his particular state. Thus [he beheld] the Blessed One... [and so forth].

Having described complete meditation with the passage ending "having seen Nārāyaṇa through the yoga of meditation," [the text] begins again with "of the Blessed One" and, up until the end of the section on increasing the hope for service to the Blessed One, [it says]: "If the descendant of Kakutstha would lead me [there], that would be worthy of him; when will my husband see me? and so forth.
Having set forth the various modes of his desire for the attainment of the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*),

and with that very intention augmented by [the Lord’s] grace, he approached the Blessed One; having prostrated from afar before the Blessed Nārāyaṇa and his entire retinue with the mantra beginning "To the whole retinue," he rose again and again.
Having performed a prostration [immediately after], this subsequent connection was stated: having become bowed down with extreme trepidation and humility,
[he was addressed] by the gatekeepers, who are the leaders of the Lord’s assembly, with words full of affection and compassion.

Having been properly gazed upon by the Blessed One with his vision and having been granted permission by each of them, he approaches the Blessed One and, requesting, "Please accept me for the sake of performing exclusive and ultimate service," he prostrates and offers himself to the Blessed One. Then, by the Blessed One...

By a glance from one whose conduct was beyond all bounds and filled with excessive affection, he was accepted and authorized for every possible state of being, appropriate for all places, all times, and all circumstances;
yet, bowing low with extreme trepidation and humility, he remained waiting, asking "What shall I do? (kiṃkurvāṇaḥ).

With palms joined in reverence, he should attend upon the Blessed One. Then, experiencing a particular state of being through unsurpassed joy, being unable to do, see, or remember anything else, he should once again pray for that very same residual state.
Beholding the Blessed One with a gaze that was like an unbroken stream, he sat there. Then the Blessed One,

having looked upon him with his own life-restoring glance, called him with a smile and placed upon his head his own glorious pair of lotus-feet, which remove all hair on the head and bestow unsurpassed bliss.
Having meditated thus, with all one's limbs submerged within the ocean of nectar, one should remain in bliss.
Furthermore, regarding the specific application of each of the three prose passages in this Yoga,
there is an abundance of world-weariness (*nirveda*) within these three prose passages that take the form of a commentary on the two [previous works].
Furthermore, due to the intensity of one's eagerness for service (*kaiṅkarya*), it is appropriate to contemplate brief prose (*mitagadya*) during the morning visit;

however, at the time of formal worship (*samārādhana*), one should especially contemplate the extensive prose (*bṛhadgadya*) concerning the essential nature, forms, qualities, manifestations, goddesses, ornaments, weapons, attendants, equipment, gatekeepers, and companions of the Lord.

Having reflected upon the expansion of His essential nature, qualities, manifestations, pastimes, and instruments exactly as they are, for the purpose of correctly connecting with them [and because He is to be connected with],
one should take refuge in Him alone through the words beginning with "akhila..."— thus, at the very beginning of worship [or: in the commencement of worship].
Thus is the reading in the Gha manuscript and elsewhere; and at the end, it was indeed employed by the author of the Bhāṣya himself:
"Having plunged into the nectar-ocean of the venerable Yāmunārya, [I have composed] the Śrīvaikuṇṭhagadya according to my understanding."
Having taken up the jewel known as the yoga of devotion, I reveal it.
Thus, because it is stated that one sees even after the initial commencement through the yoga of meditation (*dhyānayoga*),

because various distinctions of contemplation (*anusaṃdhāna*) distinct from the nature of the fruit are prescribed, and because it is explicitly stated in the text that "one should look while looking with a form like an uninterrupted stream," [this refers to] that which is conceived as the object of yoga.

The intention of the author of the Bhāṣya appears to be that this should be specifically kept in mind at the time of forming a resolution for yoga (at the time of *kāla-yogārtha-saṃkalpa*). Furthermore, one should not be misled into thinking that because it begins with the words "the jewel called the yoga of devotion" (*bhaktiyogākhyaṃ ratnam*), this treatise concerns devotion as a means (*upāya*) for those who have no other recourse.

Because surrender (*prapatti*) is taught here as a means (*upāya*); and because there is no contradiction in applying the term *bhaktiyoga* to both the specific form of mental orientation (*anusandhāna*) that constitutes the means and that which constitutes the fruit. Therefore, even by those for whom this yoga is already established as a means, it should be practiced at its proper time. Since there is no fixed rule regarding the time for yoga, it may also be performed at other times, provided they are conducive to one-pointed concentration (*aikāgrya*).
[In a corresponding interval of time, such as *ka kha ga ca jha*] it sometimes occurs. Indeed, the extraordinary sanctity of meditation performed during the night is remembered—
even for those who have taken refuge— regarding the practice of yoga.
Even one joined with minor offenses (upapātaka) or even one possessed of great sins (mahāpātaka),
should practice meditation on Brahman for at least one quarter of the night.
Thus, yoga has as its object the fivefold form of the Blessed One;
and from that—

Likewise, even while not abandoning their respective roles within the series of internal presences (*antaryāmī*)— just as in the manifestation of the worshipful descent (*arcāvataraṇa*) within the supreme multitude known as the *vyūha*— the regulations regarding their offices and so forth remain unchanged.
Having stilled your own mind within the boundless, great, and infinite ocean, free from all dependence on other things, spend this entire time fruitfully.

And among these objects of focus for the mind, beginning with the external manifestations (*paravyūha*) and so forth— [note that the letter *ca* does not appear in the list *ka kha ga jha ki*]— the Lord Muni and the other masters, being solely intent on the practice of devotion, regard even the descent in the form of an image (*arcāvatāra*) as the most easily accessible and, because there is no difference in its perfection, as something to be pursued even by those whose minds are in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*).

They took as their object the auspicious basis of the mind. In this regard, although the elders were aware that the specific mantra which serves as the cause for swift realization had its lineage interrupted, nevertheless,
they practiced according to possibility and according to tradition, either with specific mantras known to themselves or without mantras.

The pursuit of that [goal] is likewise unavoidable for this [mantra] as well—[the pursuit of that is also unavoidable] (ka ṅ ca cha jha; likewise, the pursuit in such a manner is also unavoidable) (kha). Its perfection is established by such statements as: "The sixfold excellence (*ṣāḍguṇya*) that transcends all is established within the mantra and the image (*bimba*)," and so forth.

In the *Śrīvaikhānasa* as well, the primacy of that very contemplation (*tadanusaṃdhāna*) has been established. As it is stated in the *Kriyādhikāra*, beginning with: "Mental [worship], fire-oblation (*homa*), and image-worship (*berapūjā*)—that [worship] is threefold," and so forth.
For one who has taken refuge in yoga, the primary practice is the contemplation of the *arcāvatāra* (the incarnate form),
because it is possible to perform the worship with flowers and other offerings according to one's capacity;
this is because it brings delight to the eyes and likewise to the mind (or the heart).
[The reading is found elsewhere than in the Kośa.]
From love devotion arises, and for the devotee, Hari is easily attained;
therefore, among these three, the worship of the image (berapūjā) is preeminent.
Thus it is said; and the Blessed Śaunaka spoke:
"Having seen a beautiful image of Viṣṇu, with a serene face and eyes, which brings joy to one's own self, [fashioned] from gold, silver, and other materials..."
One should worship her, bow down to her, sacrifice to her, and meditate upon her;
for one who has cast off all defects enters into her alone, whose nature is Brahman.
