Thus, therefore, wherever there is the form of the Blessed One, one should—according to one's capacity (*yathāśakti*)—maintain uninterrupted contemplation (*nirantarānusaṃdhāna*), even by those who have perfected the means (*siddhopāya*), just as the sage Nāda and others did. (Note: The phrase *yathāśakti* does not appear in the Ka, Kha, Ga, or Jha manuscripts; hence, the reading *dvacit bhagavadrūpanirantarānusaṃdhānaṃ* is adopted from the Kha manuscript.)
[To be inserted here: ka kha ga jha] | Thus, this is the summary of the ritual acts from the evening twilight until the end of sleep as taught by the Sāttvatas—
the evening twilight and so forth as prescribed by the Sāttvatas and others.
Then, when the time for twilight has arrived, having bathed as far as the hips,
he should thereafter wash himself and perform a change of garments.
Having worshipped with offerings such as *arghya* and flowers, one should likewise sacrifice to the god Agni; then,
having performed recitation (*japa*) according to one's capacity, one should thereafter resort to the bed.
Having concentrated the deity externally,
one should remain in the state of non-reliance with an undistracted and unobstructed mind.
Indeed, along with that very [state], sleep now comes upon the Yādavas.

Thus it is said; and in the Padma Purāṇa it is stated as follows: "Then, when the evening twilight has arrived, having performed there all the prescribed rites such as recitation (japa) and fire-offerings (homa), [one should worship] the Supreme Person."
Having worshipped according to the rules in their entirety, as performed previously,
he partakes of food, retires to his bed, and rises during the deep of night.
Having sipped water, become pure, and meditated upon the Supreme Person,
seated in the yoga posture, one should unite the self within the Self.
O Four-faced One, according to the manner described and to the best of one's ability,
one should dissolve the principles (tattvas) into oneself by resorting to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama).
And having arisen from yoga, one should withdraw even the self into the Supreme Self situated within the heart-lotus; thus one attains sleep that removes all afflictions.
Thus, O Brahmin, this fifth period of yoga has been described.

Yoga is to be practiced according to one's capacity. One should not remain indifferent, thinking that this continuous contemplation of the Lord— which was accomplished by Sanaka and others— is difficult for people like us to achieve, just as [one does not give up] the pursuit of health.

Like food, its flavor should not be abandoned according to one’s capacity. As it was said by the illustrious Prahlāda: "What effort is there in remembering this? Once remembered, it bestows what is auspicious."
And there is the destruction of evil for those who remember it day and night.
Thus it is said. Therefore, as it is stated—or rather, as the word "vā" does not appear in the Gha, Ṅa, Cha, and Kośa manuscripts—"O Supreme Lord, I wish to see Your divine form;
O Lord, if You think that it is possible for me to see it."
O Lord of Yoga, therefore, show me Your imperishable Self.
To Arjuna, who spoke thus regarding the manner of experiencing sleep in the form of service to the Blessed One, the Blessed One revealed his own self in its universal form (viśvarūpa);
likewise here too, [it concerns those] dependent upon their own experience.

The treasury here is open; the Blessed One himself, most magnanimous, manifests his own self according to one’s desires. Therefore, considering myself to have achieved my life’s purpose through this abundance of bliss from experiencing the Blessed One—attained effortlessly—I sit happily for as long as my faculties and body permit.

One who is disciplined in sleep and wakefulness should not ward off sleep when it approaches of its own accord for the rest of the group of organs— which, having been exhausted by various activities and being dependent on those activities, is about to become an instrument for the practice of yoga. This is because such a person is one whose sleep and wakefulness are properly regulated.

Because of the scriptural remembrance [of the Self]. At that time, sleep itself is the service [to the Lord]. Furthermore, regarding the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), the *Śārīraka-sūtra* states: "And its existence [occurs] in the channels (*nāḍī*), in the pericardium (*purītat*), and in the Self (*ātman*," according to the scriptural authority). This is explained by the analogy of the palace, the bed, and the couch (*prāsādakhaṭvāparyaṅkanyāya*). Thus, [the soul resides] in the channels, the pericardium, and Brahman.
Having contemplated his own lying down within Brahman,
he glorifies the Blessed Lord with the word *Mādhava*, which indicates the embrace of Lakṣmī;
beginning with the words "as one embraced by his beloved," [it continues] that he is embraced by the conscious self (*prājñātman*) and perceives nothing external.

Having reflected upon the specific nature of the embrace with the Supreme Self (*paramātmapariṣvaṅgaviśeṣa*) according to the scriptural method beginning with "He knows nothing within" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.3.21), and by means of the approach beginning with "Whatever you do" (Gītā 9.27).
Regarding even sleep as a form of propitiation, with his feet thoroughly cleansed and dried,

he should lie down in a suitable place according to the method prescribed in the scriptures upon a scriptural bed, with his head directed toward the prescribed direction, and endowed with the observances of purity, nakedness, and so forth.

Having placed his head at the lotus feet of the Lord who is to be worshipped by him, according to the methods prescribed in the *Śrī Śāṇḍilya-smṛti* and other texts— since there are injunctions such as [placing Him] on one's bed, seat, or vehicle—
he should meditate upon that very Mādhava in his heart and glorify Him alone.

One should sleep happily. Whenever there is an interruption of sleep, at that very moment one should meditate upon Him and recite those names again until sleep returns. This practice begins from evening and continues until the Brāhma-muhūrta.

For a period of a muhūrta, there is an opportunity for yoga, like the flow of the Sarasvatī river, which is interrupted by rest; even when one-pointedness is possible at other times, it should be accepted by withdrawing from other activities. [The reading "svīkāryam" is found in the manuscripts kha, ga, gha, and ṅcha.]
This has already been stated.
Thus, for one devoted to the five periods of yoga, every activity is of the nature of service;
for one conducting oneself in this manner, all time and all activities become fruitful.
All incidental enjoyment becomes of the nature of service;
by the maxim of the pet parrot tasting the milk, it becomes a remnant of the master's own enjoyment for one whose delight lies in performing service to the Lord.

For the supreme devotee (*paramaikāntin*), this remaining period of life stands like the break of dawn at the end of the night of beginningless *māyā* and at the onset of the infinite opportunity for liberation. This is the stated general sequence;
however, in cases of exception (*apavāda*), there occurs activity characterized by inversion, omission, and so forth. For instance:

On fasting days, such as the eleventh day (ekādaśī) and others, the secondary sacrifice (anuyāga) is omitted; at that time, the worship consists of only seven limbs. This is an exception in certain cases to the sequence of performing the five daily rites (pañcakālānuṣṭhāna).
For this very reason, the commentators did not mention it in order to indicate that the subsequent sacrifice (*anuyāga*) is not fixed.

And the time for its purpose is as follows: on that day, one should pass the time appropriately by means of one or another of the practices such as Vedic study (*svādhyāya*) or yoga; sometimes, however, on the twelfth lunar day (*dvādaśī*) and so forth.

The breaking of the fast (pāraṇa) occurs at dawn. For that purpose, even if the preliminary sacrifice (pūrvayajana) has already been performed, the midday sacrifice with its seven limbs (saptāṅga), which arrives at its own time, remains to be performed.
Furthermore, when many special worship services (vaiśeṣikārcana) occur on a single day in succession, there is a conflict between the primary rite and its subsidiary qualities (aṅgaguṇavirodha).
By the principle that "an action is for the sake of its purpose," even slight engagement in [worldly] acquisition and so forth is obstructed.

In that regard, the accomplishment of those various rites is performed with materials acquired on previous days or brought by others. And sacrifice is permitted at all times for one whose livelihood is exhausted, who is intent on other [spiritual goals], who is afflicted by illness, or who is beset by strife and other calamities.
It occurs whenever an opportunity arises prior to the meal;
however, in cases of extreme incapacity, it is performed by others equal to oneself, such as officiating priests, sons, disciples, and so forth. In that regard, this exception is maintained:
One who is destitute, a celibate student, a forest-dweller, and likewise a physician—
performing work for the sake of others, they cause [others] to fall and they themselves fall as well.

Thus, when one's capacity is slight, worship is contracted; beginning with a single offering, it is prescribed according to one's respective capacity up to the limit of a thousand offerings. On prohibited occasions—such as the equinoxes (*viṣuva*), the two solstices (*ayana*), the fifteenth day of the lunar fortnight (*pañcadaśī*), and so forth—the daily recitation (*svādhyāya*) consisting of Vedic study is suspended. At that time:
Even at that time, yogas characterized by supreme darkness assail one who is not intent on anything else.
Furthermore, some maintain that there is an exception even for this at the onset of the night of the thirteenth day;
even then, the vow of silence is to be observed, preceded by the cessation of all other activities.

One should reflect that, through the process of *sāttvika* renunciation, it is the Blessed Lord Himself who causes [the action] to be performed by me, His own devotee, for the sake of His own pleasure. Therefore, the remembrance of the Blessed Lord— stated in passages beginning with "Having churned all the scriptures" and ending with "Nārāyaṇa should always be meditated upon"— is applicable in every context.
However, qualities such as having an uninterrupted continuity of mindfulness are diminished to some degree.

Even during periods of ritual impurity (āśauca) and the like, the chanting of the Lord's names and other such practices must certainly be performed; likewise, even during times of impurity caused by death or birth (mṛtaka-sūtaka).
There would be the total abandonment of all scriptural duties that ought to be performed. At that time, however—[the reading *vilopavattadānīṃ* is in manuscript *kha*;

*vilopāttadānīṃ* is in manuscript *ga*]—the time other than the occasion for silence should be spent through chanting and remembrance. Therefore, while constantly chanting My praises, remember Me at all times.
Because such [scriptural statements] are free from exception at that time; on the contrary:
"One should always and everywhere chant the names of the wielder of the discus weapon.
There is no impurity regarding his chanting; Lord Hari is the purifier."
No impurity exists either in the recitation of his name or even in the remembrance of him.

Whether impure or pure, unclean or of improper conduct, even if he has reached every possible state of being—whosoever remembers the Lotus-Eyed One is pure both internally and externally. [The reading "apavitro vā pavitro vā" is found in the Viṣṇudharma. Whether impure or of improper conduct, even if he has reached every possible state of being—whosoever remembers the Lotus-Eyed One is pure both internally and externally.

Because it is stated by such passages that chanting and recollection are to be performed even during the period of ritual impurity (*āśauca*); furthermore: "One should chant the name of the Lord of the World, or one should recite the Veda."
What one obtains by meditating in the Kṛta age, by sacrificing with rituals in the Tretā, and by worshipping in the Dvāpara,
that one obtains in the Kali age simply by chanting the name of Keśava.

By such statements as these— without distinction of place, time, state, or qualified person (or, with distinction of qualified person and so forth)— in the place for the study, meditation, sacrifice, and worship of the Vedas, which are prescribed without distinction of qualified person and so forth.

Since it is ordained that *saṃkīrtana* (proclamation) yields a fruit equal to meditation (*dhyāna*), recitation (*japa*), worship (*arcana*), and remaining in a sacred place (*sthāna*), and since the pleasure of the Lord desired by those who have surrendered (*prapanna*) is easily attained through that alone,
*saṃkīrtana* itself— conforming to the requirements of all places, all times, and all qualified persons— is [the duty] at a time when other ritual acts are omitted.

This is appropriate, especially because it accords with the nature of the Kali age (or the law of time). Indeed, in the Kali age, even for one who strives but lacks other capabilities, this alone is fitting. As the venerable Śaunaka said: "By the mere chanting of Kṛṣṇa's names, one whose bonds are released shall go to the Supreme. Therefore...

Thus, there is never any lapse in approaching [the Lord], even for one who is not making a formal effort, provided they perform surrender preceded by mere worldly speech— consisting of recitation, prostration, joining the palms in *añjali*, and hymns of praise— even while remaining at a distance.
For that very nature is established thereby.

Now, one who has properly mastered the Vedānta from a true teacher of the Bhāgavata tradition is, by virtue of being a knower of Brahman— [the reading "bhāgavatasya" appears in manuscripts gha, ka, kha, cha, and jha].

[Objection: Since the rule for immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is prescribed, the continuity of the [usual] rules of purification is not established; how then can there be an omission of ritual action (*karmavilopa*)? [Response: Not so.
For those who are devoted solely to the secret tradition (*rahasyāmnāya*), that [omission] does not occur because of the procedure specified in the *Gṛhya-sūtra* of their own branch.

However, for those devoted to the systems of Mantrasiddhānta and the like—even for those who have been initiated (*dīkṣita*)—it applies only to those who are eligible for a great festival (*mahotsava*) that has already commenced.

This is its negation. Although their status as knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*) is undifferentiated— [as the variants *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *jha* read "their status as knowers of Brahman is also undifferentiated," while *ṅ* and *cha* read "only their status as knowers of Brahman is undifferentiated"]— nevertheless, this applies to the three beginning with Kṛta [the word "three" does not appear in the *gha* and *ca* manuscripts].

Regarding those ages as well, there is immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*); and for one endowed with good conduct and Vedic study, there is likewise no contraction [of the period]. Thus, because of the statement regarding the established rule (*vyavasthā*)—specifically the rule concerning the *ghaṭikā*s—it is prohibited in the Kali age to contract the period of impurity based on conduct or other such factors. Nor should it be argued:
A Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires and possesses the Vedas is purified in one day;
one who possesses only the Vedas is purified in three days, while one devoid of qualities is purified in ten days.

This prohibition concerns the contraction of sin caused by such factors as [knowing] the sacred fires or the Vedas, which was mentioned in the aforementioned passages, but not that caused by the state of being a knower of Brahman; [the word *iti* and the letter *gh* do not exist in the two manuscripts]. This is not so, because even for those knowers of Brahman described as above, their inclusion is possible under the term "those of virtuous conduct" (*vṛttaguṇa*), since there is no reason for restriction.

Nor can the term "knower of Brahman" (brahmavid) be taken to include only renunciants, because knowers of Brahman and renunciants are mentioned separately due to their differing eligibility for immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*). As it has been said: [this is not so].
There is no *ṅ* in the case of those who know Brahman (*brahmavedana*) and so forth; nor is there a *gha* even among those who speak of Brahman (*brahmavādin*), because they are mentioned separately.

Furthermore, the manuscripts (*kośa*) regarding those who know Brahman as described above differ in many ways according to their readings. At this point, in the *kha*, *ga*, *gha*, and *ṅ* manuscripts, [the word] "as described" (*yathokta*) follows immediately after [the previous term], and [the word] "not so" (*maivam*) precedes it.
Furthermore, signs indicating the omission of lines are visible.

In that case, for those read together with "so too" (*tathā*)—namely, the performers of sacrificial sessions (*satrin*), those observing vows (*vratī*), celibates (*brahmacārī*), donors (*dātṛ*), and knowers of Brahman (*brahmavid*)—the word *guṇa* (quality) [should apply] to the qualities of the sacrificial sessions and so forth belonging to the performers of sacrificial sessions and the others as well. [The reading *guṇa* is found in manuscripts *ka* and *kha*.]

If it is argued that because the phrase "the non-contraction of impurity (*aghasaṃkocana*)" does not exist in the *Ka*, *Kha*, *Ga*, *Ca*, and *Jha* manuscripts, this would not apply in the final age (*antimayuga*), we say no; for its establishment is based on actual practice (*anuṣṭhāna*). Indeed, even today, immediate purification (*sadyaḥśauca*) is observed among those under vows (*vratya*) and others.

It is practiced by the learned. Even among householders who possess the knowledge of Brahman established through the study of the *Śārīraka* (the *Brahma-sūtras*), such practice is observed in some instances. (Note: In the Gha manuscript, the reading is "na śārīrādhigama," whereas in other manuscripts, the reading is "na śārīrakādhigama.
It is seen that even for those who have attained the realization of Brahman through the mastery of the *Śārīraka*, there occurs at times the performance of such [Vedic] rites.

In this age where the determination of reality is confounded by the endless external false views and tenets, which is thick with the darkness of defects such as passion and the like, and where even a mere fragment of virtue is like a firefly in the middle of a deep night; in this time when the multitude of one’s own duties has been lost to the Kali age— [the word "api" is not seen in the manuscripts *ka*, *kha*, *ga*, *ca*, and *jha*].

If it is argued that there is no observation of such performance because those who know Brahman do not exist at the present time, and thus there is no observation of its performance, then for which knower of Brahman (*brahmavit*) are you now seeking to avoid the loss of ritual action through immediate purification?
For him in whose mind Govinda resides and in whose heart Acyuta dwells, it is the Kṛta Yuga during the Kali Yuga, and it is the Kali Yuga during the Kṛta Yuga.
If it is argued that, according to this principle, anyone anywhere— even a knower of Brahman— might exist, that is true; however,
such a person would have to exist in some region unseen by Vyāsa, Agastya, Bṛhaspati, Vibhīṣaṇa, and others, as well as by you.
Let him indeed practice in such a manner, witnessed by his own inner self; however,
as for others who have entered the path of the Bhāgavatas,
even if they lack the state of being knowers of the perfect Brahman— [the word "hi" does not appear in the manuscripts gha, ṅa, cha, or kośa].

Just as the status of being twice-born (*dvijatva*) is established merely by the state of having been initiated (*upanīta*), so too the status of being a Bhāgavata is established merely by the application of specific purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), dress (*veṣa*), and so forth; thus, for those characterized by that much distinction alone—
[the word *vaiśiṣṭya* does not appear elsewhere than in the *gha* manuscript].
We see no authority anywhere for restricting that basis; for this very reason, even for them, impurity (*āśauca*) is permitted in the *Pauṣkara* and other scriptures.
As for the case of a certain person who possesses specific sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) therein, even during the period of impurity—
That [practice] should be understood as being merely a mental sacrifice,

to be carried out according to the principle of casting handfuls of water preceded by the recollection of the Gāyatrī. For even the worship of Viṣṇu— [the word "hi" does not appear in the Ka, A, Jha, and Kośa manuscripts]—
is established by direct Vedic revelation and is obligatory.
It has already been stated that by the permission of the mental sacrifice alone, the prohibition of the remainder is established there as well. Thus,
in this way, the inherent attainment and the modes of exception [the mode of exception and...].
Having correctly understood both the types of exceptions that have been stated and the types of exceptions that follow from them by implication,
this Dharma must be practiced. For the manner of practicing Dharma is difficult to master.
If there were but one scripture, knowledge would be free from doubt;
however, because of the multiplicity of scriptures here, the true essence of knowledge is very difficult to find.

By means of these and other such [works], for the sake of pacifying the confusion of directions produced by the agitation of numerous scriptures—vast, dense, profound, and full of various conceptual constructions—there is a mere compendium [of all] for the sake of peace. [Variant reading: "for the sake of peace, even a mere fraction..."]

The phrase "sarvaiḥ saṃkalana iti paṅktiḥ" appears to have been written here by mistake immediately after the previously mentioned sentence "gha kośe upanītāvasthatvamātreṇa," though it has been included here for the sake of completeness. By this very method, those who are capable and whose confusion regarding the directions has been dispelled [should proceed] as far as the cognizer (pramātṛ).

All actions to be performed must be undertaken after having properly understood them, one by one, within their respective scriptures that prescribe the various procedures, primary rites, secondary alternatives, options, exceptions, and so forth. Alas, then, who [would engage] in this path which is so difficult to comprehend and so hard to practice?
Regarding the word "nām" [the word "adya" does not appear in the Ka, Ga, and Ca manuscripts]: if it is thought that this should be the governing factor for "today," do not fear thus;
for the worship of the Blessed One is constant and easy to perform.
There exists no Vedic rite more meritorious than the propitiation of Viṣṇu;
indeed, the Vaiṣṇava method is the highest among all religious duties.

Since this dharma is heard in scripture as being the supreme through such statements as "The constant worship of Viṣṇu is the highest," and as being both the most excellent and obligatory— [the word *ca* is not found in the Ka, Kha, Ga, Ca, Jha, and Kośa manuscripts]— even for one who enters into it in any manner whatsoever, just as the duty of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) does for an eight-year-old boy, [the word *api* is found in the Ka, Kha, Ga...].
Because it is logical [and is not found in the Jha manuscripts],
even a very small portion of this Dharma protects one from great fear;
for no one who performs wholesome deeds, my dear, goes to a state of misery.

"Even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Word-Brahman (*śabdabrahman*)," according to this principle— since the Lord, who is affectionate toward those who take refuge in him, has himself supplied the missing portion— and as they also remember:
By whomsoever these two syllables, "Ha-ri," are uttered even once,
by him the girdle is fastened for the journey toward liberation.
Whether uttered as a convention, in jest, as a mere exclamation, or even in derision,
the utterance of the name of Vaikuṇṭha destroys all sins without exception.
Govinda, when remembered even once, quickly burns away the heap of sins accumulated by men over hundreds of births, just as fire consumes a pile of cotton.
Hari removes sins even when remembered by those with wicked minds;
for fire indeed burns even when touched unintentionally.
For those rushing toward the shoreless wilderness of miserable saṃsāra,
the single salutation to Kṛṣṇa is the guide to the crossing-place of liberation.
Even a single prostration made to Kṛṣṇa is equal to the final purificatory bath of ten horse-sacrifices;
one who has performed ten horse-sacrifices returns to birth, but he who prostrates to Kṛṣṇa does not return to further existence.
Whether one has fasted or not, whether one is pure or impure, and even if one is bowed down in submission, Hari forcibly removes one's sin; therefore, who would not worship Hari?

For what burden, or what excessive weight, is there for the tongue in the full proclamation of Hari’s name? What exhaustion is there in its remembrance, since when remembered, it bestows auspiciousness?
And there is the destruction of evil for those who remember him day and night.
Have you not worshipped the Lord Keśava, the destroyer of afflictions? For even in the absence of material offerings, the Lord is worshipped with water alone.
Janārdana desires nothing other than a jar full of water, other than the washing of his feet, and other than inquiries regarding one's welfare.
Since leaves, flowers, fruits, and water are always available without being purchased,
why is no effort made for the sake of liberation toward the Ancient Person (Purāṇa Puruṣa), who alone is to be attained?
Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water— that offering made with devotion by one of purified soul, I accept.
Even an atom-like offering presented by devotees is sufficient for my satisfaction and enjoyment.
And so forth. It is also stated in the *Nāradīya*, within the *Śrīmat-aṣṭākṣara-brahmavidyā*, immediately after the description of the sixteen modes of service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*):
"In this way, by means of the eight-syllabled mantra alone, [one should perform] the rite of worship everywhere."
Performing these services with a mind endowed with devotion.
Having worshipped the Lord of the World with auspicious *tulasī*, lotus, *pālāśa*, and golden flowers, one enjoys infinite fruit.
One should perform the worship of the Blessed One daily with perfumes, flowers, fruits, roots, leaves, or even water, according to what is available.
The worship of the Lord Viṣṇu himself— the protector of all the worlds, the god of gods, and the wielder of the Śārṅga bow— is the fruit of one's birth.
Thus, by this, the obligatory nature, the ease of performance, and the self-sufficient purpose of the worship of the Blessed One have been clearly stated.
Furthermore, as for what is said regarding the transgression and so forth resulting from incomplete worship and the like:
Even if there is a deficiency in the daily worship, there is no fault;
just as upon seeing a snake, a man’s body trembles again and again even while he is meditating upon it.
Seeing the worshipper devoid of mantra, Janārdana became likewise afraid—indeed, greatly afraid.
If it lacks fragrance, fear arises; if it lacks flowers, there is turmoil;
if it lacks food offerings, there is famine; and if it lacks the mantra, there is death.
If worship is performed without mantras, without the proper ritual procedure, or at an improper time,
it will constantly cause fear for the kingdom, and that village shall perish. (If the reading "grāmastu" is accepted, it is correct.)
When even without being invited, one worships those who are like Piśācas or Asuras,
there will be the afflictions of disease and thieves, lack of rain for food, and great fear.

All this [beginning with the aforementioned] is for the sake of the prosperity of the king, the kingdom, and so forth; it applies to the worship performed out of desire (*kāmyārādhana*), as well as to other [rites], by one who is capable of complete performance and possesses all the necessary materials, yet— due to greed or other such factors— loses those specific items and is thus able to perform the primary rite only through a secondary substitute (*anukalpa*).

He states the fault regarding [the performance of] occasional rites (*vṛtti* / *pravṛtti*)— not, however, regarding the performance according to one's ability of obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) by one who is free from desire. And Manu and others record [this]:
One should constantly perform, without sloth, one's own duty as declared in the Vedas;
for by performing that according to one's ability, one attains the supreme goal.
And so forth. Furthermore, there is another specific quality of the Blessed One’s Dharma with reference to which this *Sāttvata-saṃgraha* was composed:
"Whether for one day, three days, seven days, a fortnight, or even a month..."
Whoever should sacrifice according to this rite, endowed with devotion and faith.
Even he would go to the supreme abode, how much more so one who is established here in yoga,
remaining firm with girded loins for as long as life lasts, O high-minded one!

Thus it is said. This very point was summarized by the sages known as Nārāyaṇa: "If a man, being pleased, should perform this rite even for a single day, he becomes a doer of good deeds; how much more so if he should practice it thus throughout his entire life!"
Thus it is said. And Ahirbudhnya stated: "O Nārada, even if you worship in this manner for but a single day, liberation stands within his grasp, as do all his desires; what more need be said?"
Again:
Thus [it is said].

This refers to those who seek a specific result (*phalārthin*). However, it has already been established previously that for others, [the study of the scriptures] is an end in itself (*svayaṃprayojana*).
With this intention, the lords of the Vaṅgivaṃśa stated:
In this way, it may last for one day, or two days, or three days;
or even for a month, or a year, or indeed for as long as one lives.
A Vaiṣṇava shall indeed proceed with supreme devotion for a very long time in happiness,
even if this rite is interrupted midway by obstacles during its commencement.
There is neither misfortune nor fruitlessness, nor the loss of the merit of what has been performed,
when other actions have been interrupted while those already commenced remain unfinished.
All this indeed applies to those who follow the Vedas as well as others;
for even a very small portion of this, once performed, remains inexhaustible for a very long time.
One who possesses faith is the qualified person for this aforementioned Vaiṣṇava rite; by one’s own power, one should indeed protect one’s own performer from the fear of worldly existence.
No other quality, such as noble lineage or conduct, is particularly required for the agent; rather,
anyone at all who desires it must be fit for this ritual action.
When that which is so difficult to obtain has been attained, compassionate action itself is the immediate task;
for even those qualified candidates who are endowed with the sequence of knowledge, austerity, and yoga [must act thus].
The loss of faith is the supreme defect, for it causes one to fall from one's spiritual qualification;
thus has the Supreme Person spoken in the Upanishads he himself revealed.
Since faith and lack of faith are directed toward one another, faith is therefore the supreme quality;
it does not depend on time, the performer, the substance, the direction, or the place.

Apart from the fact that it does not become an object of negation, there is no other quality [in the desire] such that, having abandoned either the desirer or that desire, there could be a restriction.
The cause of the Supreme Lord’s pleasure lies in the materials used for one's own acts of worship;
therefore, one should personally enumerate the substances that constitute the components of worship.

He said that even without [considering] caste, color, and so forth, merely by possessing the [essential] leaves and other [requisites], one who speaks thus of Hari attains liberation—oh, how wonderful! Oh, how wonderful!
Oh, oh! What great accessibility! Oh, oh! What compassion! There is indeed pure water on this earth, easily obtained without effort.
Auspicious *dūrvā* grasses are seen everywhere and are easily obtained;
yet the tongue within one's own mouth exists only to speak of Hari and to praise Him.
The mind is indeed capable of conceiving even one's own hands as being active;
therefore, there is no loss of mantras, nor does yoga cause any obstacle to Hari’s sacrifice.

For this collection is complete; however, even if there are errors— whether due to ignorance or knowledge— regarding each individual item such as the leaves, the reading of the verses is sealed by the speaker and others.
For one who is endowed with true resolve, omniscient, and omnipotent, there is only this single prayer: "Forgive me; accept my atonement."
To her who possesses eternal, faultless, and boundless great majesty;
to her who is the sovereign of all things, both conscious and unconscious, who are entirely subordinate to her.
To Him who reclines upon the ocean of the treasury of stainless and infinite consciousness,
in whom the birth, dissolution, and maintenance of the entire universe are brought about by His own volition;
Since no one is exempt from failing in matters such as worship,
one should therefore disregard all consideration of the faults of the agent, which are not part of the essential practice.
By the grace of this deity alone, everyone is worthy of performing that rite.

Thus, because of the general designation "that action" (*tatkriyām*) here, everything is included according to one's specific qualification: direct worship, causing others to perform it, service through providing what is required for worship, and so forth. By the aforementioned logic, all matters such as the performance of supplementary or excessive services are also established.
This must be considered.
Furthermore, the worship of the Blessed One is recorded in the Smṛti even by means of internal flowers and the like, which are obtained without effort;
thus, internal flowers and the like hold primacy in the propitiation of the Blessed One.
Knowledge is a flower, austerity is a flower, and meditation is the seventh flower;
truth alone is the eighth flower, for by it the Lord of the World is pleased.
Thus it is said, and the Blessed Śaunaka declared:
"A heart free from passion and the like, speech free from falsehood and other faults,
and a body free from violence and the like— this triad is the worship of Keśava."
Thus, the meaning is that there is equality of fruit for one who performs the rite in its entirety and for one who performs it by collecting [the parts] together;
that is, each constitutes a complete propitiation. Therefore, according to one's qualification and according to one's ability, in this matter—
By those who possess faith, having entered [the path] preceded by the instructions of a teacher whose heart is moistened by compassion, and who—

having gathered [the requirements] flawlessly and in due order according to the suitability of place, time, and circumstance— perform [the practice] with no other motive, being supreme and exclusive devotees.

It is established that the sovereignty of liberation, consisting of the service of the feet of the infinite Supreme Person, must be enjoyed right here, according to one's health and as is appropriate.
Conclusion of the Text:
Having extended the left foot which removes the misfortunes of those who take refuge in it,
and having bent the right leg while placing the other arm upon the knee of the former, [the Lord remains in this posture].

Jha; having placed his other arm upon the coils of the serpent with his right hand, and subsequently holding the conch and the discus with his two rear arms for the subduing of adversaries (or: for the pacification of great fear).

May the Lord of Vaikuṇṭha, adorned with divine ornaments and so forth, be victorious; may He, who resembles a fresh rain-cloud, grant peace to the worlds—thus is the reading seen at the commencement of the sacrifice in this very work (on page 137): "May the divine Supreme protect us."

May the Sāttvatas, who have mastered the boundaries of the Vedas, who have raised the banner of victory before many assemblies in the presence of Lord Veṅkaṭeśa, attain attentive mindfulness at every step.
This protection of the five periods has been prescribed for the assembly.

Let certain dull-witted people, itching for a quarrel and their minds clouded by the soot of strife, cry out fruitlessly with those who roam the heavens and are terrified by the exchange of offerings;
yet, while hope is in vain toward such as they, it is not in vain toward noble ones who are never false— where indeed could it fail?
Therefore, with the thought that this practice yields the great fruit of supreme sovereignty, let this conduct be practiced intensely.
Was the scripture abandoned by those such as A-le-pa-ka because of that? What did he gain from it?
By those blinded by day, the world’s single eye was hated; what did that bring him?
Was milk rejected by those afflicted with bile, and what did that do for them? Thus, what did the wicked gain by rejecting it?
Even if what I have composed is abandoned, why would it be rejected by the teachers if it is truly beautiful?

Thus ends the section titled "The Daily Exposition" within the *Śrīpāñcarātrarakṣā*, among the works of the venerable Vedāntācārya Śrī Veṅkaṭanātha, the lion among poets and logicians, who is independent in all philosophical systems.
The third section,
the Śrīpāñcarātrarakṣā, is complete.
